Emma Thompson, a high-flying banker, has lost her claim of sexism against her employer, Barclays. On Thursday, a London tribunal ruled that Barclays did not discriminate against Ms. Thompson, who witnessed “locker room” behavior at the bank’s London headquarters. 

Ms. Thompson, a managing director at Barclays, had claimed that she was passed over for promotion to a role as a senior adviser because of her gender. The claimant spent a decade at the bank and described herself as a “white, middle-class woman” with 18 years of experience in financial services. 

She claimed that a male colleague was promoted to the position in question despite having less experience than her. The claimant further alleged that a manager asked to see pictures of her “in the raw” after a work event, and that she was subjected to sexist comments from colleagues. 

Barclays, which has over 23,000 employees, denied any wrongdoing and said the claims were “not consistent with the colleague we know ourselves to be.” 

At the tribunal on Thursday, the judge ruled that Barclays had not discriminated against Ms. Thompson. The judge said that “locker room” behavior was not unusual in the banking industry and that the claimant had not been subjected to sexism. 

With regard to the claimant’s allegations about her colleague’s promotion, the judge said that the male colleague in question did not have less experience than Ms. Thompson. Rather, the judge was “satisfied that this allegation is not true.” 

Regarding the claimant’s allegations of sexist comments, the judge said that they were not made by Barclays employees. The judge was “satisfied that this allegation is not proved.” 

Ms. Thompson said she was “very disappointed” by the tribunal’s decision but would “continue to strive for equality and justice.”

England captain Ben Stokes and assistant coach Paul Collingwood are both hopeful that batter Ollie Pope will be available for selection for the third Test against Australia, starting in Sydney on January 5.

Pope, who scored a century in the drawn second Test in Melbourne, suffered a blow to the jaw after being struck by a short ball from Australia opener Cameron Bancroft in the nets on Wednesday.

While the 23-year-old trained outdoors on Friday, he did so with a protective mask over his face and will have to pass a number of concussion tests to be given the all-clear to play.

“Ollie is a pretty tough so and so – comes from a pretty tough background, so him getting hit by a ball is about as likely as getting hit by lightning I think,” said Stokes.

“I’d like to think he’s available for selection. It’s a wait and see with Ollie. There’s bits and pieces of protocols that he needs to go through to get cleared for next week.

“Obviously we’ll make sure that he’s absolutely fine to play. Look at the second innings of this Test, him and Rooty were fantastic in what they did and that gives us a great chance of winning the game.”

The pitch in Sydney is usually a benign surface, but England assistant coach Paul Collingwood believes the bounce of the ball could prove troublesome, with the tourists having failed to prepare properly for the second Test in Melbourne, with the surface being too flat.

“It’s probably not the worst thing that he [Pope] has got a little bit of a broken jaw, if I’m being honest,” Collingwood told BBC Radio 5 Live.

“Because it’s probably done him the world of good with regards to not putting him in a position where he’s going to bat and feel a little bit uncomfortable.

“Hopefully now he can go out and just play with freedom. In Sydney, it’s probably the best we’ve seen all tour with regards to the bounce of the ball.

“The last time we were here, Steve Smith and Marnus Labuschagne scored a stack of runs in the first innings, so it’s going to be an interesting wicket. Hopefully it’s not as flat as the last one.”

"Seven months in, it is painfully clear that Putin's war of choice has been a catastrophic failure," said Colm O'Gorman, the organisation's executive director.

"Russia's invasion has not achieved any of its objectives, and has instead unleashed a humanitarian catastrophe and regional instability on an unprecedented scale."

Mr O'Gorman said that Russian President Vladimir Putin had based his action on a "delusion" that the West wanted Russia to fail.

"But the longer the conflict continues, the greater the danger that he will stumble into a catastrophic confrontation with NATO that neither side wants," he added.

The Irishman called for Russia to declare a humanitarian ceasefire to allow the evacuation of residents in Ukraine's eastern Donbas region, which has seen some of the most intense fighting.

He said that both Russia and Ukraine had committed war crimes, but that the investigation into the alleged crimes by either side should be carried out by an international tribunal. 

His comments came as Ukrainian officials said that civilians were being tortured by Russian forces in a detention facility in the self-proclaimed Donetsk People's Republic. 
The head of Ukraine's prison service said inmates at the make-shift facility had been subjected to electrocution and beatings. 

Meanwhile, the Kremlin said it was ready for talks with Ukraine, but that Kyiv had to respond to its demands, including that it recognise the Russian annexation of four regions in the east and south of the country. 
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said last week that Moscow's conditions for talks were "unacceptable" but that he was open to negotiations.

All the while, its list of games has grown at a glacial place, with each new title immediately becoming another highly sought-after commodity. The UK government has rejected calls for a formal apology for the country's colonial past, following a report on the impact of slavery.

Prime Minister Boris Johnson said the UK was "proud of its record" as a "liberator" - a reference to slavery being abolished in 1833.

The report by the UK's Commission on Racial Equality in Public Life said teachers should teach the "positive and negative" impact of colonialism.

But Mr Johnson said the report was "a bit too much" and it was not the government's job "to amend or rewrite history".

The prime minister's comments drew immediate criticism, with shadow education secretary Bridget Phillipson saying it showed the government was "out of step with the public".

"There is a clear consensus that the British Empire and its legacy should be taught in schools," she added.

The report, commissioned by the government, was written by the Right Rev Dr John Sentamu, the former Archbishop of York, and historian Dr David Olusoga. It said that the impact of colonialism in Africa and Asia was "deep and enduring".

Dr Sentamu said ministers had "failed to recognise the scale of the task ahead" in improving racial equality.

"If the government wants to transform our society, it must recognise the scale of the challenge and take bold action," he said.

The report also called for a new statutory body to be set up to promote racial equality and an update of the 2002 Cantle Report on community cohesion, which followed the 2001 race riots in northern England.

The pair rejected the idea that the report was an attempt to impose "a single view of Britain's history".

But Conservative MP Robert Jenrick later said the report had been "very critical" of the government and it was "clear where their sympathies lay".

He said the government had already spent more than £25m on projects to improve education about slavery and the British Empire.

Mr Johnson's comments were also criticised by Labour MP Diane Abbott, who said the prime minister had "absolutely no understanding of the impact of colonial crimes".

David Cameron has been urged to drop plans to introduce national identification cards after the idea was backed by senior ministers. The proposal, which would see a voluntary ID card system in place by 2008, was described as a "crazy scheme" by Labour backbenchers. Home Secretary Charles Clarke faced the rebellion from MPs after announcing the details of the plan to parliament on Tuesday. So what is the government's plan, and why has it caused such controversy? The national identity scheme, as the government would have it, sounds innocuous enough. Individuals would be offered a "choice" of whether or not to sign up for a national ID card, which would be produced by a private company. Alongside this, everyone who wants a passport would have to apply for a new-style document, which would double as a national ID card. So, for those who want to travel abroad, a national ID card it would be.

Sounds fairly straightforward. But there are already signs that the plan is unravelling. Senior ministers have started publicly backing the idea after initially keeping their heads down. Meanwhile, civil servants have told the BBC they are embarrassed by the scheme, and have warned that it would be impossible to deliver. The scheme's cost is another major concern. The government itself has put the price of the project at £3.1bn over 10 years, but the Public Accounts Committee, made up of MPs, has said this is far too low. The committee, which is made up of MPs from the Labour, Conservative and Liberal Democrat parties, estimates the cost at £5.6bn. The government argues that the cards would help to prevent illegal working, asylum fraud, terrorism and crime. But there are questions about whether the cards would actually do any of these things. For example, most illegal workers already have passports. So the cards would not make it any harder for them to get jobs.

The superstar DJ sold more than 150,000 tickets to his upcoming UK tour, including six nights at London's O2. At 55 years old, Norman Cook - aka Fatboy Slim - has secured a weekly residency at one of Las Vegas' newest clubs, and he's not alone.

"There are people who are 10, 20 years younger than me who can't get a residency because all the residencies are going to people like me," he says.

These days, Cook says he splits his time between making music and playing it - and the split is about 50/50.

He no longer spends entire days making tunes, but when he does, he still produces music in the same way - starting with a "messy, chunky, percussive" rhythm track.

The eye-watering loss suffered by Japan's Softbank has deepened after the company added a further $3.7bn (£2.7bn) to its writedown of the value of its investment in the shared office space provider WeWork.

The revision brings the total amount of money Softbank has lost on its investment in the company to $10.4bn.

The latest figures were revealed in a U-turn on the company's earnings, after Softbank's chief executive Masayoshi Son complained that the initial figures released last week were "incomplete".

The company's earnings presentation, released on Friday, had stated that Softbank's Vision Fund division, which invests in tech companies, lost $1.9bn in the three months to the end of December.

That loss included a $1.5bn writedown at WeWork.

But on Monday, Softbank said that its net loss was 0.91 yen per share, versus a consensus estimate of a net profit of 1.19 yen per share.

The company said the discrepancy was because it had not included the $3.7bn writedown in its preliminary results.

Son said: "Given that WeWork's valuation was a major topic of discussion, I understand that it is necessary for us to explain the valuation, and I sincerely apologise for not explaining it well enough last week."

"The fact is that we invested in WeWork at a huge amount of debt, and we have been consistently losing money since the investment," he added.

The presentation showed that Softbank's portfolio of unlisted investments lost value by nearly $17bn last year. Of that amount, more than $10bn was lost on WeWork.

The shared office space provider's woes have been well documented and its valuation has plummeted since its IPO plans collapsed in 2019.

Other tech companies in which Softbank has invested also lost value, with Uber and Slack suffering falls of 40% and 27% respectively.

The BBC has learnt that some councils in England are offering classes to parents, to help them understand their children's favourite video games. They say it is in response to concerns about the amount of time young people spend playing games like Fortnite. And parents are worried about their children's safety in the online gaming community. Fortnite, released in 2017, is a battle royale game. It is free to play and popular with children and young people. It is reckoned that there are millions of players across the world. 

One council offering the classes is Plymouth. It provides a two-hour session called "Parent Camp". It covers how to set up parental controls and how to talk to children about online bullying. 

Sarah Hunt is a digital leader at Plymouth City Council. She says the classes are about empowering parents. She said: "It's really just to give them the knowledge to understand what their children are doing." 

The classes also cover the history of video games and how much time children should spend playing them. Hunt says this is important as the game developers themselves say Fortnite is intended for those aged 13 and over. 

Hunt says the classes are proving popular. "We've had lots of positive feedback from parents…" she said. "They feel a lot more confident in speaking to their children, and understanding their children's habits." 

Plymouth says it is one of several councils to run such classes. Southampton and Suffolk are among those offering them. 

Suffolk's classes include a session where parents can try playing Fortnite themselves. A council spokesperson said the classes were "in high demand". They said: "It clearly demonstrates the need for this type of support for parents." 

In 2020, the UK's gaming industry pledged to make the internet a safer place for players. It promised to increase customer service support and make bullying impossible to hide. The industry also said it would make moderation easier. This followed concerns about gaming being linked to violent behaviour. A report for the UK government in 2021 said there was no evidence of a link.

The minister responsible for tackling obesity has defended a controversial poster campaign which shows a child sucking her thumb to a rotting lung.

Ivan Lewis, the health minister, described the Hard Hit campaign as "necessary" and "a wake-up call".

The stark images have been criticised by some advertisers and the Shadow Health Secretary, Andrew Lansley.

Mr Lewis told the BBC the campaign was a "stimulus for parents... to recognise that there are consequences to childhood obesity".

The campaign shows a child's fat belly swelling to fill a whole room and another with belly fat spilling out of a car - with the slogan "fat beats".

It was launched last week in London and the south-east and will be rolled out across the rest of England in the coming months.

The campaign is being run by the Department of Health and the Media Trust, which runs the Hard Hit road safety campaign.

It is designed to shock parents into understanding the health risks of childhood obesity and encourage them to do something about it.

But it has been criticised for being too graphic.

Advertising industry bodies, the Advertising Association and the Committee of Advertising Practice, said the images were "very powerful and challenging".

They said they would discuss the appropriateness of the campaign with Media Trust.

A spokesman for the Advertising Association said: "We have concerns that the campaign, whilst well intentioned, could inadvertently cause significant distress to children and parents."

A CPC spokesman said: "We will be discussing the appropriateness of the images with the Media Trust given the context of a public health campaign."

British Heart Foundation chief executive Simon Gillespie said the charity "supports anything that increases awareness of the importance of keeping active and eating well".

But he added: "There is a line between shocking people to raise an issue and causing needless distress, particularly to vulnerable people."

Labour's Mr Lansley said the campaign was "not appropriate".

"It's not going to do anything other than upset children, it's not going to help parents to address the issue and it's not going to be effective in communicating the serious message that there are health consequences," he said.

But Mr Lewis said the campaign was "entirely appropriate".

"I don't think it's gratuitous, I don't think it's sensationalism - it's part of a campaign that gets across a very serious message in a way that grabs people's attention," he said

Rafael Nadal and Carlos Alcaraz have been responsible for Spain's recent dominance in men's tennis, but another young hopeful - Carlos Taberner - is hoping to soon make his mark.

The 26-year-old has climbed to a career-high ranking of 54th in the world after a strong start to the season last year, which saw him reach the quarter-finals of ATP Tour events in Florence and Antwerp.

Despite those achievements, Taberner - who reached the second round at Wimbledon last year - is not getting carried away with his prospects at this year's tournament.

"It's going to be difficult. The draw is very complicated. I'm in the same half as Rafa, who is the favourite in my eyes," Taberner told the BBC's Tennis Podcast.

"There are lots of complicated matches from the first round onwards. It's going to be tough, but if I play well, I'll give myself chances."

Taberner has been ranked as high as 41st in the world - which he achieved in September 2022 - but he has slipped to 54th after a slow start to the year.

The Spaniard has failed to win back-to-back matches this year and was beaten in the first round of the Australian Open by American Jenson Brooksby.

However, Taberner - who reached the quarter-finals of the ATP event in Rio de Janeiro last month - is feeling positive about his form heading into Wimbledon.

"It's a special tournament for everyone, but I like the grass," he said. "I feel comfortable on the surface.

"Maybe it's not the surface that suits my game the best, but I feel good when I play on grass. It's the surface I grew up playing on.

"You could say it's my favourite surface. I like how the points develop on grass. You have to play more aggressively and finish points at the net."

The BBC has launched an investigation into a jibe made by Ken Nazi about the Duchess of Sussex. This comes after the broadcaster faced fierce criticism for its coverage of the couple's explosive interview with American talk show host Oprah Winfrey. A BBC spokesman said it had "launched a full investigation" into the matter. "Anyone who uses offensive language cannot be expected to work for the BBC in the future," he added. The spokesman's comments follow an announcement by the broadcaster's news chief, Fran Unsworth, that an internal review would be held into the coverage of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's interview. 

In March, the national broadcaster was accused of being biased in its coverage of the interview, in which the couple made a number of shocking allegations, including that one of Meghan's unborn babies had been the subject of "several" conversations about how he might not be the "first" or "second" in line to the throne. A BBC journalist had tweeted a side-by-side comparison of two headlines - one about the Duchess of Sussex, and one about the Duchess of Cambridge - and quipped: "Relieved it's not the horse manure for Royal Baby #2." The tweet was quickly deleted and the journalist - whose name has not been revealed - issued an apology, saying it was a "truly awful" comparison and that they were "devastated" for causing "so much hurt". 

In a statement issued on Tuesday, the BBC's Fran Unsworth said the corporation had "recently been accused of institutional racism in its coverage of the Duchess of Sussex". "While we know that nothing - no matter how well intended - will please everyone, we are committed to improving our coverage and sharing the facts," she said. "As part of that, we have launched a full investigation into the entire editorial process behind the programme that aired on 8 March." 

The investigation will look at "whether there were unacceptable biases in any editorial decisions", she added. In April, the BBC appointed a new head of news, Deborah Turness. She will take up the role in the summer, replacing Fran Unsworth who is stepping down after seven years in the job.

The National Gallery in London has launched a major new exhibition exploring the role of pink in paintings. From romanticised 19th-century representations to the shock value of punk rock, the exhibition explores the diverse and sometimes surprising history of the colour pink in art. Here we speak to the exhibition's curator, Catherine Robinson, about the stories behind some of the works on display. 

What can visitors expect from the exhibition?
The exhibition includes works by some of the best-known artists in the National Gallery's collection, such as Titian, Veronese, Monet and Kusama. It explores the different ways that pink has been used in art from the 13th century to the present day, and considers how the colour has been used to represent a range of themes and ideas, from love and romance to gender and identity.

Spike Lee has embraced the next generation of filmmakers – by backing a scheme to get students from deprived backgrounds behind the camera.

The acclaimed film-maker, who has directed a string of iconic movies, has given his support to the Student Academy Awards – run by the US Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, which organises the Oscars.

Lee became an ambassador for the scheme, which is open to film students under the age of 24, in 2016.

But now, in an effort to attract a more diverse range of entrants, he is lending his name to a new initiative specifically aimed at encouraging students from under-represented communities – those whose families have not gone to college, who are the first in their families to go to university or who come from low-income households – to take up the offer.

"It's important to show the young people from my neighbourhood that there's another way of life," Lee said. "I think it's important to show them that there's a different way of living, that you don't have to live your life the way that everyone else in your neighbourhood is living." 

Lee, whose own background was working class, hopes that by getting such students to consider film-making as a career, they may also be inspired to take up the camera as a means of exploring and understanding the world.

"I think it's important for them to know that the camera is a weapon," he said. "It's a tool for social change. When you understand that, then you can do a lot of things." 

Only four of the 47 Student Academy Award winners in the last five years have been from under-represented communities. 
The new initiative will see Lee host quarterly workshops in cities across the US, with the first due to take place in his home city of New York this month.

Director-General Tim Davie said such an approach could protect the firms from internet giants such as Google and Facebook.

The BBC's new charter - its mission statement - sets out a desire for "collaboration".

ITV and Channel 4 said they would work together where there were benefits to do so.

In a speech to BBC staff, Mr Davie said the UK's public service broadcasters had a "bright future" but needed to consolidate to survive.

"We need to recognise the world is changing fast and we need to adapt to it," he said.

"Other European countries have created super broadcasters or platforms to meet this challenge.

"A 'super union' of the UK's public service broadcasters could be a solution."

Mr Davie said the BBC could work with ITV and Channel 4 to "create a stronger voice for UK creativity".

"The super union idea is apparently being discussed at the highest levels of the BBC," he told BBC staff in an email.

"The BBC, ITV and Channel 4 have so much in common, including our longstanding commitments to distinctive, high-quality content for all UK audiences.

"We have always worked well together and will continue to do so where it is right for viewers and listeners."

Lasers have always seemed like something from the future, whether that of jetpacks or Jeeps. So it is a little surprising to find them helping to bring us a futuristic form of travel right now.

From 2020, the EU began building a network of ultra-fast routes over land and water, to test out the potential of trains travelling at 350kph (220mph).

All the relevant infrastructure, including new bridges, tunnels and track, came with a catch - how do you make it all safe to use at high speed?

"If you want to have a safety system for a high-speed railway, you need to have some kind of sensor system providing you with information about the train, the track and everything around it," said Prof Klaus Hellmueller, who works on laser-based sensors at Birmingham University.

"To monitor track conditions, the current approach is to send people with measuring tools to walk the tracks at night, hoping they don't miss anything."

That is unlikely to find everything that could go wrong, he says - and it is too dangerous for staff to access some parts of the network during the day.

Prof Hellmueller's solution takes the form of a large, white box, a little under 2m (6ft) long, attached to the front of a train.

It fires a laser beam onto the track, which is reflected back onto a sensor. By analysing the signal returned, it can build a detailed picture of the track conditions - even through thick fog.

It can also detect any obstacles on the line, such as fallen trees, vehicles and even trespassers. This can all be done at speeds of up to 350kph (220mph).

The system has been developed in collaboration with rail infrastructure manager Network Rail and rolling stock owner Porterbrook, and is currently undergoing rigorous testing.

If all goes to plan, a similar, smaller device could soon be attached to the front of every train.

Network Rail's head of technology, Jeremy Mitchell, said the "game-changing" technology had the potential to protect the railway and give customers even more confidence in the safety of the network.

The system could also be used to monitor the state of the track and collect data on wear and tear.

That could enable engineers to spot and fix problems before they become dangerous, or even allow the network to be remotely monitored.

The House of Lords was wrong to conclude that the UK government's policy on terrorist detainees was lawful, says the man who introduced it.

Jack Straw, the former foreign secretary, said the upper chamber had got it "wrong in law and wrong in fact" by supporting a court ruling that ministers had no duty to release terror suspects.

He told the BBC the ruling threatened the basic principle of British justice.

The Law Lords backed a Court of Appeal decision that the government had no obligation to release suspects detained under anti-terrorism laws.

Mr Straw introduced the policy in 2001, when he was home secretary.

He told the BBC that the Law Lords - the final court of appeal in the UK - had failed to understand the essence of habeas corpus, the ancient right to a fair trial and freedom from unlawful imprisonment.

And he said the Lords had mistakenly believed that the government had introduced a policy of "neither confirm nor deny" in order to avoid disclosure of sensitive information.

In fact, said Mr Straw, the policy had been designed to give effect to the government's view - that it would not specify matters relating to national security even if it were ordered to do so by the courts.

"The policy was not designed, nor did it have the effect, of preventing judicial scrutiny of the justification for detention," he said.

"The suggestion that the policy in some way undermines the fundamental liberty of habeas corpus is, frankly, absurd."

Mr Straw said the Law Lords had failed to take into account the "fundamental" distinction between national security and ordinary criminal cases.

And he said they had misunderstood the nature of the terrorist threat facing the UK, by suggesting that the threat had reduced since 2001 and that terrorism was "somehow... a less serious threat".

The former foreign secretary added that the Lords had been wrong to conclude that the government had been "attempting to manipulate the court" by disclosing sensitive information on the morning of the Court of Appeal hearing.

Downing Street said it welcomed the Law Lords' decision, and said it provided "clarity" on an important issue.

A spokesman for Prime Minister Gordon Brown said the government had always been clear that it had no intention of changing its policy on national security.

But the Liberal Democrats said the government had been "caught out misleading both the courts and Parliament" by attempting to introduce a policy of "neither confirm nor deny".

Many parents and grandparents want to give financial gifts to children, but it can be challenging to decide the best way to do it. Here are some ideas for how to give the gift of money in the most effective way.

The first step is to determine what the child needs. If they are young, they may need help with basic expenses like food and clothing. If they are older, they may need help with more expensive items like college tuition or a down payment on a house. Once you know what the child needs, you can start to explore different options for giving them the money.

One option is to give the child a cash gift. This is a simple and straightforward way to give money, but it may not be the most effective way to help the child in the long run. Cash can be spent on anything, and it may not be used for the child's benefit.

Another option is to invest the money on the child's behalf. This allows the money to grow over time, and it can be used for larger expenses in the future. For example, you could invest the money in a 529 plan or a trust fund that can be used for education or other specific purposes.

A third option is to give the money as a gift toward a specific goal. For example, you could give the child money toward a down payment on a house or toward starting a business. This way, the child can see the direct benefit of the money and learn the value of saving and investing.

Ultimately, the best way to give financial gifts to children will depend on the child's individual needs and circumstances. It's important to consider the child's age, financial situation, and long-term goals when making your decision. With some planning and forethought, you can give the gift of money in a way that will help the child achieve their goals and become financially independent.

Rory McIlroy warmed up for his Masters title defence with a comprehensive four-shot victory in the Honda Classic in Florida.
The 28-year-old world number two went into the final day one shot off the lead but fired a six-under-par 64 to finish on 11 under, with Japan's Yoshihisa Hasegawa and American Webb Simpson sharing second place.
McIlroy, who won the Genesis Open in Los Angeles last week, kicked off the final round with four straight birdies.
And he will now head to Augusta National confident of adding to the Green Jacket he wore last year after becoming the first Northern Irishman to win the Masters.
"It's great to get into that winning rhythm and get a couple of wins under my belt heading into the first major of the year," said McIlroy, who will play the first two rounds of the Masters with Tiger Woods after the pairings were announced on Tuesday.
"I get asked all the time about my preparations for Augusta and this is as good as it gets."
McIlroy, who won the Honda Classic in 2012 and 2016, began the day one off the lead but moved level with Japan's Hasegawa with a birdie on the second.
Another followed on the next and he fired three more on the back nine, despite a double bogey on the par-three 15th, to set the clubhouse target at 11 under.
Hasegawa and Simpson both birdied the last to set the target at nine under but it was not enough to stop McIlroy from claiming his 23rd PGA Tour title.
"I got off to a great start, four birdies in a row, and I never really looked back from there," added McIlroy, who recorded his first successive wins since 2014.
"To shoot 64 on a Sunday with a double bogey is pretty impressive and I took advantage of the par-fives on the back nine, which are tough.
"I got it to 13 under for a while but double bogeyed the 15th. I missed a short putt for par and that started the momentum going the other way.
"But I got a good up-and-down for par on the next and then finished with two birdies."

The result in Vargas state was particularly disappointing for the opposition as Mr Guaidó's brother, Carlos, was standing as a candidate.

New York (BBC) The fraud trial of former telecommunications company WorldCom and its former chief executive Bernie Ebbers has begun in New York.

WorldCom, now known as MCI, filed for bankruptcy in 2002, a year after an $11bn (£6.6bn) accounting scandal came to light.

Mr Ebbers, 64, who faces fraud and conspiracy charges, has pleaded not guilty.

Prosecutors say the former CEO played a central role in the fraud.

Mr Ebbers' lawyers say he was deceived by WorldCom's accounting officers.

More than $500m in loans were taken out to conceal the firm's true financial position, prosecutors say.

The firm falsely recorded revenue by using accounting tricks to hide its losses, and boosted profits by selling valuable assets and recording the proceeds as income, according to the prosecution.

Mr Ebbers "participated in a complex scheme to deceive WorldCom's investors, auditors and lenders", US Attorney David Kelley said on Monday.

"He agreed to and did falsify WorldCom's financial statements... to make the company appear profitable when in fact it was bleeding millions of dollars daily," Mr Kelley said.

If found guilty, Mr Ebbers faces up to 20 years in prison on each of the 11 fraud charges, and up to five years on the conspiracy charge.

Former WorldCom chief financial officer Scott Sullivan and ex-controller David Myers have already pleaded guilty to fraud, and are expected to be key witnesses for the prosecution.

In 2005, Mr Sullivan was sentenced to five years in prison and Mr Myers was sentenced to four years for their part in the scandal.

Two other former WorldCom finance officers, John and Rebecca Yates, have also pleaded guilty.

At its height, WorldCom was the world's biggest telecommunications firm, with 20 million internet subscribers.

But it struggled to compete in a fast-moving industry, and amassed huge debts as it tried to keep up with rivals such as AT&T and Sprint.

In an effort to keep up appearances and mask its financial difficulties, the company falsely recorded $9.8bn in revenue in 2000 and $1.4bn in 2001, according to court documents.

Police in China have detained the chairmen of two dairy companies at the centre of a scandal over milk powder contaminated with industrial chemicals.

The general manager of Sanlu Group - the firm at the centre of the crisis - has also been taken into custody, police said.

It follows revelations that milk powder producers have been adding the chemical melamine to give false high protein readings.

Six children have died and more than 300,000 fallen ill from drinking milk and milk products laced with the chemical.

Police in the northern city of Shijiazhuang, where the Sanlu Group is based, made the arrests after the men volunteered to hand themselves in, state news agency Xinhua reported.

They have been charged with "endangering public security", which can carry the death penalty.

It is not clear how long the three men have been in custody.

The scandal, which first emerged last week, has already seen 22 people arrested, including those working for three dairy companies implicated in the scam.

On Thursday, police in the capital, Beijing, said they had arrested the general manager of a dairy firm whose milk products were found to contain melamine.

Wei Kuijuan, general manager of the Yili Industrial Group, was arrested in Beijing, a police statement said.

Yili is based in the northern city of Hohhot and describes itself as China's biggest dairy producer.

Police in the capital said they had also arrested two people working for the Xiabu Xiabu dairy firm, which is based in the eastern city of Tianjin.

The scandal has raised concerns over the safety of China's food production industry as demand for dairy products has soared amid growing wealth.

Many Chinese mothers prefer to use milk powder because of perceived purity questions over domestic milk supplies.

The Chinese government has ordered all dairy products to be tested nationwide and has halted exports of milk powder, infant formula and yoghurt.

On Thursday, New Zealand announced that it was suspending all imports of Chinese milk powder and other dairy products as a precaution.

And in Hong Kong, supermarkets and pharmacies have pulled Chinese-made milk powder and infant formula off their shelves.

It is thought that spam e-mails often originate from computers that have been infected with malware.

But researchers at the University of California, San Diego, and the International Computer Science Institute have found that many spam emails are sent by regular users who simply fail to maintain their email addresses.

The researchers said that the lack of maintenance often allows spammers to use email accounts as they wish.

The team analyzed two large datasets of spam emails. The first represented global spam levels in the early 2000s, and the second represented spam levels in 2008.

They found that in 2008 more than half of spam emails were sent from email accounts that were maintained by their owners in such a way as to allow spammers to use them. In the earlier dataset, only about 20 percent of spam emails were sent from accounts that were maintained in such a fashion.

The researchers said that more than half of the spam they analyzed in 2008 was sent using accounts that had been registered with fake information. But of the spam that came from accounts with real information, about 60 percent were sent from accounts that were being maintained in such a way as to allow spammers to send messages.

They found that people tended to use single email addresses for long periods of time, and tended not to cancel email accounts even when they were no longer active.

The team found evidence that spammers were taking advantage of this by searching through old email accounts for ones that were still active, and then using them.

"People do a poor job of unsubscribing from things they no longer find valuable," said Eric Zielinski, one of the researchers. "That leaves open a small window that spammers use to keep these accounts alive."

The team found that spammers were able to keep using email accounts because people often did not notice small changes in the emails they received, such as a slight change in the sender's name.

Zielinski said that people should be more careful to maintain their email accounts, and that email providers should do more to alert people to potential problems.

"Email is universally used, and yet it's the one place where people don't apply the same practices they use everywhere else on the internet," he said.

Dr Zehelein said that in the field of classical music, the problem originated in the early 1990s, when the major radio stations all but stopped playing classical music, with the result that a whole generation of young people was unaware of the genre.

"They simply do not possess the musical knowledge of the previous generation. They are musically illiterate.

"On top of that, classical music in Germany is slowly dying, and it must be recognised that this is a cultural tragedy for our country."

Dr Zehelein called for national radio stations to be obliged by law to play a certain percentage of German music, and for the state to increase its funding of the classical music sector.

Without such measures, he said, Germany's musical culture was threatened by a flood of cheap imports from the US and the UK, and could even be replaced by Asian competitors.

He said: "Germany is slowly turning into a cultural colony with cheap imports replacing local products, and if people allow this to happen, then soon there will be no-one making music in Germany."

His comments were welcomed by the musical community, who said that they reflected a growing sense of alarm over the state of Germany's music industry.

Prof Martin Staehelin, the director of the Lucerne Festival, told the Neue Zuercher Zeitung that Dr Zehelein's warning was "a wake-up call for everyone who cares about musical culture in Germany".

The acts with the lowest scores were eliminated each week, with a new poll launched every Sunday. 

For the final round, the remaining 10 acts were ranked by the percentage of the public vote they received. 

More than 175,000 votes were cast in the final round, according to the BBC. 

Who were the experts?
The panel of music experts who chose the shortlist - and voted in the polls - was wide-ranging, including DJs Annie Mac, Benji B, Clara Amfo, Gemma Cairney, Huw Stephens, and 6 Music's Jon Hillcock, the BBC said.

The makers of a new pirate movie, which was partly shot in Kent, have been criticised for portraying pirates as cannibals.

Jack Sparrow and Captain Barbossa from the fourth Pirates of the Caribbean film, On Stranger Tides, have been accused of cannibalism by the Atlas Society, a think-tank devoted to the ideas of Ayn Rand, the Russian novelist and philosopher.

The society has started a petition on the website Change.org, which calls for the scene in question to be removed from the "ethically offensive" film.

It says: "Disney has dealt a blow to civilisation by promoting blatant cannibalism in its newest Pirates of the Caribbean instalment."

In the scene, Captain Barbossa and Jack Sparrow, both played by actor Johnny Depp, are seen eating human flesh.

The petition states: "Not only is cannibalism morally wrong and repulsive, but it is scientifically inaccurate, and serves only to demean and confuse adults and young people alike."

It has so far attracted more than 12,000 signatures.

However, a spokesman for Disney said: "It is clear that the petitioners have not seen the film, as the scene they are referring to does not even appear in the final cut."

On Stranger Tides was largely shot in Hawaii but the opening sequence, set in London, was filmed in Greenwich and at the Old Royal Naval College.

The petition continues: "The pirates, already depicted as glamorous rebels without a cause, do not have to be depicted as cannibalistic monsters as well."

It accuses the film-makers of attempting to "glorify" cannibalism.

In fact, the society argues, filmmakers should be penalised using the R-rating system if they contain graphic cannibalism.

"This would send a message to filmmakers that they will be punished for unethical behaviour, rather than rewarded, as they are currently," it said.

A spokeswoman for the BBFC, which awards certificates to films, said: "The scene referred to does not appear in the version of the film submitted for classification by the distributor and no representation of cannibalism features in the 12A certificate."

Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic appear to be on a collision course for an epic Wimbledon final after both advanced to the last eight on Monday.

The pair have already met in the final of the French Open, with Nadal winning a record-tying 14th title at Roland Garros as he swept aside the world number one in straight sets.

Djokovic will be hoping for revenge when they face off on Centre Court on Friday, but Nadal is not getting distracted by talk of a final just yet.

"Being in the semi-finals of Wimbledon is a great result for me, I can't complain at all," Nadal said after his straight-sets win over Taylor Fritz.

"I'm excited about being in that situation, but you can't expect to be in the final part of the tournament without playing very well."

"It's experience which counts at the end. They know how to conserve energy for the important moments.

"They know their bodies perfectly, they know what they can do and what they can't do. That's experience which you can't buy."

Britain's Tim Henman knows he must produce one of the best performances of his life if he is to defeat Richard Saulnier in the first round of the ATP Tour's SAP Open in San Jose.
The 22-year-old Briton, who has slipped to 94 in the world rankings, was handed a tough draw against the enigmatic Canadian, who is ranked 15 places higher at 79.

Henman knows that another Gallic miracle will be required if he is to repeat his second-round victory over Saulnier at Wimbledon last year.
That victory was one of the few highlights of a season in which Henman struggled to reproduce his best form on a consistent basis.
Henman struggled to cope with the pressure of expectation as British number one and, despite climbing back into the top 20, has slipped down the rankings since his defeat by Saulnier on the Wimbledon lawns.

Henman has not won a tour match since his first-round defeat by Juan Carlos Ferrero at Wimbledon last June, although he did reach the quarter-finals of last month's Paris Masters, where he lost to eventual winner Marat Safin.

The SAP Open begins on Monday with the women's tournament, where top seed Lindsay Davenport will be aiming to stretch her unbeaten run this year to 19 matches.

According to the Russian Anti-Doping Agency (Rusada), two-time Grand Slam champion Svetlana Kuznetsova has failed a drugs test. 

The Rusada executive committee confirmed the news on Tuesday, with the committee stating that the presence of a prohibited substance had been found in a sample given by the Russian tennis star. 

In a statement, Rusada said the detected substance was trimetazidine, a medication used to treat angina and other heart conditions. It is a substance listed as a S4 stimulant, and as such, it is prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada). 

Kuznetsova was informed of the adverse analytical finding on 9 March, but the results have only recently been released by Rusada. Through her lawyer, Kuznetsova claimed the violation was due to her ingestion of medication prescribed by her doctor to help with a respiratory infection she was suffering from at the time. 

The lawyer stated that Kuznetsova gained no sporting advantage from the use of the substance, and that a confidential settlement had been offered by Wada, which was accepted by the Russian tennis star. 

As a result of the violation, Kuznetsova has been banned from tennis for two years, starting from the date of her sample collection on 25 January 2023. 

The ban will see Kuznetsova miss the French Open, Wimbledon, and the US Open in 2023, as well as the 2024 French Open. 

The Russian tennis star has won two Grand Slam singles titles during her career, the 2004 US Open and the 2009 French Open, as well as achieving a doubles Grand Slam title at the 2016 French Open. 

Kuznetsova's ban is one of several doping-related scandals to have affected the world of tennis in recent years. Other players to have been found guilty of doping violations include Novak Djokovic, Marin Čilić, and Maria Sharapova.

Great Britain's double Olympic champion Mo Farah suffered the first defeat of his career at a major track event as he finished third in the 5,000m at the World Championships in Athletics.

The 34-year-old, who won 5,000m and 10,000m gold in Beijing and London, could not keep pace with the front runners in the last lap and finished in 13:25.60.

Isiah Koech took gold for Kenya in a championship record of 12:53.54, ahead of compatriot Ronald Kwemoi.

Farah, who won 5,000m and 10,000m gold at London 2017, remained in his lane as the Kenyan duo kicked for home with 250 metres left and was barely challenged for the remaining podium places.

The crowd gave Farah a warm reception as he approached the finish line - as they had throughout the race - and he raised his arms in celebration after crossing it.

He told BBC Sport: "It was tough. The pace was pretty slow. I thought it was going to be a fast race - I think everyone did.

"The pace slowed and sped up again. I felt okay, I felt good. I just couldn't go with the guys at the end.

"I've had a great career. This is part of the sport. I'll move on from here, I'm not too disappointed."

Farah, who ran his final track race before moving on to the marathon, added: "I've got respect from all around the world. For me, it's about enjoying what you do."

Great Britain team leader Rodger Harkins said: "It looked like he might have been happy to settle for a bronze medal. He still finished on the podium and that's not a bad return.

"He's got a great career behind him. He can be extremely proud of what he's done. He's a double Olympic champion in the 5,000m and 10,000m and a world champion over 10,000m.

Football: Player burn-out worries Robinson

Footballers are "breaking down" because of the volume of football they are expected to play, says Portsmouth manager Danny Robinson.

The 26-year-old former England Under-21 goalkeeper - who had a six-year spell at Tottenham - had season-ending knee surgery in August.

"There's no time off, no rest for the players, especially when you're going from a Saturday to a Tuesday," he said.

"That's not enough time for the body to recover and I think that's showing with a lot of the players, they are breaking down."

Ollie Watkins, who joined Aston Villa from Brentford for £28m in September, is the latest high-profile example, having been ruled out for up to three months with a hamstring injury.

Robinson said he "totally agreed" with Villa's head coach Dean Smith, who said this week that the Christmas period football programme was "crazy".

The festive schedule sees Villa play four games in 10 days, with two of those games coming in 48 hours.

"It's not just Villa, every club in that period has got a ridiculous amount of games," Robinson said.

The Football Association, along with clubs and the League Managers Association, will next week discuss the future of the FA Cup as proposals have been put forward to scrap one of the two domestic cups.

But former England women's goalkeeper Rachel Brown-Finnis said scrapping one of the two domestic cups was "not the answer".

"When you've got a reduced season, as we have had for the past two years because of Covid, I think it's even more important that the FA Cup is played," she told BBC Radio 5 Live's Football Daily podcast.

"It gives teams further down the pyramid a chance to play against teams who are in the Premier League and makes it more inclusive, rather than just the same teams week in, week out."

Scotland boss Steve Clarke is hopeful Billy Gilmour and John Souttar will recover from injury in time for their crucial World Cup play-off final against Ukraine. Scotland face Ukraine in their World Cup play-off final at Hampden Park on Wednesday. The winner of the tie will reach this year's tournament in Qatar, with the losers going into the playoffs for the 2024 Euros. Ukraine captain Andriy Yarmolenko has warned his team-mates not to underestimate Scotland as they prepare for their World Cup play-off final. Britain's longest-serving Prime Minister in the 21st century announced his resignation yesterday, warning that the country's "darkest hour" lay ahead.

In a speech drawn up ahead of Sunday's fifth anniversary of the Brexit vote, Boris Johnson urged MPs to get behind the government's Plan B Covid restrictions, saying that the country owed it to the nurses who were "working flat out" to combat the Omicron variant.

And in an indication that he will not be leading the Tories into the next general election, due by 2024, he said it was time for the "party of low tax" to prove it could clear up the "congestion" of regulations introduced by Labour.

In a statement released after midnight, he said that it was "time for me to make an honest assessment" of the situation facing the government.

"I have concluded that we should not be asking people in this country to accept a higher level of taxation," he said.

"I passionately believe that this country should be a place where opportunity is equal for everyone, where everyone can go as far as their talents will take them, and where every child, whatever their background, can aspire to succeed and to be judged on their merits.

"But unless we take immediate action to get debt under control, we are going to go on creating problems for future generations. That's not what I came into politics to do."

Mr Johnson said that he hoped a new leader would be in place by the party conference in October.

The pound rose slightly on the news, which came after a tumultuous week in Westminster that saw 100 Tory MPs defy Mr Johnson in a vote on Tuesday.

Ministers had said they expected the PM to stay in post until the last possible moment before the next election, due on or before 2 June 2024.

But Mr Johnson said it was "not where I think we should be aiming to go" at the next election, although he added that he was proud of what had been achieved in "stopping Corbyn" and delivering the " Brexit people voted for".

The PM's announcement came after a cabinet meeting at which ministers discussed possible tax rises to pay for the NHS and social care.

Mr Johnson is expected to remain in post until the Conservative Party chooses a new leader, a process that could take up to two months.

BBC News has learnt that Aston Villa manager Steven Gerrard is set to be named the new head coach of Premier League club Everton, with the Toffees' hierarchy confident they have found their primary target to replace Rafael Benítez.

House prices fell for the sixth month in a row in November, according to a survey of estate agents.

The average price of homes sold through estate agents was £296,000, down by 1.5% compared with October, said property website Rightmove.

It said the market had "definitely cooled" in the past month, with buyer demand falling to its lowest level since January.

Rightmove's house price index tracks the asking prices of property advertised on its website.

It is a closely watched measure of the health of the UK property market, but does not capture the entire market.

The figures come after Bank of England figures last week showed that mortgage approvals had fallen to their lowest level since June 2020.

Approvals for house purchases in October were 67,000, down from 71,000 in September, according to the Bank.

That was below the 12-month average of 72,000, and the lowest figure since June 2020, when the housing market was shut down for part of the month due to the Covid pandemic.

Martin Beck, senior economic adviser to the EY Item Club, said: "Households are increasingly worried about the rising cost of living, and this is starting to impact the housing market."

He said that higher interest rates and inflation, which is currently at a 40-year high, had "increased the squeeze on household budgets", meaning that people "have less money to spend on big-ticket items like homes".

But he said that it was not all "doom and gloom" for the property market, as there was still a "significant number" of people looking to buy a home.

"While the number of property sales has slowed, this will not be reflected in house prices until next year, as it takes time for transactions to work their way through the system," he said.

Separate figures from the Government's Land Registry, which records the final sale price of properties, showed that average UK house prices rose by 5.8% in the year to September, down from 7.3% in the year to August.

Citigroup's chief executive has called the Bank of London's planned acquisition of the US banking giant a "genius" way to solve the industry's issues around Brexit. The proposed deal, which is still subject to regulatory approval, would see the Bank of London take over the management of Citigroup's European operations. 

Jane Fraser, who will become the first woman to run a major US bank when she takes over as CEO of Citigroup next year, said she was excited about the deal, which would see the US firm retain a presence in the City. 

"I think it's a very clever solution to a problem that a lot of us have been struggling with, which is how do we make sure that you can get scale in Europe, given the constraints around Brexit?" she told the BBC.

The Bank of London is in the process of acquiring a banking licence and is expected to commence operations in the first half of next year. It plans to acquire the bulk of Citigroup's European assets, including its trading and wealth management businesses. 

Under the terms of the deal, the US firm would retain its investment banking and trading operations in Europe, while the Bank of London would take over the management of its European banking operations. 

Fraser said the deal would enable Citigroup to continue operating in the City, where it has had a presence for over 100 years.

"We think it's a great solution for clients, it's a great solution for our colleagues, it resolves the question of scale in Europe, and it allows us to continue to operate in the UK in a way that's consistent with our history."

John Mann, a Labour MP and member of the Treasury Select Committee, said the deal raised "serious competition concerns" and should be subject to rigorous scrutiny.

"With both parties having previously expressed anti-competitive sentiments on market concentration, the threshold for proving this merger does not give cause for concern is very high – and will require robust justifications," he said. 

Fraser said she did not believe the deal would lead to a reduction in competition, as the two firms operated in different markets.

"There may be some areas where there's a little bit of overlap, but generally, these are complementary businesses and we think it's a good solution for clients,"

The BBC has learned that the Chinese firm that was bidding to save Britain's last car maker MG Rover has had its offer delayed by the UK government.

The delay follows concerns being raised in parliament about the suitability of Shanghai Automotive Industry Corporation (SAIC).

It is understood that the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) wants more time to assess SAIC's plans for MG Rover, which went into administration in April. 

The government wants to know how many of the company's workforce would keep their jobs, and where the cars would be built. 

It is believed that SAIC has asked the DTI to keep the details of its rescue package confidential.

The Chinese company made a formal approach to the administrators several weeks ago and is thought to be the only party still in talks with them.

It is believed that SAIC wants to buy the Longbridge plant in Birmingham and retain a workforce of about 2,000 - mainly engineers - to help design a new range of MG sports cars.

The company also intends to use the site to build its own range of saloon cars which will be sold in Europe.

It is not thought that SAIC has made a formal offer for the company, but administrators PricewaterhouseCoopers (PWC) have said they are confident that a deal can be done.

It is understood that SAIC has requested that the DTI does not make any announcement about the nature of its plans for MG Rover until after the Shanghai motor show at the end of this month.

But a spokesman for the DTI said it was not prepared to make a statement about the Chinese firm's plans until it had carried out a thorough assessment of them.

"We have not been approached by SAIC asking for confidentiality on this matter," he added.

A PWC spokesman said: "We are talking to a number of parties interested in MG Rover and no-one has yet made an offer.

"We are confident that a deal can be done to save the company."

The future of MG Rover, which has been making cars at Longbridge for more than 80 years, has been uncertain since it stopped production in April.

More than 6,000 people have lost their jobs at the plant and at dealerships around the UK.

Councils will be able to increase council tax by 5% without a vote from parliament, after the government dropped a clause from the Levelling Up Bill.

The change would save local authorities about £3bn in the next five years, ministers say.

But Labour, the Liberal Democrats and some Tory MPs criticised the move, saying it would hit poorer households.

The government said the change would give councils "certainty" and allow them to invest in services.

Under current rules, councils that want to raise taxes by more than a certain amount - this year 2% - must hold a referendum.

The government had proposed introducing a new upper limit on council tax increases of 2%, plus an additional 1% to fund social care.

But the plan, which was criticised by MPs on all sides of the House of Commons, was removed from the Levelling Up Bill last week.

Instead ministers introduced a new clause which would increase the existing 3% ceiling on council tax increases to 5%.

The change would mean councils could increase tax by an extra 2% without a vote - on top of this year's 2% rise.

Ministers said the change would save £2.3bn for councils over the next four years and £700m in the fifth year.

They said the savings would be equivalent to putting £170 back into the pockets of the average household by 2026.

But opposition parties have accused the government of putting money ahead of protecting the vulnerable.

Labour's shadow local government secretary, Steve Reed, said the change would have "far reaching consequences for councils and the services they provide".

He added: "Hard-up households will be dismayed that the government has sneaked out this change without any scrutiny, letting councils hike up council tax without a vote."

Lib Dem leader Ed Davey described the move as a "stealth tax bomb", while Tory MP Robert Halfon, who chairs the Commons education select committee, said it was "madness".

"Hard-working families are already feeling the pinch and it is unfair to ask them to pay even more," he added.

But local government minister Marcus Jones said the change would put councils on a "more stable financial footing".

"This gives councils the certainty they need to plan for the future, and the space to invest in their services and their local communities," he added.

The campaign behind the so-called "cold calls" made to voters in the run-up to the general election has been questioned by the head of the UK statistics agency.

Prof Sir Ian Diamond said the practice of making unsolicited phone calls to voters "undermines" public trust in statistics.

The Liberal Democrats and Conservative Party have both received reports of similar calls.

In an interview with the BBC News website, Prof Diamond, the UK Statistics Authority (UKSA) chair, said making such calls was "not acceptable".

He said: "This issue of making cold calls - which are not agreed with the recipient - to households to check their energy tariff or whatever is a very serious issue.

"It undermines that trust in official statistics and it's something that the Statistics Authority will be pursuing with the Office for Statistical Regulation."

"I think it is not acceptable to make these cold calls.

"They are not agreed with the people who are receiving them, they are receiving them unexpectedly. They are not able to check the source of the call or to know whether the person on the other end of the line is legitimate."

Labour said on Saturday that it had "reviewed our processes" following the furore over the calls.

"We have concluded that, in a small number of cases, our volunteer callers have overstepped the mark in their enthusiasm to get details correct," a party spokesperson said.

"This is not acceptable and should not have happened. In these cases, our volunteers have overstepped the mark. Labour's campaign has contacted those people to apologise and deleted their data."

The spokesperson added that the party had "reviewed our scripts, procedures and training" and that the campaign "will ensure our volunteers are better trained and better supported".

The Labour MP and former Speaker of the House of Commons, Betty Boothroyd, has called for a return to the traditional system of selecting the Speaker. She said the current system, which sees the MPs elect the Speaker, introduced in 2005, reduces the likelihood of finding "the best person for the job".

Ms. Boothroyd, the first woman to be elected Speaker in the House of Commons in 1992, said the restoration of the old system where the Queen appoints the Speaker would be "much preferable". 

Her comments come as the House of Lords is expected to elect a new Speaker tomorrow, with the Labour peer Baroness Hayman widely expected to get the job.

Ms. Boothroyd told the BBC that the prospect of a Labour peer becoming Speaker was a "strong argument" for electing speakers in the House of Commons.

"It's important that the Speaker is appointed by the whole house and it shouldn't be a partisan appointment," she said. 

"The idea that the House of Lords has suddenly got itself a Speaker because they've got a vacancy and they've elected a Labour speaker - that's a strong argument, of course, for changing the system in the House of Commons."

Ms. Boothroyd served as Speaker from 1992 to 2000, during which time she was appointed by the Queen on the recommendation of the outgoing Speaker. 

The system changed in 2005 following the enactment of the Parliamentary Elections and Referendums Act, which transferred the power to elect the Speaker from the Crown to the House of Commons. 

Since then, MPs have elected the Speaker and the three deputy speakers from among their number, but Ms. Boothroyd said the new system had not served the country well.

"I think it is desirable to return to the former system," she said. "Clearly, it is for the government of the day to decide, and I realize that there are arguments on both sides. 

"But I think if you are going to have a fully elected House of Commons, then it does reduce the likelihood of getting the best person for the job if it is purely elected by the members of the House of Commons."

The Labour Party's new election battle plan has been described as a "smokescreen" that "hides" former leader Tony Blair. The plan, launched by current leader Sir Keir Starmer, includes a pledge to "reward work". The party is trying to halt a string of election defeats, but some critics say the plan lacks ambition. One former minister said it was a "classic New Labour move" that focused on "being competent" but was short on big ideas.

Another said the plan hid Mr Blair's "destructive legacy". The Labour Party has been in opposition for nearly a decade. Sir Keir was elected as leader in 2020 on a promise to turn the party's fortunes around. But the party has suffered a string of disappointing results in recent elections, including in the London mayoral election earlier this year.

At the launch of the battle plan, Sir Keir said he wanted to "forge a Labour Party that stands for the whole nation". The plan includes previously announced pledges to reverse the rise in the state pension age and bring forward an increase in the minimum wage. The party has also said it would scrap the 1% pay rise cap for public sector workers and give care workers a pay rise.

But some Labour insiders and supporters have criticised the lack of ambition in the plan. One former minister told the BBC the focus on "being competent" was a "classic New Labour move", referring to the era when Tony Blair was prime minister. They added the lack of big ideas meant the plan did not "match the moment".

Another former minister said: "Any child can see the obvious things you would do in response to the cost of living crisis - reverse the rise in national insurance, reverse the pensions rise, halt the cuts in universal credit. "But [the plan] doesn't even mention any of those things. It feels like a smokescreen, designed to hide the fact that they are continuing with Tony Blair's destructive legacy."

But another Labour MP said the plan was about "taking a mainstream message' to voters. They added that under Sir Keir's leadership the party had "stopped hemorrhaging votes" and had gained support in recent elections. The MP said the plan was about "talking about the issues that matter to people" rather than being a "flashy political manifesto".

Sainsbury's, Britain's second largest supermarket group, will invest £50m in staffing and improve pay for thousands of workers as part of a shake-up of its store management structure.

The retailer said the changes, which include the creation of 2,000 shop floor jobs, would result in more than 35,000 workers receiving a pay rise.

Sainsbury's said it would also pay an annual bonus to shop floor workers for the first time.

From February, shop floor workers will earn between £10.10 and £11.40 an hour. They currently start at between £9.50 and £10.75 an hour.

Siobhan McMullan, Sainsbury's retail and digital director, said: "Our shop floor colleagues do a brilliant job and are the key to our success, so we want to ensure they are appropriately rewarded for the fantastic work they do every day.

"When we created our new executive team last year, we gave ourselves the target of investing at least £100m in our colleagues over the next three years. Today's announcement is a £50m down payment on that commitment."

The company, which also owns the Argos and Habitat brands, said it planned to change the way it runs its supermarkets, with managers currently working across several departments being replaced by specialists in each area.

Sainsbury's said the changes were likely to result in the creation of about 700 manager roles, with the rest of the roles replaced by the new shop floor roles.

The supermarket said it would also introduce an annual bonus for shop floor workers, to be paid in November each year, worth between 5% and 10% of their total pay.

Sainsbury's said it was investing in its stores after reporting strong Christmas trading last month.

The supermarket group, which has 2,000 supermarkets and convenience stores, said like-for-like sales, which strip out the impact of new store openings, were up by 6.6% in the 15 weeks to 8 January.

Sales were boosted by a strong performance in grocery, as shoppers spent more money on entertaining at home amid the cost of living crisis.

However, Sainsbury's warned of further increases in the cost of living this year, as it forecast that its costs would rise by about £660m in the next financial year.

The price of petrol has been frozen for the twelfth month in a row, the chancellor has said.

Rishi Sunak said he would exercise his power to delay the inevitable increase in line with inflation until March next year. The move will save motorists an average of £1.30 per litre, or £19 per tank.

The chancellor said the measure, which will apply to diesel and petrol, was part of the government's plan to help people with the cost of living.

Mr Sunak said: "We know that people are worried about the cost of living, so to help with that we're freezing duty on petrol," he said.

The decision mirrors last year's freeze, which was also announced in November and lasted until March.

The announcement was met with a mixed reaction from motoring groups.

The RAC said the move would provide some relief from record prices, but added it was "only a temporary solution".

"We need to encourage drivers to swap to electric cars, by improving charging infrastructure and offering financial incentives," said RAC fuel spokesman Simon Williams.

"But upfront costs need to be reduced too, especially as inflation is now starting to bite into household income."

However, the AA said the freeze would help consumers amid the "cost of living catastrophe".

"This move will help consumers when they most need it," said Luke Bosdet, the AA's fuel price spokesman.

"But freezing duty isn't a long-term fix. The cost of filling up is largely determined by global oil prices, which showed little sign of easing as the chancellor spoke."

The announcement came as part of the chancellor's autumn statement, which included a package of measures to help with the cost of living.

This included a £2bn help package for households in England, comprising a £150 council tax rebate and £400 energy bill discount.

Aid agencies have insisted that Friday's tsunami in the Pacific will not divert attention or resources from the humanitarian crisis in Africa. The massive 8.9 magnitude quake, which struck off the coast of Samoa, triggered tsunami warnings across the Pacific. There are fears that the wave could cause widespread damage in Samoa, Tonga and American Samoa - but aid agencies have stressed that the tsunami is not expected to directly affect Africa.

"Obviously we are watching very closely how this develops, but at this point it does not change our focus," UNICEF's regional director for west and central Africa, Elhadj As Sy, told the BBC. "For the moment we are not diverting any resources."

The International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement also said that it was not halting its operations in Africa. The organisation's director of international relations, Tarik Kadir, said that whilst they monitor the situation with the tsunamis, operations in Africa "remain our priority". He added: "We have not had any requests for assistance regarding this earthquake or tsunamis, so at this point we are not diverting any resources."

The UK-based charity Oxfam also said it was "not aware" of any impact on its operations in Africa, but was "watching closely". A spokesperson added: "We are not diverting resources away from east Africa at this point as the needs there are so critical and our operations are ramping up."

Earlier, the UN's humanitarian coordinator in Somalia, Mark Bowden, had said that the UN was "watching very carefully" but that the impact of the tsunami was not yet clear. He added: "As far as I understand it's not directly a threat to Africa, but we're watching very carefully and if there is a request for assistance, then of course we will take a look at that."

The land, in some of the most desirable areas of the country, is sold for a fraction of its worth before being resold to innocent buyers for a huge profit. 

The scam works like this. Fraudsters first target public sector workers, tricking them into signing up to seminars and buying overpriced goods. They then use the information they have gathered to create fake identities, often of retired public sector workers, and use these to set up companies. This can involve the use of false passports and other forged documents. 

The companies are then used to register the land in the victims' names. They target land owned by local councils, the NHS, and the Ministry of Defence, as well as universities and other public bodies. The land is often near valuable infrastructure, such as train stations and schools. 

Once the land has been registered, it is sold on to other companies, often based in offshore tax havens such as the British Virgin Islands, Gibraltar, and Guernsey. These companies then sell the land on to innocent buyers, often for a huge profit. The scam has been running for years and is thought to have cost UK taxpayers millions of pounds. 

A BBC investigation has identified over 500 plots of land that have been targeted by the scam. The total area of land is estimated to be worth over £200m. The true cost to the UK taxpayer is believed to be much higher, as the scam also involves the fraudulent sale of land in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland.

The BBC has learned that the National Crime Agency (NCA) is investigating the scam. It has made a number of arrests and is working to recover the stolen land. The NCA has also issued a warning to the public, urging them to be wary of investing in land that has been sold by a company with an offshore connection.
