The EU parliament has once again delayed the vote on the software patent directive, amid intense lobbying from both sides of the debate. The latest delay comes after a narrow victory for the parliament's pro-patent camp last month, when a draft law written by German Christian Democrat MEP Axel Voss was amended in a way that satisfied many of the opponents who had previously fought against it.

The original draft directive, written in 2017, would have required member states to offer patent protection for computer-implemented inventions, including software. After 18 months of debate, Voss's draft was approved by the European Parliament's legal affairs committee in June this year, but in October a deal was struck that limited the scope of the legislation to cover only "computer-implemented inventions which make a technical contribution".

The deal was seen as a victory for medium and small-sized software developers, who argued that the original directive would have put them at risk of lawsuits from larger companies. However, the agreement was not enough to win over all opponents, and the vote was delayed for a second time to allow for further negotiations.

Speaking after the decision was taken to delay the vote, Voss said he was "disappointed" that the parliament had not voted on his revised draft, but added that he wanted to give his negotiators time to convince the opponents that the legislation will not harm software developers. "We want to find a good solution for all sides and I think we will achieve this," he said.

The latest delay is a blow to the European Commission, which has made the software patent directive a priority and has been pushing for it to be approved before the EU parliament's summer recess. The commission originally proposed the legislation in 2017, and has been working on it ever since.

 opponents of the legislation said they were pleased that the vote had been delayed, but warned that they would continue to fight against it. "We are glad that the vote has been delayed, but we are concerned that this may just be a delay and not a cancellation of the proposal," said Julia Reda, a German member of the European Parliament who has been leading the opposition to the legislation. "We will continue to campaign against it."

Sales of consumer electronics are expected to rise by more than 10% this year, the biggest increase since 2017.

But figures from OMDIA, a research consultancy, suggest that the boom could lead to a sharp rise in toxic waste.

It estimates that 57 million tonnes of waste electronic and electrical equipment (WEEE) was generated in 2021, up from 53.6 million tonnes in 2020.

Most of the waste - about 70% - came from small devices including smartphones, tablets, and headphones. The remainder was made up of large household devices such as fridges, washing machines, and TVs.

Under the Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE) Directive, consumers are entitled to dispose of old electronics free of charge at designated collection points.

But the Local Government Association, which represents councils in England and Wales, said that in some areas, household recycling sites were so full that they had to turn away people with electronic waste.

Simon Blackburn, the chair of the Local Government Association's environment, economy, and climate board, said: "Councils are doing all they can to provide accessible and efficient services, but [are] battling against a backdrop of government cuts, with recycling services particularly hit.

"Increased producer responsibility - making brands that produce electronic goods contribute to towards the cost of disposal - would help alleviate the financial burden on councils and encourage manufacturers to take more responsibility for the lifespan of their products," he added.

Most of these devices are sent to landfills, even though they could be refurbished or recycled to extract the valuable metals and minerals on board.

Now, a growing number of initiatives are pushing to give old devices a second life—whether by refurbishing them for those in need or by extracting valuable components from them.

“We believe that reuse and recycling are important parts of the circular economy,” Brightstar spokesperson Liz Hyman told The Washington Post. “We are proud to say that our mission—to make it easy for people to get a new device and give them a simple and responsible way to recycle their old one—is aligned with the principles of reducing e-waste.” 

Still, only a fraction of devices are recycled.

According to EPA data, Americans recycled approximately 152 million devices in 2021, which represents less than 15 percent of the devices that became obsolete that year.

In a café in Baghdad's decaying Ottoman-era quarter, a group of young men hunch over their laptops, caffeine and Wi-Fi fuelling their creativity.

They are the founders of Iraq's first professional video-game development company. It is called Rabid Wolves Studio, and in a few weeks' time, the team will release their first game, called The Broken Mask.

"We face many problems here every day. There is no electricity, no internet, but we have found a way to do it," says Raad Abdul-Amir, the company's 25-year-old founder and CEO, as he shows me the game. 

It is a 2D platform adventure, similar to Super Mario, and tells the story of a Iraqi policeman who is trying to save his daughter from kidnappers.

The game has been a year in the making, and Raad is proud of it. But he is prouder still of something else: earlier this year, the company signed a deal with Iraqi cinema legend Mohamed Said Abu Al-Wail, to make a film based on Raad's life.

The film, also called The Broken Mask, and directed by Abu Al-Wail, will tell the story of a young man from a noble family, who abandons his studies in the UK to return to his home city of Baghdad, and make video games.

The film takes the form of a thriller, and there are shades of the video-game industry's own back-story in Iraq's recent history of violence and upheaval.

The idea of a "super union" between the BBC, ITV and Channel 4 has been raised again by a senior BBC figure.

Director-General Tim Davie said such an alliance would give the UK media a "fighting chance" in the face of competition from streaming giants like Netflix.

He said it would be akin to the "railway analogy" - referring to the merger of British railways into Network Rail.

But his counterpart at Channel 4, Catherine Newman, said she was "not convinced" of the benefits.

Under the plan, the BBC, ITV and Channel 4 would form a not-for-profit organisation that would be jointly owned by their public and commercial shareholders. It would be funded by a levy on UK broadcasters and video-on-demand services.

The proposal was first put forward in 2019 by former BBC director-general Lord Hall, who said the public were "fed up" of in-house monopolies and wanted a choice of media provision.

But the plan was opposed by Culture Secretary Nadine Dorries, who said local TV channels could be "wiped out" if channel numbers were reduced as a result.

Mr Davie said the "super union" would help UK media compete in the face of the "global tech giants", such as Netflix, which have "a very different idea of success".

"We have to be honest, the BBC on its own won't solve this," he said. "It requires a railway analogy - let's bring the tracks together, let's make it one track to compete."

Mr Davie said the plan would stop the BBC, Channel 4 and ITV "rowing in opposite directions", adding that it was not about "cutting costs".

But Channel 4's Chief Executive, Ms Newman, said she was "not convinced of the benefits of a super union".

"The principle of public service broadcasting is important," she told the BBC. "But I think there are more elegant ways of trying to protect it and evolve it for the future than a super union."

She added that any partnership should focus on "content and brand" rather than "structure and process".

The government is to change the law to allow judges to strip people who flout child access orders of their passports and driving licences. The move is designed to stop so-called “parental abductions”, where one parent takes a child against the wishes of the other.

At present, the courts can only issue orders to stop a parent taking a child if there is already evidence they have done so – for example, if they have crossed a border.

But ministers believe the current system is too slow and that it is better to head off such incidents before they happen.

The plan is to give the courts the power to impose financial penalties and strip parental rights, such as the right to a passport, if a parent is not complying with an access order.

The Ministry of Justice said the move would send a strong message to parents who flout court orders.

Ministers will also consider whether to introduce a specific offence of parental abduction, which could result in prison sentences. at present, cases are dealt with under the general offence of child abduction.

The proposals, which will be announced by Justice Secretary Dominic Raab on Monday, follow a campaign by a charity, the Domestic Abuse Legal Fund, and come after a rise in parental order breaches during the pandemic.

The charity’s founder, Jane Robey, whose daughter was abducted by her father 14 years ago when she was 12, welcomed the move.

“When a child is abducted it is often the start of a campaign of coercive control – it is the first step in removing the child from all they know and often from the other parent too,” she said.

“These changes… will give courts the tools they need to deter and tackle parental abduction at the outset, providing better protection for children and hope for parents who find themselves facing this terrible situation.”

It has been 15 years since Doves last released an album. The wait for the Manchester band's fifth record has been prolonged by the pandemic, but also partly by the group's own relentless perfectionism.

The newly released "Clash" has been worth the wait, topping the UK album charts in its first week of release. It is Doves' fourth album to do so - more than any other band in the past two decades.

Frontman Jimi Goodwin says he is "delighted" the album has connected with people in this way, adding that making it during lockdown "kept us focused on something positive".

"It saved our lives, really," he says. "We didn't have anything else to do. It just consumed us, in a nice way. Little did we know it would then go on to sell quite a few copies… That's the icing on the cake."

"Clash" is an enigmatic title for an album that is directly inspired by the world shutting down around the band.

The first single, "Carousel", began life as a poem written by Goodwin about his experience of going through cancer treatment during lockdown, while his wife and children lived 180 miles away.

Growing up in Manchester, Doves singer Jimi Goodwin met bandmates Jez Williams and Andy Williams - who are twins - at school.

They formed the band in 1998, retiring their previous moniker, Sub Sub, at the same time that Britpop was ceding ground to the nascent dubstep and new rave scenes.

Doves' first two records, Lost Souls and The Last Broadcast, married the spiritual and the psychedelic with bouts of Britpop brilliance, but it was their third, Some Cities, that really put them on the map.

It included the Manchester anthem "There Goes the Fear", which became the most played record on UK radio in 2005. It was also the year Goodwin felt he could finally "breathe and relax" as the band found their audience.

A change in approach for the more electronic-led Kingdom of Rust followed in 2009, and while it was a bold move, it didn't quite have the same acclaim as their previous records.

By the time they got around to making the follow-up, Goodwin had become a father and the band had been through their fair share of trauma.

Touring Kingdom of Rust had taken its toll on the singer's mental health, and he was diagnosed with tinnitus and anxiety.

The consortium includes the University of London, City University, the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC), and the Science Museum.

The money will be used to develop the virtual learning environment and to establish the e-university's governing body.

The DfES has made available a further £140m for the running of the e-university in 2006-7 should the consortium's bid be successful.

A spokesman for the OU said the consortium's virtual learning environment would "revolutionise" home study.

The company, which has apologized over the incident, said the affected product accounted for about 0.08 percent of its total production in China this year.

It's astonishing how many people still haven't learned proper email etiquette. Despite the surge in spam and the introduction of laws such as the CAN-SPAM Act in the US, people still don't seem to get it. Here are some of the worst habits I've noticed when it comes to email. Are you guilty of any of these?

Not including an unsubscribe link: If you're sending an email to a list of people, you should always include an unsubscribe link. If someone doesn't want to receive your emails, they should be able to easily opt-out. This is a legal requirement in many countries.

Not getting permission: If you're sending an email to someone, make sure they've given you permission to do so. Don't buy email lists or send emails to people who haven't opted in to receive them. This is the best way to get marked as spam.

Not using a real email address: If you're sending an email, use a real email address that people can reply to. Don't use a fake or anonymous email address. This just looks suspicious and can get your email marked as spam.

Not including a signature: If you're sending an email, include a signature with your name, title, and contact information. This helps people identify who you are and why they're receiving an email from you.

Not proofreading: Before you hit send, make sure you proofread your email for any spelling or grammar mistakes. A professional email should be free of errors.

Not using proper formatting: Use proper formatting, such as paragraphs and bullet points, to make your email easier to read. Don't use all caps or excessive punctuation.

Not considering the recipient's time zone: Make sure you consider the recipient's time zone when sending an email. You don't want to wake someone up with an email at 3 am their time.

Not using email tracking: If you're sending an important email, consider using email tracking to see if the recipient has opened it. This can help you follow up appropriately.

Not using a professional email address: Use a professional email address, such as your name@company.com, rather than a personal email address, such as yourname123@gmail.com.

If you can avoid these bad habits, you'll be on your way to better email etiquette and more effective communication.

"Patents are a tool for monopolizing innovation and restricting access to technology," said Linus Torvalds, the creator of the Linux operating system and a prominent open source advocate. "They are a barrier to progress and should be abolished."

Open source leaders also argued that patents can lead to unnecessary litigation and can be used to extort money from small businesses and individuals. Google, Microsoft and other companies have been involved in costly patent lawsuits over the years.

"Patents are a form of legalized extortion," said Richard Stallman, founder of the Free Software Foundation. "They give the owner the right to demand payment from anyone who uses the patented technology, even if the use is harmless and non-commercial."

In response to these concerns, some companies have begun to reevaluate their approach to patents. For example, Google has launched the Open Patent Project, which makes some of the company's patents available for free to anyone who wants to use them.

"We believe that patents should be used to protect innovation, not to restrict it," said Kent Walker, Google's general counsel. "Through the Open Patent Project, we hope to encourage the development of new technologies and help to reduce the burden of patent litigation on small businesses and individuals."

Despite these efforts, open source leaders remain skeptical about the role of patents in the software industry. They argue that patents are an anachronism in an age of open collaboration and free sharing and that they should be abolished in order to foster innovation and protect small developers. 

Ultimately, it remains to be seen whether patents will continue to play a role in the software industry, or whether they will be replaced by alternative forms of intellectual property protection.

The government is planning to launch a pilot project on mobile ticketing in four to five cities, including Mumbai, Delhi, Bengaluru, Chennai, and Kolkata. "We are working on a pilot project on mobile ticketing. In the first phase, we plan to launch it in four or five cities. We have identified the cities and they include Mumbai, Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai and Bengaluru," Union Minister for Road Transport and Highways, Nitin Gadkari, told the Times of India. 

The ticketing system would be optional, and passengers could continue to use their existing travel cards if they chose. According to the report, the government is planning to partner with state governments and urban local bodies for the project. 

There will be a provision for giving a discount to passengers who will use the mobile ticketing system. Besides, the government is also planning to introduce a common mobility card that can be used for travel as well as shopping, the minister said without giving details.

This development comes after the Ministry of Railways announced plans to introduce a similar system for train travel. Earlier this month, the Ministry of Railways announced that it was planning to introduce a mobile ticketing system, allowing passengers to use their smartphones to book and pay for train tickets. 

The new system is expected to be launched by the end of this year, starting with a few trains and eventually expanding to include all trains.

The mobile phone has become the central hub for music fans, creating new challenges and opportunities for artists and labels to break through and be discovered in an increasingly crowded market.

It's little wonder that artists and labels are focusing their attention on mobile. According to the IFPI, 50% of all music listeners use music streaming apps on mobile devices, a higher proportion than use them on computers or via smart speakers.

Mobile listeners are also passionate about music. Figures from MRC Data, formerly the Music Consumer Insights survey, show that mobile listeners stream more frequently, spend more time streaming and are more likely to pay for a music subscription.

Mobile listening has been supercharged in recent years by the rise of in-car infotainment systems, better Bluetooth connections and the arrival of affordable true wireless earbuds, such as AirPods.

England's rocker prince has been called out by audience members for "fat-shaming" during a live onstage interview. 

Singer Liam Gallagher, 47, has faced backlash from fans at the Park Stage at Glastonbury Festival after he appeared to make a snide comment about singer and TV personality Peter Doherty, who was in the audience.

Doherty, 53, rose to fame as the guitarist of indie rock band The Libertines, as well as for his high-profile relationship with model Kate Moss. 

He has since struggled with drug addiction and homelessness and became a patron of the charity Focus 12, which provides residential rehab treatment for people suffering from drug and alcohol addiction. 

Doherty received a standing ovation from other festival-goers during the Q&A, which came after he had introduced a film about the charity at the festival's Cabaret Tent. 

But then, when interviewer Jo Whiley asked Gallagher if he had ever been tempted to "go off the rails", he replied: "Not until I saw Peter Doherty in the audience." 

An audible groan went up from some in the crowd, while others shouted: "Respect!"

Doherty, who has struggled with weight loss and gain through his life, wore a black shirt and trousers with a yellow jacket and sat cross-legged to one side during the show. 

He did not comment on the comment during the live broadcast, but shared a clip of the exchange on his Instagram story with the words: "Fat-shaming is never cool."

Doherty's patron charity also posted the clip on Instagram, with the words: "That was a low blow."

The exchange came on the final night of the festival, which has been taking place near Pilton in Somerset over the past five days. 

More than 250,000 people have attended, with headlines coming from the likes of Billie Eilish, Sir Paul McCartney, and Kendrick Lamar. 

The festival has been running since 1970 and is considered one of the most prestigious and well-known music festivals in the world.

Few names are as synonymous with comic books as Stan Lee. As the co-creator of Marvel Comics' instantly recognizable stable of superheroes, including the Fantastic Four, Spider-Man, the Avengers, and the X-Men, Lee's impact on the genre is undeniable. Yet, for all of his success, Lee remained grounded, and was known for his trademark wit, and an ability to connect with fans that transcended the page.

Born as Stanley Martin Lieber on December 28, 1922, in New York City, Lee grew up in a vibrant neighborhood filled with immigrants from around the world. As a child, he was fascinated by movies and books, and dreamed of one day becoming a writer.

After graduating from high school in 1939, Lee got his start in the comic book industry as an assistant at Timely Comics, which would eventually become Marvel Comics. Initially, he performed menial tasks, such as filling in watercolors and proofreading, but soon began writing his own scripts.

Lee's career took off in the early 1960s when he and artist Jack Kirby created the Fantastic Four. The title's success spurred Lee to create even more superheroes, including the Hulk, Thor, and Iron Man.

What set Lee's creations apart from other comic book heroes was their relatable, human qualities. Despite their superhuman powers, characters like Spider-Man and the X-Men faced the same struggles as everyday people, such as paying rent and dealing with relationships.

Lee's impact on the comic book industry was unparalleled. He introduced a level of complexity and emotional depth to his characters that set them apart from the traditional archetypes of the time. Additionally, he was a master of the cliffhanger, and his stories were filled with twists and turns that kept readers coming back for more.

Lee was also a pioneer in the realm of multimedia franchising. He saw the potential for his characters to thrive in other formats, and successfully expanded the Marvel Universe into television, film, and even video games.

As Lee's fame grew, so did his reputation as a pop culture icon. He made appearances in numerous Marvel films, and was beloved by fans for his trademark wit and charm.

Lee's legacy extends far beyond the page. He was a true pioneer in the world of superhero comics, and his creations have become a timeless part of popular culture. He will be remembered as a true visionary who helped to shape the industry into what it is today.

Music is at a "zombie" state in Germany, dominated by US pop and chart-topping hits from the 1990s and early 2000s, according to a prominent classical music critic.
Daniel Barenboim warned that the country was no longer producing music which was " competitve on the international market" and risked becoming a "museum" of its own musical history.
The conductor and pianist, who is Spanish-Argentinian and has lived in Germany for 40 years, said he felt a "sense of panic" about the lack of infrastructure to support young musicians.

His comments came in a interview to be published on Sunday in the weekly Der Spiegel on the eve of his 80th birthday on 15 November.

Barenboim accused the country's arts establishment of ignoring the current generation of musicians in favour of celebrities and vintage stars who appealed to a mainstream audience.

"Pop and old stars are booked for the next 10 years. There is no space for young musicians," he said.

"Nothing happens anymore, and that's why Germany has become a museum country. Either you play Bach and Beethoven or you play pop music. There is no in-between."

He said that the days when Germany could produce world-class musicians such as Anne-Sophie Mutter and Herbert von Karajan, who had "filled the major concert halls of the world", were over.

"Germany is no longer a music-producing country. It's a catastrophe," he added. "The infrastructure is collapsing. There used to be a musical education in Germany that was the best in the world. Now it's a zombie state."

Barenboim, who was born in Buenos Aires in 1942, said that he had moved to Germany in 1982 because he had been offered the chance to establish the Berlin Philharmonic Orchestra as a world-class ensemble - a dream that had been realised.

But he added that he had a "sense of panic" about the lack of opportunities for young musicians in Germany, once considered the centre of the classical music world.

"There is not enough being done in Germany to help young musicians find their place," he said. "All they can do is emigrate and that breaks my heart."

He won a second Grammy in 1988 for Best Original Score for his work on the film Fatal Attraction.

The decision announced by a Pennsylvania court yesterday not to file charges against Bill Cosby, the famed TV dad, was a severe blow to the scores of women who accused the comedian of drugging and sexually assaulting them.

The district attorney, Bruce Castor, declared that his office had concluded after a thorough investigation that it could not “satisfy the burden of proof” required to bring a criminal case against the 90-year-old celebrity.

Mr Castor said too much time had passed since the alleged incidents and the accusers themselves had contributed to the problem by failing to report the offences at the time. 

“We conclude this investigation without sufficient evidence to file any criminal charges,” he told a press conference. “To the women who reported these allegations, I promise you that you were heard.”

Mr Cosby’s lawyer, Brian McMonagle, claimed the decision proved his client’s innocence. “He has been accused by some as being the monster that these accusers have claimed,” he said. “Today that narrative was destroyed.” 

The decision capped a remarkable comeback for Mr Cosby, whose career seemed over after he was convicted in April 2018 of three counts of sexual assault.

Mr Cosby, who rose to fame as the wholesome patriarch Dr Heathcliff Huxtable on the TV sitcom The Cosby Show, spent three years in prison before a court overturned his conviction, citing flaws in the prosecution. 

The district attorney’s office had three years to decide whether to retry Mr Cosby on the original charges or bring new ones against him. Several of his accusers had accused him of drugging and molesting them at a hotel in Philadelphia in 2004. Mr Cosby has repeatedly denied the accusations.

The media regulator has fined Viacom £1.8m for airing a documentary that it ruled was indecent.

Ofcom ruled that the Channel 5 show, Murder at the Cottage, did not need a warning despite "graphic" scenes.

The watchdog launched an investigation last year into the show, which included footage of a dead body.

Channel 5 said it did not agree with Ofcom's ruling and planned to appeal.

The fine is the latest in a series of high-profile decisions on TV standards.

Ofcom said Murder at the Cottage, which was aired in September 2021, broke rules on offensive content.

The documentary showed the bodies of two murder victims being removed from a house, Ofcom said, adding that it "judged the footage to be graphic and explicit".

But the regulator ruled that a warning at the start of the programme would have "undermined the editorial value of the footage".

Instead, it said a "precise and factual" introduction to the programme - which was broadcast at 10pm - was sufficient.

Under the rules, broadcasters must include a warning at the start of a programme if there is "material that is likely to offend generally accepted standards".

Ofcom said its decision took into account the fact that Channel 5 had taken a number of steps to alert viewers to the nature of the programme.

These included a "high-profile publicity campaign", a warning at the start of the channel's news and an introduction from journalist Mark Austin.

A Channel 5 spokesperson said: "We do not agree with Ofcom's ruling and we will be appealing against it.

"The programme was carefully compiled with editorial standards at its heart, including significant warnings to viewers ahead of broadcast. It was broadcast after the 9pm watershed and we believe it was in line with Ofcom's rules."

The fine comes after the BBC was fined £1m by Ofcom for a BBC Three documentary on fat-shaming.

Ofcom ruled that the BBC had "failed to take due care over the handling of offensive content" in the programme, which was hosted by actress Roxanne Pallett.

Its stars, Leonardo DiCaprio and Cate Blanchett, lost out on best actor and best actress awards but director Martin Scorsese triumphed.

It also won actress Julie Walters, who played the title role of the 1950s midwife, the Bafta for best supporting actress.

The BBC must "get with the times" or face being broken up by the government, warns a former director general.

In a speech to Cambridge University students on Tuesday, he will argue the BBC has become a "monolith" and needs an "overhaul".

It was once one of the most ubiquitous sights in Britain - a landline phone perched on a table, with a spiral cord stretching onto the sofa where someone sat, idly chatting away.

But the era of the home phone may be coming to an end - signalled by telecoms giant BT's decision to stop selling them altogether.

Landlines - once considered a vital component of the information superhighway - have been supplanted by mobile phones. The telecoms regulator Ofcom says that 65% of households now have a "phone-free" home, with adults and children communicating via mobile phones.

According to market research firm GfK, there were 16 million residential landlines in Britain at the end of 2021, down from 18 million two years earlier.

And Ofcom said last year that landlines were likely to disappear completely within the next decade. It found that even older people, who might have relied on landlines in the past, were turning to mobile phones.

The switch away from landlines has been rapid. Ten years ago, almost every home had one.

Since then, many have decided they do not need an additional phone socket in their homes, and have cancelled their landlines, or not taken one out when moving into a new property. Some have even ripped out the wiring altogether.

BT's decision to stop selling landlines - which Ofcom approved - is not expected to have an immediate impact on existing customers.

The company said landline connections were increasingly being used only for broadband, and that its focus would be on providing digital phone services, such as VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol), which allows people to make calls over the internet.

But what does the disappearance of the home phone mean for Britain - and could it leave people behind?

Less socially inclusive

The end of the landline "may risk further isolating those who are already socially excluded", Ofcom warned last year.

It pointed to older people and those on low incomes as potentially being most affected, because they are less likely to own a mobile phone.

In 2019, Ofcom found that 8% of people did not have a mobile phone and 7% did not have home broadband, with low-income households significantly less likely to have access to the internet.

Although Ofcom does not link these figures directly to landlines, it says that for those who do not have internet access, "retaining landline connectivity will be important".

Air China has launched its $1bn (£815m) flotation on the London Stock Exchange, as the country continues to open up its economy.

The airline's shares were priced at £2.68 each, at the bottom of their expected range, in a sign that the global recovery in air travel is still some way off.

The listing is a rare chance for investors to buy into one of China's biggest state-owned companies.

Only last week, the ruling Communist Party announced it would accelerate the opening of its financial sector to foreign investors.

Air China's flotation is part of a plan by China's government to revive its flag carrier, which has been losing money for years.

In a sign of the times, prospective investors were not able to attend in person but had to pore over a 3,000-page prospectus posted on a web portal.

They will get just a sliver of the company - the flotation will raise just over $1bn for the airline, with the rest staying in the hands of the Chinese government.

But it is the first time in more than a decade that a company has floated on the London market worth more than £700m.

The timing appears to be linked to China's political calendar, with the country's leaders gathering in Beijing this week for their once-every-five-years national congress.

It is being seen as a chance for China's leaders to lay out their vision for the next five years, and to announce any number of policy changes.

Last week, in a move seen as symbolic, the Chinese government announced it was easing restrictions on foreign ownership in the country's financial sector.

For example, it said foreign companies would be allowed to take large stakes in Chinese banks and financial management companies.

Also last week, the UK prime minister, Boris Johnson, visited China, where he spoke of a "golden era" in relations between the two countries.

One analyst said the Air China flotation appeared to be part of a wider strategy to improve relations with the West.

"This is a signal from Beijing that they are still happy to do business with the West," said Charles Robertson, a China economist at Renaissance Capital.

The e-university was announced in 1997 as part of the government's strategy for increasing the number of people with access to higher education. It was intended to be a "virtual" university, without a campus, offering courses predominantly through the internet. But the project has been hit by a series of problems and has been the subject of criticism from academics who said that it would not attract students because of the lack of face-to-face teaching.

Last month, the government's spending watchdog said that there was no clear business plan for the e-university and that value for money was not proven. The ECB's governing council left the rate on its main refinancing operations at 0%, while the rate on its marginal lending facility remained at 0.25%.

The ECB also said it would accelerate its bond purchases under its 1.85 trillion euro ($2.1 trillion) pandemic emergency purchase programme (Pepp).

The moves came as inflation in the eurozone hit a record high of 5% in December, well ahead of the ECB's 2% target.

The central bank had already said it expected inflation to be higher for longer and that it would keep rates at their current, or lower levels until it saw inflation reaching 2% consistently.

Portugal's central bank chief, Mario Centeno, who is also the ECB's governor, said: "We are witnessing a phenomenon that is not a generalised inflationary spiral in the euro area."

He said that the ECB did not want to "surprise" markets by changing its policy stance prematurely and that any exit from its current policies would be gradual.

The Pepp is due to run until March, but the ECB has said it would assess whether its duration should be extended in light of the continued uncertainty over the outlook for the economy.

It has also said it would create a new tool to cope with government bond yields that "deviate substantially, and persistently" from their levels seen before the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

The ECB's move came on the same day as the US Federal Reserve increased its key interest rate by 0.25% to a target range of 4.5% to 4.75%, its highest level since 2007.

In the UK, the Bank of England also increased interest rates, raising them to 4% from 3.5%, their highest level in over a decade.

US trade gap narrows as exports rise

The US trade deficit narrowed in November for the third straight month, as exports of agricultural products and machinery rose, official data shows.

The gap between what the US sells and what it buys from other countries fell to $67.0bn, a decline of nearly 11% from $75.4bn in October, the Commerce Department said.

The improvement was driven by a 6.2% rise in exports to $224.9bn, with soybean shipments rising ahead of the harvest in Brazil, and an increase in exports of capital goods.

Imports were up 0.9% at $292.9bn, with increases in foreign-made cars and consumer goods.

The monthly trade gap is closely watched as it is considered an important barometer of the US economy.

But it also matters because the gap represents the difference between what the US buys from abroad and what it sells to other countries. 

When the trade gap is as large as it has been over the past year, it means the US is buying more from other countries than it is selling overseas, with the shortfall having to be financed by foreign capital.

That can contribute to a wider current account deficit, which means the US is paying out more money than it is taking in, increasing its need to attract foreign capital to finance the shortfall.

That can put pressure on the dollar, which fell after the release of the data on Thursday.

The improvement in the trade gap comes as central bankers and policymakers struggle to tackle inflation, which has been driven up by the supply chain problems and shortages caused by the Covid-19 pandemic and the recovery from the pandemic.

The Federal Reserve, which has kept interest rates low to support the economic recovery, has started to wind down its large-scale bond-buying stimulus scheme from November, and signalled that it plans to raise interest rates three times next year.

In the UK, the Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in three years this month, and analysts expect the Fed to raise rates at its meeting next month.

"Had the West provided Ukraine with the weapons it needed, when it needed them, Russian troops would have been forced to divert resources from the battle for Kyiv and other cities," Amnesty said.

"This failure to provide the weapons Ukraine requested cost lives, multiplied casualties, and enabled Russia to mount a credible claim that it is acting in self-defence," the organisation added.

Ukraine has made repeated requests for Western countries to supply it with fighter jets, with its defence minister asking for aircraft from NATO members in November last year.

Several countries have sent missiles and other weapons to Ukraine since the invasion, but Western nations have been wary of providing fighter jets or other aircraft for fear of being drawn into the conflict.

Last month, US President Joe Biden announced that Washington would supply Ukraine with the more advanced NASAMS air defence system, as well as up to 350 missiles for the system, amid reports of continuing Russian air strikes on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure.

Softbank has invested heavily in British telecoms firm BT, but the value of its holdings dropped by £1.6bn.

The performance of Softbank's Chinese investments also dragged on its overall performance, with its holdings in ride-hailing firm Didi Chuxing and mobile phone firm Tencent falling in value.

The minister said he was "confident" that the posters were an effective deterrent, but added that there was "no hard evidence" to prove it.

Prosecutors have launched an investigation into UK MP Ken Clarke over claims he compared the Jewish community to the Islamic State group.

The Board of Deputies said it had reported the matter to the Metropolitan Police.

Ms Shah apologised for the "completely unacceptable" posts on Saturday, adding that she had not intended to cause offence.

UK's National Gallery in the pink

London's National Gallery has reopened after a major renovation of its main building, which has taken nearly five years and £215m.

The gallery in Trafalgar Square has been closed since August 2018, except for a brief period in the run-up to Christmas 2020, when it reopened for a few weeks.

The refurbishment of the Grade I listed building has seen improvements to ventilation, lighting and accessibility. New spaces have also been created, including a Creativity Studio and dedicated spaces for learning and interpretation.

The gallery's directors said it was "an important moment for the National Gallery".

"This is, at heart, a project about access and inclusion," said Nicholas Penny, director of the National Gallery. "We have created a beautiful space for everyone to enjoy."

The gallery boasts one of the greatest collections of European art in the world, with masterpieces from Leonardo da Vinci, Rembrandt, Vincent van Gogh and Claude Monet among its holdings.

Tiles in the main entrance have been cleaned or replaced, while ventilation has been improved in galleries and new lighting installed.

A new Learning Centre has opened on the ground floor, along with the Creativity Studio, a space for drawing and other creative activities for visitors of all ages.

A new entrance on Trafalgar Square has been created, while the St. Martin's Entrance off Orange Street has been renovated.

The East Wing has been partially reopened, with the new entrance on Trafalgar Square opening up that part of the building. The East Wing will fully reopen in the autumn, along with the rest of the building.

The gallery said it had achieved a "world-class" environmental standard, and that it was on track to achieve net zero carbon emissions by 2030.

Works of art from the collection have been lent to museums and galleries around the UK while the building work took place, with some due to remain on loan for several years.

The National Gallery is also due to open a new gallery at the Tate Modern in October, which will show experimental and interdisciplinary works from the collection.

Film director Spike Lee has backed a group of students who have been banned from filming a TV advert about racial profiling in the UK.

The College of Production Assistants (CPA) rejected the script for the short film, which features the experiences of three British Asian men.

The students, from the University of West London, plan to go ahead with the project.

Spike Lee, who won an Oscar in 2019, has offered to pay for the film to be finished.

The CPA, which licenses commercial production assistants in the UK, rejected the script for the short film because it was "too political".

The script for the film, called Trigger, features three British Asian men who share their experiences of being stopped by the police because of their race.

One of the men, Anjam Singh, said he was detained and strip-searched after being mistaken for a terrorist while travelling to London from India. Another, Shahlaa Ahmed, said he was repeatedly stopped by police while driving a car with tinted windows.

The students have launched a crowdfunding page to raise money for the film and have received support from Spike Lee.

The Oscar-winning director has offered to finish the film if they are unable to do so.

In a tweet, he said: "I'm so excited & proud of u guys, u have accomplished what others couldn't, by making something real, raw & provocative!"

The students have raised more than £8,000 ($10,600) - double their original target - in just two days.

Mahad Ahmed, who is behind the project, said he was grateful for Lee's support.

"It means a lot, not only to me but to my colleagues as well, we're meant to be in our 20s and he's been in the industry for 50 years and he's still passionate about the issues we're talking about right now," he said.

"We all grew up watching his films and cannot believe he has offered to pay for post-production services for our short."

The News Media Association (NMA), which represents UK news media outlets, made the proposal to merge the National Union of Journalists (NUJ) and the Broadcasting, Entertainment, Communications and Theatre Union (BECTU) at the weekend.

The plan would create a union of more than 40,000 journalists, making it the largest journalists' union in the world and one of the biggest in the UK.

BECTU's general secretary, Gerry Morrissey, said the union would "engage in constructive discussions" with the NUJ about the proposal.

It is not clear how the plan would be funded or how the two unions would merge their operations.

Laser beams carrying internet data can help connect remote areas where laying cables is challenging, researchers say.

Two teams of scientists have used lasers to transmit data at high speeds over long distances.

One team sent images and high-quality video between two mountain tops in Switzerland.

The other team connected two universities in Mexico, but eventually hopes to link a town to the internet.

Both projects are small-scale but could be used to deliver internet in places where laying fibre is too difficult or expensive.

"We are trying to find solutions for the last mile," said Prof Gerald Fabre from the University of Southampton, UK, who led the Mexican project.

"There are many remote areas, for example in the UK we have hundreds of kilometres of coastline where laying fibre is not easy," he told the BBC.

"There are also other applications where you don't want to have any physical contact - in the Arctic or Antarctic, for example."

Ordinarily, the "last mile" problem - the final leg of getting from a telecommunications hub to a user - is solved by laying fibre-optic cable, which can be slow and expensive.

But laser light in the mid-infrared range can be sent along tiny glass fibres, and carry far more data than current technologies.

The researchers in Mexico used a beam with a wavelength of 1,550 nanometres - a similar wavelength to that used in traditional fibre-optic cables - to send data at speeds of 2.89Gbps over a distance of 20km (12 miles) between the cities of Puebla and Toluca.

Their apparatus cost less than £2,000 ($2,730) - about 100 times less than a similar experiment a few years ago.

What's more, the laser they used was powered by the USB port of a laptop, and its energy use was negligible, said Prof Fabre.

In a separate project, researchers from the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne (EPFL) used a similar technique to send data over a record-breaking 143km.

Their low-power, wavelength-tunable laser sent information at speeds of up to 1.4Tbps through the air between the peaks of two mountains, at a distance of up to 120km.

The former foreign secretary, Jack Straw, has told the BBC the House of Lords was wrong to argue in a landmark decision that it was always illegal to hold foreign nationals without trial.

And he predicted that the government would not accept the verdict - reached by a majority of three - and would seek to change the law.

The Lords ruled on Thursday that the Detention Authority Act 1994 meant that no minister could authorise the detention of foreign nationals indefinitely.

But Mr Straw said that when the legislation was passed, as well as when he used these powers when he was home secretary, it was assumed that it was legal to hold foreign nationals indefinitely.

He added that the then government believed that it would be impractical and foolish to have foreign nationals with no right to be in the UK - such as asylum seekers whose applications had been turned down - walking the streets at will. 

"That is the background against which this legislation was passed and it is entirely unreasonable for the House of Lords to make a judgment about the legislative intent against a background which they themselves have created," he said.

Mr Straw added that the decision would create huge practical problems because there were many foreign nationals who were currently unable to return to their own countries. 

He said the decision would also have serious consequences for the government's counter-terrorism strategy.

"I cannot believe that any government, any parliamentary democracy would allow the situation to develop whereby those suspected of involvement in terrorist activities, where evidence is scarce and it may take months to get hold of it, that they could not be held for the period of time necessary to enable the authorities to gather the evidence," he said. 

"The idea that they can simply be released, whether they are British or not, in the meantime seems to me to be a very dangerous development."

Mr Straw also said he did not think the decision would be respected in other commonwealth countries, adding that this was likely to affect the treatment of British nationals abroad.

The Hollywood star, who has sued the Sun newspaper over libel, spoke as he received a honorary award from the Critics' Choice Awards.

He was not in attendance when a High Court judge ruled that the allegations against him in the article, published in April 2018, were "substantially true".

Depp has been asked to resign from his role in the Harry Potter spin-off franchise Fantastic Beasts by the film's director David Yates and studio Warner Bros, following the court ruling.

The actor is also involved in a separate $50m (£38m) defamation lawsuit in the US against Heard over an op-ed she wrote for the Washington Post in which she said she had suffered domestic abuse.

His appearance at the Critics' Choice Awards in Los Angeles on Sunday was his first major showbiz event since the ruling.

Depp was introduced by his Rum Diary co-star Amber Heard, who appeared by video link-up from Australia, where she is filming.

Heard, 34, who donated her $7m divorce settlement to charity, introduced Depp as "a true artist, a consummate actor, and a humble man".

Depp appeared shocked when he was handed the award, telling the audience: "I came here tonight as an honourary award winner.

The Beatles may be coming to iTunes, but for now, downloads are still ruled by the King. Elvis Presley's classic 1960s singles collection Elvis Presley Singles Collection: Volume 1 is this week's top-selling download album, according to Nielsen SoundScan, bumping the Beatles' greatest hits collection from the top of the chart after just one week.

Presley collected three new downloads this week from the album, for a total of 7,000, while the Beatles' album sold 6,000, for a two-week total of 63,000.

Sales of individual downloads were led by Justin Timberlake's "LoveStoned/I Think She Knows," which moved 172,000 downloads, according to SoundScan. That's just ahead of Presley's "A Little Less Conversation," which sold 169,000 downloads.

Downloads are a growing part of the music business. According to Nielsen, digital sales accounted for 20 percent of the overall market last year, and grew by 30 percent in 2007.

This is the first time downloads have shown up in the Billboard singles chart. Billboard plans to include downloads in the Hot 100 singles chart beginning in 2012.

This week's other top downloads included Josh Groban's "You Raise Me Up" at number three, followed by Journey's "Don't Stop Believin'," Glen Campbell's "Rhinestone Cowboy," and Johnny Cash's "Man in Black." Rounding out the top 10 were Eagle-Eye Cherry's "Save Tonight," Simon & Garfunkel's "Bridge Over Troubled Water," Guns N' Roses' "Sweet Child O' Mine," and Black Sabbath's "Iron Man."

Overall album sales were led by the soundtrack to the film "Dreamgirls," which sold more than 140,000 copies to top Billboard's list. That was followed by the Eagles' Long Road Out of Eden, Presley's classic hits collection Elvis 30 #1 Hits, and the soundtrack to "Now That's What I Call Christmas." Rounding out the top five were the Def Leppard/Poison collection Def Leppard/Poison – Best Of, and Radiohead's 2007 release In Rainbows.

In other music news, Coldplay scored its fifth straight number one album this week, as Viva La Vida moved more than 302,000 copies, according to SoundScan.

A documentary about the Van Gogh festival has been withdrawn from a Dutch film festival after allegations of "toxic" working conditions behind the project.

Tilburg University withdrew Vincent: A Life in Colour following criticism of the way the festival was organised.

One staff member told broadcaster NOS that volunteers were put on standby to fill in for workers who protested against poor conditions.

The university said it "deeply regretted" the situation.

The team behind the documentary has denied any wrongdoing.

The festival in the town of Brabant celebrated the life and work of the famous Dutch artist who cut off his ear before shooting himself and has attracted more than 600,000 visitors over the past two years.

This year's event was supposed to be even more ambitious but three days before it was due to start, the team behind the documentary about the festival's development was dropped from the programme.

"The reason is that several participants have indicated that they are confronted with unacceptable working conditions," the festival's organisers said in a statement.

Volunteers were put on standby

One employee told NOS that volunteers were asked to sign a confidentiality agreement, adding that if they spoke about the "toxic" working atmosphere, they would have to pay a fine of €10,000 (£8,600).

The worker said there was a "culture of fear and power" and that organisers had put together a list of people who had complained about their work conditions.

They were then confronted and bullied, the employee added.

The team behind the film, which was being shown at the festival for a second year, said in a statement that it had done "nothing wrong".

It said it had "devoted attention and care to the organisation of the staff and its working conditions" and had "not violated any laws".

The university, which was a co-producer on the film, said it had launched an investigation into the allegations.

"If it appears that the organisers have not lived up to their obligations, then we will draw consequences," it added.

The US box office is on course to break records in 2022, with ticket sales expected to top $8.5bn (£6.9bn) for the first time.

Revenue has rebounded after the pandemic shut cinemas and crushed the industry in 2020.

Ticket sales have been boosted by Marvel films such as Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness and Black Panther: Wakanda Forever.

But analysts warn that admissions are still below pre-pandemic levels.

Box office figures are generally divided between the number of tickets sold and the higher average ticket price.

In 2022, the average price of a movie ticket in the US is expected to be more than $9 for the first time, a new record.

That is up from $8.85 in 2021 and $8.63 in 2020, but still below the $9.11 recorded in 2019 before the pandemic.

Analysts say that the rise in ticket prices is one of the main reasons why the box office is set to break records this year, despite lower attendance.

"When you have a situation where you don't have as many tickets sold, but the average ticket price is $9, that's $9 that is counted towards the box office and that is what is driving these record numbers," said Comscore's media analyst Paul Dergarabedian.

The Walt Disney Company, which owns Marvel, has enjoyed huge successes in 2022 thanks in part to the release of seven Marvel films this year, including Black Panther: Wakanda Forever which has taken more than $800m worldwide.

That film was released in November, a month that is traditionally a strong one for the box office.

But admissions in 2022 are still below pre-pandemic levels.

In 2019, the last pre-pandemic year, the box office took $11.32bn. It fell to $2.3bn in 2020 when cinemas were shut.

"We're still well below where we were pre-pandemic," said Dergarabedian. "A record-breaking year in terms of box office is still a far cry from what we were at in 2019."

The cinema industry has faced a difficult 2022, with strong competition from streaming as well as the aftermath of the pandemic.

Sir Ian Corbett, the former director-general of the BBC, has attacked the "dumbing down" of television, arguing that the public service channels are in danger of "losing their way".

Corbett, who was director-general of the BBC from 1982 to 1987, was speaking at the launch of a new book about his predecessor, Hugh Greene.

"There are signs that some broadcasters are already moving in that direction [of dumbing down]," he said.

"I think they are misunderstanding their publics. I think they are doing themselves a disservice and, in the end, they will do the public a disservice."

He argued that the public service channels - BBC1, BBC2, Channel 4 and Channel 5 - were "in danger of losing their way".

"They should be providing alternative views," he said. "They should be providing stuff that isn't immediately accessible but which is worthwhile because it stretches your mind.

"I think they are in danger of forgetting that. They think their job is to satisfy as many people as possible of a certain level of intelligence."

Corbett said the BBC had "got much better" at reflecting the whole of the UK than when he was director-general.

But he added that it was still biased towards London and the south-east of England.

"I think the BBC reflects, far more than it did, the whole of the UK," he said. "But is it still London-oriented? Yes, it is.

"Is it as bad as it was? No, it's much better. But it is still the major problem for the BBC."

Corbett said the corporation still had too many senior managers and producers based in London.

"It is still the way the BBC works," he said. "It is still assuming that the centre of the universe is London and everybody else comes second.

"That's a pretty unhealthy approach for an organisation that is supposed to be supporting the whole of the UK."

He also had some advice for BBC director-general Mark Thompson, who is due to leave soon: "The most important thing is to have a really strong relationship with the government of the day.

"It's absolutely fundamental. If you haven't got that, it's very difficult to have the influence that you need."

The Anglo-Nigerian writer Bernardine Evaristo has won the Booker Prize for her novel Girl, Woman, Other.

The novel tells the stories of 12 characters, mostly black women, living in Britain.

The 63-year-old reacted to winning the prize, worth £52,500 ($66,000), by lifting her arms in the air and laughing.

She described the book as "a celebration of heterogeneity".

The book is Evaristo's eighth novel and the judges called it "a dazzling, vivid and engaging novel".

The announcement was made at a dinner in London's Guildhall, with the shortlisted authors watching.

It is only the second time in the history of the prize that it has been won by a woman author.

The previous winner was Anna Burns in 2018 for her novel Milkman.

Organizers of the prize, which has been running for 51 years, said they made the decision to change the rules because "no woman has ever won the prize twice, or men either come to that".

They also wanted to encourage authors to enter their novels for the prize.

Prior to the rule change, authors could only win the Booker Prize once in their lifetime.

The change means that three previous winners - Margaret Atwood, Hilary Mantel, and John Banville - would now be eligible to win it again.

Atwood, who won in 2000 for The Blind Assassin, said she would "think about" entering her novel The Testaments, which follows on from The Handmaid's Tale, for the prize.

The Testaments was published in September and Atwood described it as a "sequel, not a sequel", because it picks up on characters from the earlier novel, but is also a standalone story.

The Booker Prize is open to writers of any nationality, writing in English.

The prize money for the Booker has increased this year from £50,000 to £52,500.

The increase marks the first time the prize has risen above £50,000 in its history.

Arthur Hailey has made a fortune from fiction. His books have sold more than 170 million copies worldwide and have been translated into 40 languages. He is the author of a string of bestsellers, including Hotel, Airport and Wheels.

The success of these books saw him dubbed "the king of the bestseller".

The one thing his readers could rely on was that Arthur Hailey would never surprise them.

His formula was simple. Take a large organisation oozing with ambition, cynicism and greed. Throw in a ruthless businessman as protagonist. Add a strong female character as the moral compass.

Mix well and place in a container. Then take a large pinch of suspense, a generous scoop of romance, and a heap of insider information about the workings of the organisation concerned.

Bake until the plot is thick and juicy, and serve in small portions. A chapter a night is about right.

Some authors have admitted emulating Hailey's recipe for success. Stephen King, for one. "Hotel was one of the books that made me want to be a writer," he said. "I thought, 'I can do this. This is not rocket science.'"

Others have criticised Hailey for making writing look easy. Michael Crichton, creator of Jurassic Park, described Hailey as "a lazy writer".

"He works occasionally," he said, "but not hard."

The son of a police officer, Hailey was born in Luton in 1920. After leaving school at 14, he had a variety of jobs - including as a vacuum cleaner salesman and a touring actor with the BBC's repertory company - before joining the RAF during World War Two.

After the war he worked as a journalist in London and, in 1951, moved to Canada where he wrote for the Toronto Star. It was there that he started to write novels.

His breakthrough came with the publication of his seventh novel, Hotel, in 1965.

The book became an instant hit, turning Hailey into a millionaire.

He wrote a string of bestselling novels in the same vein - using real-life locations such as airports, railways and hospitals as the backdrop to his stories of big business and ambitious men.

His method was to carry out extensive research until he knew more about his subject than anyone else.

"I'm not a very bright fellow," he once said. "But I stay with it until I know as much as anybody about it."

The former Labour MP said he had been "horrified" to read comments on the party's website after he joined on Saturday.

Mr. Kilroy-Silk - who joined UKIP after quitting the BBC's Question Time panel - said the comments revealed a "dark, destructive and divisive" force within the party.

The year's first major consumer electronics show, held in Las Vegas last week, showed a industry waking up to the fact that the MP3 player is now mainstream.

Last year, the MP3 player was the star of the show. This year, it was taken for granted.

Instead, the buzz was about larger, higher-resolution screens and flashy new photo capabilities.

The new Pocket PC phones, with their colour screens, built-in cameras and MP3 players, got most of the attention.

But the star of the show was a handheld game console, not a phone or a music player.

The Nintendo DS, launched in the US last month, is a gaming handheld with two screens, one of which is a touchscreen.

Its most exciting feature, however, is its wireless connectivity. Nintendo has partnered with a company called Broadcom to create an 802.11b Wi-Fi chip for the DS, which can be used to connect to the Internet, for multiplayer games, and eventually to download games and other content from the Web.

At the show, Nintendo demonstrated the device's Web browsing capabilities, although it was unclear when Nintendo plans to enable the feature, and whether Americans will be able to surf the net with it anytime soon.

The DS's Wi-Fi capabilities may be a prelude to a new generation of always-on, always-connected handheld devices.

Last year, when the MP3 player was the star, it was surrounded by devices, such as phones and PDAs, that could, in theory, do much more.

This year's show made good on some of those promises.

The most exciting products were not the star of the show, but they were also not the also-rans of last year.

They were simply cool, new gadgets that help us communicate, organise our lives and, of course, play music and games.

The parties are launching their manifestos ahead of the election - with the Tories defending their record on taxation.

The Liberal Democrats have accused the Conservatives of putting the country's finances in jeopardy, while Labour says the Tories are not ambitious enough in their spending plans.

The BBC's political editor, Laura Kuenssberg, says it is an unusual move for opponents to agree on anything, but that the parties are "united" in their criticism.

The Conservative manifesto will be launched on Thursday, with the party defending its record on taxation, saying it has "cut taxes for 30 million people".

The party has come under pressure over the cost of living, with Labour, the Lib Dems and SNP all promising to scrap the rise in National Insurance payments that kicks in this year.

At Prime Minister's Questions, Labour leader Sir Keir Starmer accused the Tories of putting up taxes by £700 a year for anyone on an average wage - £1,500 for families - with the National Insurance rise, VAT going up on household energy bills and higher council tax bills.

He asked: "Isn't the truth that millions of working people are worried they are going to see an increase in their taxes under the Conservatives?"

But Boris Johnson insisted the government was "cutting taxes for everyone".

The prime minister said: "We are helping people on low incomes by reducing the basic rate of tax, we are helping people with the cost of fuel by reducing the surcharge on fuel and we are helping young people with the cost of living by increasing the National Living Wage, but Labour wants to put up taxes."

In his reply, Sir Keir again accused the prime minister of breaking his promise not to put up taxes, saying: "Taxes are going up next year by £700. That is the cost of living crisis created by this prime minister."

Mr Johnson insisted that he had not raised taxes, and that all government budgets were set out in the autumn statement.

Former Labour Cabinet Minister Peter Mandelson has warned the BBC that it risks "getting into a proper mess" if it does not tackle the "dark forces" arrayed against it.

In an interview with the BBC's Newsnight programme, Lord Mandelson said the corporation should stand up more for itself and not be "cowed" by critics.

The BBC should also "drop Jonathan Ross" because he was the "wrong person to hire in the first place", he added.

Lord Mandelson was speaking as the BBC prepared to announce the findings of its own inquiry into the Ross and Brand show.

The corporation has been under pressure from the government after the BBC admitted it had overspent on Brand and Ross by £350,000.

The BBC has agreed to make savings of £2.25bn over the next six years, but the government has said it will impose top-up fees for the BBC if it does not make bigger cuts.

Speaking to Newsnight's Jeremy Paxman, Lord Mandelson said the BBC should not get "drawn into this endless... discussion about whether the licence fee should be cut or whether top-up fees should be introduced".

He added: "The BBC should stand up for itself and say... we are entitled to the licence fee we currently receive.

"We are the world's greatest broadcaster, we are entitled to that and frankly the government ought to stand up for the BBC and say... you lot in Westminster, you lot in Whitehall, you lot in media city, you just shut up, you leave the BBC alone.

"And if the government won't do that, the BBC should say it loud and clear itself. That's what I would do if I were running the BBC."

On whether the BBC should drop Jonathan Ross, he said: "In the end, it's [BBC director general] Mark Thompson's decision.

"But my own view is that Jonathan Ross was the wrong person to hire in the first place and now is the time to move on.

"Because frankly, the BBC... risks getting into a proper mess on this if it doesn't sort it out soon."

On whether the BBC should cut back on its spending on TV talent, he said: "Of course they should. They should hire better, they should hire equally well-known, equally talented people but pay them less.

Germany has called for sweeping changes to how the European Union operates, in a bid to accelerate decision-making and strengthen its economic sovereignty.

Outlining a series of proposals in a government paper, Berlin said the EU's existing system was "not working well".

The plans include allowing some member states to team up in coalitions to advance their interests.

Germany's Foreign Minister Heiko Maas, whose country currently holds the EU's rotating presidency, said the bloc needed to become more "proud" of its achievements and more "capable" of acting.

The paper calls for the existing system of requiring every single member state to agree on all major decisions to be replaced by what it calls a "double majority".

In future, key decisions would have to be agreed by a simple majority of member states - representing at least 65% of the EU's population.

Currently, all member states have an equal say on all matters, regardless of their size.

But the system has become increasingly difficult to manage, with the EU facing a series of major crises, from the debt crisis in the eurozone to the coronavirus pandemic and the conflict in Ukraine.

"We have to be honest: The EU's decision-making machinery is not working well," the paper said.

"It is too complex, it is taking too long and it is not able to react quickly enough to new challenges."

The paper also calls for the EU to be more "economically sovereign" and to do more to reduce its dependence on foreign suppliers, especially in key sectors such as energy.

To achieve this, it suggests the EU should become more competitive by improving its innovation and technology performance.

And it says the bloc should do more to increase its domestic production of renewable energy, as part of its transition towards a carbon-neutral future.

BBC Sport - Andy Murray's hopes of a deep run at the Australian Open received a boost with the announcement that Dan Evans and Kyle Edmund have received wild cards for the Grand Slam.

British number one Evans and world number 50 Edmund join Murray and Cameron Norrie in a strong contingent from these shores in Melbourne.

Evans' ranking of 33 is higher than his career-high of 39, while Edmund has climbed from 68th to 50th in the world since September.

The wild cards for Evans and Edmund were announced at lunchtime on Sunday UK time ahead of the 2 February start of the 2022 tournament.

Australian Open tournament director Craig Tiley said the British pair were given the wild cards because "they help elevate the tournament".

"We get to see some amazing matches and with the way they can play, we feel they can go deep into the second week."

Evans, who has earned £1.8m this year, reached the third round of the Australian Open in 2017 and won the ATP title in Melbourne in 2017.

He said: "I am really excited to be playing in Melbourne again. I have great memories from winning here in 2017 and I can't wait to step back out on court at Melbourne Park."

Edmund, 25, has yet to progress beyond the third round of a Grand Slam but reached the semi-finals of the Australian Open in 2018.

He is ranked ahead of Evans and has earned £2.5m this year, with his best result a run to the final of the ATP event in Vienna in October.

"I have good memories of playing in Australia and hopefully I can play well again," said Edmund.

"I'd like to thank Craig and all those involved for the opportunity."

It is the first time in a decade that Britain has had four representatives in the main draw of a Grand Slam.

The last time was at Wimbledon in 2013 when Murray, Evans, Edmund and James Ward were all in action.

Murray is still on the comeback trail following surgery on his hip in January 2019 and having had two rounds of chemotherapy after testing positive for Covid-19 in March 2020.

The three-time Grand Slam champion has been handed a wild card for the Australian Open main draw by the tournament organisers but his ranking of 135 means he is likely to need to win two qualifying matches to progress.

Tan, who appointed Warnock in 2011, said the 70-year-old might struggle to handle "big names" in the future.

The Welsh side avoided relegation from the Premier League on the final day of the season despite finishing 18th in the table.

They have already announced the departures of midfielder Peter Whittingham and goalkeeper David Marshall, who are out of contract.

"But when it comes to the players, I have never brought a player in that was not of value. That is a little bit disrespectful."

Tan bought a controlling interest in Cardiff City in 2010 and, at the end of the following season, sacked manager Dave Jones - who had led the club to the Championship play-off final - despite having previously said he would remain in charge regardless of the outcome.

Canadian tennis player Bianca Andreescu has pulled out of the Australian Open, with a leg injury that she says was caused by "complications" from a blood clot in her arm.

The men's champion at the 2019 US Open - who had been scheduled to play in Melbourne on Monday - said the clot had been "triggered by a recent medication for a liver condition that I have been treating".

Canadian tennis player Bianca Andreescu has withdrawn from the Australian Open with a leg injury
The Toronto native, 24, said she was "devastated" not to be able to play in the Grand Slam event.

"I'm incredibly disappointed to not be able to play today," she wrote on Instagram.

"I was really excited to make my comeback today, but unfortunately, I will not be able to play.

"On the advice of my medical team, I have been advised that I cannot risk the possibility of an adverse event occurring during play that could cause me to miss out on the rest of the season."

Andreescu - who has not played a competitive match since September - said she began feeling "sharp pain" in her leg during training and a MRI scan on Saturday evening local time revealed a "small lesion" on her lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.

She wrote: "To manage this condition, I will be taking some time off to recover once I return to Canada.

"This unfortunately means that I will not be able to play in this year's Australian Open.

"I'm devastated by this news as I was really excited to make my comeback especially at one of my favourite tournaments, but I promise I will be back stronger and better than ever."

Andreescu won her first Grand Slam in New York three years ago and followed that with a victory at the WTA Finals in Shenzhen.

But the Canadian has been affected by a series of injuries since, prompting her to announce in September that year she was taking a break from the sport "to recover mentally and physically".

Prior to the Australian Open, Andreescu - who has been ranked as high as fourth in the world - said she was "hungry for more".

Zambia's president has said he is "confident and cautious" as the country becomes the first on the African continent to receive COVID-19 vaccines through the UN-backed COVAX scheme.

Ruling party leader Edgar Lungu received his shot live on TV on Friday, urging others to follow suit.

But the event itself was not without controversy. Main opposition leader Hakainde Hichilema criticised the handling of the process, and questioned the timing of the president's vaccination.

Mr Hichilema, who disputed last year's presidential election results, said the vaccine should have been administered at a hospital, rather than at State House.

He added that as the leader of an opposition party, he did not believe Mr Lungu should have been given "preferential treatment" in receiving the vaccine ahead of healthcare workers.

Hasn't Zambia had its share of tragedy?

Yes. Zambia is among the African countries that have suffered countless tragedies as a result of the pandemic.

It has recorded more than 27,000 cases and over 220 deaths - but the actual numbers are thought to be higher as testing is limited.

In the capital, Lusaka, mortuaries ran out of space for bodies in December, and funeral parlours say they are overrun.

Reverend Pauline Nalley, a senior administrator at the University of Zambia, said she had seen an increase in the number of funerals at her church.

She said it was a race against time to bury bodies because of the rapid decomposition of the deceased.

Lactalis' boss said he was "sincerely sorry" for the "injustice" suffered by thousands of investors who lost savings in the dairy group's financial crisis two decades ago.

French police have now released Lactalis chairman Emmanuel Besnier, who was being held in custody over the scandal, after he was questioned for two days.

Mr Besnier was detained on Tuesday under a European warrant. 

The detention order was issued in 2013 when Italian authorities requested his arrest for alleged fraud in the collapse of the dairy group Parmalat two decades ago. 

Parmalat, once one of the world's biggest dairy producers, collapsed in 2003 after admitting it had found €14bn ($15.3bn) hole in its accounts through the systematic use of fraudulent accounting.

The company, which operated in more than 30 countries, was placed into administration and eventually split up. 

Thousands of investors lost money, including small shareholders and pensioners who were unable to recover their savings.

"I wish to tell the thousands of small investors in Italy and elsewhere in Europe who were harmed that I am sincerely sorry they suffered such injustice," Mr Besnier said in a statement released by his lawyers on Thursday.

He said he had always declared that he had "nothing to do" with the events which led to the crisis and that he had "never been charged with any offence in France or elsewhere".

Mr Besnier described his detention as "a mistake" and said he had immediately agreed to be interviewed by police once he was made aware of the warrant.

His lawyers said that he had been released without any charges being laid and that he would soon return to France. 

A spokesperson for the Italian justice ministry said Mr Besnier could still face an extradition request from Italy in the coming days.
