ANKARA (BBC) - Turkey's government has approved a draft law that would pave the way for Kurdish parties to enter parliament - if approved in a referendum.

The bill would change the way Turkey's political parties are formed, allowing them to appeal to voters from a specific ethnic background.

Prime Minister Tayyip Erdogan has promised to deliver "a new, democratised political system" to voters in the referendum.

The changes would also limit the powers of the president - albeit after Erdogan himself assumed the office.

The draft law approved by ministers on Tuesday will be put to a referendum, probably in March.

If passed, it would make Turkey the latest country to adopt what politicians call a "proportional representation" system.

Currently, parties in Turkey elect MPs from closed lists of candidates, a system that often results in vote-winning parties winning far more seats than their share of the vote.

The new system would lower the threshold for winning seats in parliament - currently set at 10% - giving smaller parties a better chance of representation.

One of the consequences of the change would be to allow the pro-Kurdish Democratic Society Party (DTP) - closed down last year for alleged ties with the rebel Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) - to re-enter parliament.

The DTP won almost six percent of the vote in 2007, but took no seats because the 10% threshold ruled them out.

The change is one element in a package of reforms put forward by the government designed to address concerns over Turkey's democracy.

Another element, also to be put to a referendum, would change the way the president is elected, reducing the powers of the office.

The changes were agreed in a consensus between the government and opposition parties, but critics say the reforms do not go far enough.

"This system will bring about change, a new, democratised political system," Prime Minister Tayyip Erdogan said last week.

"Our people will decide on this change, on these reforms in a referendum," he said. "I am confident our people will give the right decision."

The reforms have been closely watched by Europe, as Turkey seeks to begin accession talks with the European Union.

The EU has made clear that it wants to see the democratisation package passed into law.

Sara Nathan has told how her father, who died in 2016, "would be thrilled" with the progress of their Indian beer venture.

Sara Nathan is the daughter of Stanley Metcalf Nathan, who founded the company in 1740.

S&N said it would invest in a new brewery and a "state-of-the-art" bottle manufacturing plant in the southern Indian state of Karnataka.

The firm did not reveal an exact location for the new facilities, but said they would be developed in "close proximity" to its existing brewery near Bangalore, the state's capital.

'Metcalf's moment'

Ms. Nathan, S&N's interim chief executive, said: "My father, who passed away in 2016, would be thrilled with how well our Indian business has performed.

"This feels like Metcalf's moment - investing in our Indian beer business to create a long-term sustainable future for our flagship ale brand, Newcastle Brown Ale."

She said the company had undertaken "extensive due diligence" before deciding to invest.

"This includes comprehensive research into the premium beer segment in India, which demonstrates the potential for our business to continue to grow sustainably."

S&N's Indian subsidiary, United Breweries, is the country's second-largest beer company by market share.

It was founded in 1915 by Sir Thomas Leishman, a Scottish businessman who settled in Bangalore.

It is now controlled by his descendants, who are joint shareholders with the Nathens and the Primos in S&N.

The dollar's decline ahead of this week's G7 meeting in London prompted European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde to blame the US for not doing enough to bolster the world's primary reserve currency, whose global strength is seen as vital for economic stability.

"It is more reflective of the US economic situation and the US economic policy choices than it is on the international community and on the choices that have been made abroad," she said.

Ms. Lagarde, who will step down as ECB president at the end of her eight-year term in October, made the remarks in a question-and-answer session in the Dutch parliament.

Her comments come as central bankers and finance ministers from the G7 group of wealthy nations meet in London on Thursday and Friday.

The US dollar is widely regarded as a haven currency, and its decline has been accelerated by Russia's invasion of Ukraine. This has led to a marked increase in volatility across financial markets.

A weakening dollar can help US exporters and reduce imported inflation, but it can also lead to financial instability in some emerging markets that have borrowed in dollars.

It can also roil global markets as investors reassess what is supposed to be the safest asset of all. This creates problems for markets such as government bonds.

Interest rate differentials between the US and other major economies have been a key driver of the dollar's decline.

The US central bank, the Federal Reserve, is expected to raise interest rates by 50 basis points next month, but the ECB is not expected to raise rates at all this year.

In the Netherlands, Ms. Lagarde also spoke about the importance of the independence of central banks.

She said that political interference in central banking had led in the past "to disastrous consequences".

She cited the example of the Austrian central bank before the First World War and more recent examples of "political interference leading to outcomes that many would regret".

Tech giant Google's parent company Alphabet has seen its shares drop 2.3% after its employees were offered the chance to sell shares worth up to $45,000 each.

The sale came as part of a pre-arranged trading plan, which lets staff sell a certain number of shares at pre-set times.

It comes as several tech firms, including Google, face challenges due to the economic crisis sparked by the Covid-19 pandemic and changing consumer habits.

Alphabet's shares were down ($15.90) to $695.85 in afternoon trading in New York.

The stock has fallen substantially from last year when it was trading above $1,300.

"That's a reflection of the broader sell-off in tech stocks that we've seen this year," said Greg Martin, co-founder of Alphabet employee advocacy group MOVE.

He added that the trading plan had been in place for a while and was not a result of current economic conditions.

In a note to employees, Alphabet and Google's chief financial officer Ruth Porat said that staff need to exercise caution when trading shares, "given the volatility in the stock market".

"While we are in a period of uncertainty, it's important to remember that our business fundamentals remain strong," she wrote.

The drop in Alphabet's share price has been driven partly by the advertising market being hit by the pandemic as companies cut marketing budgets.

Google makes the majority of its money from advertising and like much of the tech sector is facing questions over its business practices.

The company has been the subject of antitrust lawsuits from the US government and regulators in India and Europe, who say it has abused its dominance in search and other areas.

The company's YouTube subsidiary is also facing questions over its role in political campaigning ahead of the US presidential election in November.

Last week, US President Donald Trump accused the video-sharing platform of "tying" political ad placements to favourable news coverage.

YouTube rejected the claim and said it had introduced measures to protect against misinformation in political ads.

A French billionaire has challenged the London Stock Exchange's (LSE) rejection of his £1.5bn ($2.1bn) takeover bid.

 Xavier Niel - a telecoms and technology entrepreneur who is also a minority shareholder in the LSE - held talks with the exchange's management on Thursday.

The LSE said earlier this month that Mr. Niel's bid was not in the "best interests" of the company or its shareholders.

Mr. Niel has until 19 October to make an offer or announce a firm intention to make an offer.

The LSE's rejection came after the UK government announced plans to increase its shareholding in the exchange to up to 25% .

The move was part of a plan to keep London as a global financial hub after the UK leaves the European Union.

Stock exchanges in the EU are required to be regulated by the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), and many fear that London will lose its access to the EU single market because of Brexit.

Last week, EU officials also announced that they were working on plans to lure the LSE to Amsterdam.

Why is Mr. Niel interested?

Mr. Niel is the founder of telecoms company Iliad, which operates the low-cost Free Mobile service in France.

He also owns about 4% of the LSE, and is its largest shareholder who is not a member of the exchange's board.

His interest in taking over the exchange has been seen as an attempt to ward off a takeover by the Shanghai Stock Exchange, which last month entered into an agreement to access the LSE's trading technology.

What has the LSE said?

The LSE said it had noted Mr. Niel's statement regarding his meeting with senior management on Thursday and that its response to his proposal "remains the same".

"The London Stock Exchange Group Board is confident that it can deliver greater value for shareholders as a listed company than would be available from the offer," it added in a statement.

The head of the UN's food security agency has warned that billions of dollars of subsidies for fossil fuels are putting healthy food out of the reach of millions of people.

Qu Dongyu, director-general of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), said the subsidies were skewing markets and harming farmers.

He said energy prices were affecting the cost of fertilisers, pesticides and farming equipment.

Mr Dongyu called for the reform of energy subsidies to help protect farmers and consumers.

His comments came as the FAO released its annual State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World report.

It showed that global hunger remains higher than before the Covid-19 pandemic, with around 1 in 10 people - 680 million - going hungry.

The report said hunger had increased in around 40 countries last year, with acute hunger rising in Afghanistan, Ethiopia, Haiti, Somalia and Sudan.

It also warned that other forms of malnutrition - such as obesity - were on the rise, with nearly a billion people overweight.

Mr Dongyu said the cost of fossil fuels was making it impossible for many people to maintain a healthy diet.

"Forty percent of the world's population cannot afford a healthy diet and healthy diets are getting more and more expensive," he said.

"This is not only a crisis of food affordability, but it is also a crisis of affordability of healthy diets and the cost of energy, the cost of fertilisers, the cost of pesticides, the cost of equipment, the cost of logistics and these are all converging and affecting each other."

He said the impact of Russia's invasion of Ukraine - which together account for about 30% of global wheat exports - had played a role in increasing food prices.

The war has also affected fertiliser prices, as Russia is a major exporter of natural gas, which is used to produce fertiliser.

Mr Dongyu called for an end to "distorted and harmful" subsidies for fossil fuels that were benefiting big businesses, and for the money to instead be used to help farmers and consumers.

He said there was a need to support small farmers, who produce most of the world's food and are most vulnerable to food price hikes.

The FAO chief said it was important to ensure farmers received a fair price for what they produced to avoid another "food crisis".

Beijing's government has cancelled a plan to charge drivers per entry into the city's central business district (CBD) after it sparked an angry response from the public.

The scheme, which was supposed to start on Friday, would have charged drivers of non-electric vehicles 3 yuan (£0.32; $0.43) each time they entered the district.

But it was suspended on Tuesday after online criticism and protests.

Many also questioned why two-wheeled motorbikes were not included in the plan.

"I thought Beijing was about to become a world city, but it turns out we're still living in a feudal society where the rich get special treatment," one person wrote on China's Twitter-like Weibo.

Beijing's CBD is home to many upscale shops, offices and government buildings.

Drivers entering the area in Beijing's east would have had to pay the charge every working day. The city government says the fees were intended to reduce traffic congestion and pollution in the area.

But the plan quickly sparked an online backlash, with many complaining that they were being charged for going to work.

On Sunday, a group of a few dozen people gathered at a major road in the CBD to protest the plan, according to a photo blog on Sina Weibo. The blogger said that some protesters were taken away by police.

The city's government announced on Tuesday that the plan had been suspended and that the policy would be revised.

"After listening to opinions…the relevant plan shall be thoroughly revised, and the revision shall be reported to the standing committee of the municipal people's congress for decision," a statement published online said.

The statement also said that the government would crack down on "maliciously fabricating rumours and causing chaos".

But suspending the plan has not quelled all the anger, with many Beijingers complaining that they still had no solution for parking in the area.

"Now I'm happy that the policy has been cancelled, but where are we supposed to park?" one Weibo user wrote.

CHICAGO -(Dow Jones)- A major MCI shareholder is suing to stop the telecommunications company's $37 billion takeover by Verizon Communications (VZ), arguing that the deal undervalues MCI and robs shareholders of a better offer.

The complaint, filed late Friday in Delaware Chancery Court on behalf of shareholder Robert M. Wason, claims that Verizon and MCI violated their fiduciary duties by entering into the merger agreement.

The proposed deal, which was announced Oct. 7, has already been approved by the MCI board and is expected to close by the middle of next year, pending regulatory and shareholder approval.

Mr. Wason, who owns 2.3 million shares of MCI, is seeking an injunction to prevent the companies from proceeding with the merger until they disclose more information about the deal's terms.

His lawyer, David A. Katz, a partner with Cohen Milstein Hausfeld & Toll PLLC, said Monday that they believe MCI's management orchestrated a bidding process that effectively shut out other potential buyers and forced shareholders to accept an unfair price.

"Our allegation is that this process was rigged from the beginning," Mr. Katz said. "The merger agreement contains a $750 million termination fee, which is so high that no other bidder could afford to top Verizon's offer and still expect to make a profit."

An MCI spokesman wasn't immediately available for comment.

Mr. Wason's lawsuit comes after another MCI shareholder, the University of Illinois Board of Trustees, filed a similar complaint against MCI and Verizon in Illinois state court last week.

The University of Illinois, which owns more than 400,000 shares of MCI, is seeking an injunction to stop the merger, as well as unspecified damages.

Like Mr. Wason, the university claims that MCI and Verizon violated their fiduciary duties by agreeing to the deal without shopping around for the highest bidder.

MCI has said it believes the complaints are without merit. Verizon declined to comment on the lawsuits.

Continental warned on Thursday it may run out of cash as the German automotive supplier continued to struggle with a global shortage of semiconductors, which has led to a sharp fall in production.

The news weighed on Continental's shares, which were down 6.5% in early trade, wiping off about €1.6bn ($1.8bn) of the company's market value.

Chief Financial Officer Wolfgang Schäfer said Continental had seen a significant recovery in its operations in the second quarter as lockdowns were eased, including in key markets such as China.

But he said that recovery had stalled in the third quarter due to the shortage of semiconductors, as well as rising costs and supply chain problems that were causing delays in production.

"We currently expect that we will generate positive cash flow in the third quarter, but that this will be significantly lower than in the second quarter," Schäfer said.

"We are doing everything in our power to ensure that Continental does not run out of cash. At the same time, we are making advances in securing additional financing for the company."

 Continental, which is due to report third-quarter results on Oct. 28, had cash and cash equivalents of €4.3bn ($4.9bn) at the end of June.

The automotive industry has been hit by a global shortage of semiconductors, which are key components in electronic devices used in cars, including power steering and cruise control systems.

The problem has led major carmakers such as Volkswagen, Toyota and General Motors to cut production and warn of a significant hit to their sales and profits.

At the same time, automakers are facing rising costs for raw materials such as copper, as well as higher shipping costs.

Continental, which is due to spin off its interior unit, is looking to save costs by cutting jobs and investing in new technologies such as hydrogen fuel cells and battery management systems for electric vehicles.

The company has said it expects the global semiconductor shortage to remain a major challenge through 2023.

A UK-based mining firm is facing a land dispute in Venezuela that has so far seen a British businessman briefly arrested.

Mr. Maduro said the company had not met its commitments to develop the project.

The firm said it had not been notified of any such decision and that it had received no reply to inquiries. 

This week, Gold Reserve's vice president for communications, Keith Edelman, traveled to the country in an attempt to find out more.

On Wednesday, he was briefly arrested by intelligence agents at the airport as he was about to board an airplane back to the US.

The US state department said it was "deeply concerned" about the detention of Edelman and urged Venezuela to guarantee the safety and well-being of all US citizens in the country.

How did the company respond?

Gold Reserve said it was "alarmed" at the arrest and that it had filed a missing persons report for its employees at the mine.

Ask Jeeves has launched a new service which offers small businesses affordable and simple internet advertising.

The company said its new service, Ask Ad Solutions, fills a gap in the market.

"Many small and medium sized businesses have been left behind by the complexities and costs associated with online advertising," said Greg Sterling from the Interactive Advertising Bureau.

"While search engines, online directories and other web sites offer a range of advertising options, they are still difficult and too expensive for many small businesses," he added.

Ask Jeeves said it had developed its new service after research revealed many small businesses felt "left out" of online advertising.

"We saw a need to streamline and simplify the process, making it easy and cost-effective for local businesses to tap into the power of internet search and attract new customers," said Brian McAndrews, chief executive of Ask Jeeves.

"We believe this service will be particularly appealing to the vast majority of local businesses that do not have websites," he added.

Ask Ad Solutions allows businesses to create and place ads on the Ask Jeeves website, and appears alongside search results when users look for a particular product or service in a specific region.

The ads can be updated daily, to feature special offers or to announce new services.

Mr Sterling said small businesses had been "underserved" by the online advertising industry.

"Most local businesses don't have websites, and the cost and complexity of buying online ads has been a barrier for them," he said.

"The reality is that maintaining a consistent and effective ad campaign, even with these simplified tools, requires time and money," said Kate Morris, chief executive of Buy.com.

House prices suffered a festive fall as inflation and rising interest rates put the brakes on the property market, according to an industry survey.

The Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (Rics) said its monthly price balance fell to -44 in December, its lowest level since May 2020.

It said that demand from potential buyers and the number of properties on the market were also flat.

The survey comes a day after data from lender Nationwide showed a surprise pick-up in UK house prices in November, but that was before the Bank of England's recent interest rate rises.

Rics said that, taking into account its monthly data going back to 2006, house prices were now close to "peak-to-trough" trends.

The organisation's chief economist, Simon Rubin, said the market had seen a "significant shift" in the last three months.

"Following a long period of imbalance between demand and supply, the recent rise in interest rates has helped tilt the balance more towards homeowners," he said.

"Going forward, we expect that trend to continue, but it remains too early to say if this will be reflected in a material decline in house prices."

The trend was reflected in all parts of the UK, with London seeing a particularly sharp drop, the survey suggested.

Mr Rubin said that, in the capital, prices were falling at a faster pace than elsewhere in the country "due to the combination of base rate hikes and a shift in investor activity".

He said that, while London house prices had surged in the years after the global financial crisis due to demand from investors, that had now changed.

"Following a trend which began last year, investor demand has now turned into a negative, dragging down activity levels and prices," he added.

But estate agents also reported that buyers were still in the market in December, despite the traditional Christmas slowdown.

The report said that 44% of respondents had seen an increase in the number of properties for sale, while 11% said that figure had decreased.

That was the lowest proportion of respondents reporting a fall in supply since January 2015, it said.

The UK government will announce a reduction in the legal driving limit for alcohol in England and Wales, the BBC can reveal.

It says the move, to cut the drink-drive limit to 50mg of alcohol per 100ml of blood, will save up to 95 lives a year.

The current limit, of 80mg, is one of the highest in Europe.

The planned change, to take effect in spring 2022, has been welcomed by road safety and medical groups.

But the British Beer and Pub Association said the move would punish responsible drinkers.

The Department for Transport said the reduction would bring England and Wales into line with the other devolved nations of Scotland and Northern Ireland, where the limit was reduced to 50mg in December 2014.

The new limit will apply to motorists in England and Wales who drive on Sunday morning, after a Saturday night out.

The government estimates that the current limit of 80mg sees an estimated 300 people killed in alcohol-related crashes each year.

It says this could be reduced by a fifth, saving some 95 lives annually.

Its head of road safety, Nick Lloyd, said: "We have been campaigning for this for a long time because we know it will save lives.

The British Medical Association (BMA) said it welcomed the "common-sense move".

The UK has been refusing asylum to some of the world's most vulnerable people almost every 11 minutes on average since the start of the pandemic, according to a leading charity.

Refugee Council analysis of government data obtained through a freedom of information request showed that between March 2020 and March 2022, the UK refused asylum to more than 43,000 people.

The charity said it amounted to a refusal every 11 minutes on average.

The figures also showed a sharp rise in the number of people who had successfully claimed asylum in the UK - rising from 2,283 in 2019-20 to 10,661 in 2020-21.

The Refugee Council said this showed that judge's decisions were being made "more quickly" and were "largely in favour" of asylum seekers.

The Home Office said it would not comment on the accuracy of the figures as it was due to reply to the freedom of information request shortly.

But it said it was important to distinguish between those making legitimate claims and those who attempted to "abuse the system".

"We have stopped criminals, people who've served a prison sentence or been convicted of a serious crime in their home country, travelling to the UK anonymously to claim asylum and bypassing normal security checks," it said in a statement.

"Last year we introduced major reforms to the asylum system to make it fairer and faster, including introducing a five-year time limit on asylum claims and providing certainty to those with successful claims to stay in the UK."

The charity's analysis showed that the largest group of people who had successfully claimed asylum in the UK were from Iran, with 4,551 granted permission to stay in 2020-21.

This was followed by Syria (2,730), Myanmar (1,510), Iraq (1,447) and Eritrea (1,081).

The figures also showed a sharp rise in the number of people who had their asylum claims rejected after attending a hearing - rising from 1,408 in 2019-20 to 8,429 in 2020-21.

The Refugee Council said its analysis showed "a high number of people who are given the right to remain in the UK are only given that right after a decision by a judge".

"Given how few people are arriving in the UK, it is clear the government can afford to give people the time to tell their stories and have their claims properly assessed," it added.

Former British prime minister Tony Blair has said the deal between the European Union and Turkey to restart migrant talks is "a very substantial step forward".

Mr Blair, the Middle East envoy for the EU and United Nations, said the accord offered hope for refugees.

His comments came as leaders prepared to meet in Brussels to sign the deal.

Turkey's PM said the deal would "turn a new page" in relations with the EU.

Ahmet Davutoglu said Turkey would fulfil its obligations on curbing migration and terrorism.

Under the deal, Turkey will take back migrants who enter Greece illegally, in return for the EU taking in thousands of Syrian refugees directly from Turkey.

It also includes proposals for upgrading Turkey's customs union with the EU and accelerating its EU accession process.

Mr Blair, the former Labour prime minister who led Britain from 1997 to 2007, said the deal addressed the issue of migration while also helping refugees.

He said the agreement offered hope to those refugees who were in Turkey, and the prospect of returning to Syria once the fighting there ended.

"The deal that has been struck is a very substantial step forward in dealing with the crisis that has enveloped the European Union since the beginning of 2015," he said.

"It deals with the issue of migration because it establishes a clear understanding between Europe and Turkey about the return of migrants.

"But it also deals with the issue of refugees because it says to the nearly three million refugees in Turkey that there is now a prospect for them of returning to Syria once the fighting ends."

Mr Blair said the details of the deal - including an action plan on counter-terrorism - were complex, but the overall approach was the right one.

"I think this is a good deal for Europe, it's a good deal for Turkey, it's a good deal for Syria, and therefore it's a good deal for the world," he said.

The deal has been criticised by the opposition in Turkey, human rights groups and some European politicians who say it is too harsh on Turkey and overlooks the human rights concerns in the country.

About 750,000 migrants and refugees have entered Europe since 2015, according to the United Nations.

Tens of thousands of migrants have massed in Greece, caught in limbo as countries farther north in Europe shut their borders.

The Mac mini 2022 has faster M2 processor chips, better graphics and a new discounted price tag.

Both versions come with 256GB of solid state drive storage, twice as much as the previous generation.

"We removed the power adapter, as most customers will already have a USB-C power adapter," said Apple's environment report, published alongside the launch.

It was the year that search engines became infinitely more useful – as personal assistants for the pocket, purse or wrist. 

Five years after Google launched Voice Search on its android platform, the rush to make our machines understand our spoken words hit full stride. Apple joined the fray, Microsoft beefed up Bing and Amazon's Alexa took voice recognition out of our hands and into our homes. 

Voice recognition has been a mainstay of science fiction for decades. But 2015 was the year that the technology broke into the mainstream, transforming the way we interact with machines. 

Voice recognition has been possible in one form or another since the 1980s. But it has taken massive improvements in the accuracy of speech recognition software, the rise of powerful mobile processors, and the arrival of always-on personal assistants for the technology to become part of our daily lives. 

In 2015, these three factors combined to create a perfect storm for voice recognition.

The launch of Apple's Siri on the iPhone in 2011 began the popularization of voice recognition. But Siri's limited capabilities, and the fact that it was primarily a novelty, meant that voice recognition remained a niche technology. 

All that changed in 2015 when Google launched Voice Search on Android. With Google's massive investments in machine learning and speech recognition, Voice Search was incredibly accurate. And with Android's growing market share, it quickly became one of the most widely used voice recognition services.

Voice Search wasn't the only game in town. Microsoft beefed up Bing's voice recognition capabilities, while Amazon's Alexa took the technology out of our hands and into our homes. Alexa became the voice-controlled brain behind the Amazon Echo, a always-on, always listening speaker that acts as a personal assistant and smart home hub.

The impact of these developments is hard to overstate. Voice recognition has transformed the way we interact with machines, moving from a keyboard and mouse to spoken words. It has made our devices more accessible, not just to people with disabilities but to anyone who wants a more intuitive way to use technology. 

And it has opened up new possibilities for how we use technology, from smart homes to wearable devices. It's not too much of a stretch to imagine a future where voice recognition is the primary way we interact with machines. 

2015 was the year that search became personal. And it's a safe bet that voice recognition will continue to play a central role in how we search for information in the years to come.

What high-definition will do to DVDs

If you have a library of DVDs, you might want to think about transferring them to a hard drive before the discs become obsolete.

It's happening already.

Even a modestly-sized HD television will reveal dust particles on the DVD and the blocks of pixels that make up the image.

The picture is often blurred, and there's a softness to the image that is absent from high-definition (HD).

This is not the fault of the DVD format, which is of excellent quality, particularly for the standard definition (SD) television sets for which they were designed.

It's the television that is at fault.

The picture information stored on a DVD is a series of dots, known in the trade as pixels.

In SD, there are 352,000 pixels, or blocks of colour, across the screen, while in HD there are 1,920,000.

That's more than five times as many.

A DVD player sends the information on the disc to a television at a constant rate of 25 megabits per second.

This information includes not only the pixels but also other data, such as sound.

To accommodate all this information, the data is compressed.

When it is decompressed inside the television, the picture is reconstructed from the dots.

Each dot relates to a point on the screen where a beam of light - a pixel - is required.

The position of the pixel and its colour is calculated from the dot.

That's fine for SD television, which has fewer pixels and therefore less information to handle.

But with HD, the television has to calculate almost six times as many positions for the pixels on the screen, and thus needs much more information, or data, from the disc.

The result is that a DVD will not give you a high-definition picture, however good the disc might be.

Some new machines are advertised as up-converting your DVDs, giving you a higher resolution picture.

In fact, they are simply sharpening the image, and the result is often disappointing.

A sharp, crisp HD image is a beauty to behold - but it needs a lot of data.

To get it, you will need to think about copying your DVDs on to a hard drive and compressing them to a format that can be played back through an HD television set.

As voters in Indonesia prepare to vote in the country's presidential election, a look at how ink is used to combat vote rigging.

For election officials, making sure that each vote is cast only once is a perennial problem.

But in many countries in Asia, a simple solution has been found - marking voters' fingers with ink.

The ink is usually applied to the finger with a rubber stamp immediately after voting.

And it is usually indelible - designed to last several days. That makes it difficult for people to go and vote again, or vote multiple times for different candidates.

The idea behind it is to make voting more honest.

"There are still people who believe that if they vote many times, then their voice will be heard," said Ahmadi, an election official in Jakarta.

"But that's not true. This is a democratic method, we just need one vote, not many."

Indonesia has used indelible ink in elections since 2004. The ink - a deep purple - is applied to the finger using a rubber stamp, with the voter then pressing their finger onto a piece of paper to leave a print as proof.

He said in a statement: "It's time for me to move on.

They scored their first big hit in 1996 with the album Korn, which featured the single " Freak on a Leash".

That was the first of a series of Top 10 hits for the group, whose core members are Jonathan Davis, James "Munky" Shaffer and Reginald "Fieldy" Arvizu.

Welch, who is also known as "Head", joined the group in 1998 after the departure of their original guitarist, Brian "Crash" Dickey.

Home phones face uncertain future as mobiles dominate communications

The demise of the landline in the UK is confirmed in a new study which shows it has dropped below 50% of households for the first time.

Industry regulator Ofcom said phones plugged into the wall were now in just under 50% of homes. It said this trend was likely to continue as mobile phone use exploded.

The study also revealed that the typical UK adult now owns 1.75 mobile phones.

Ofcom said this "exploding" use of mobiles had promoted a culture of "continuous connectivity".

The regulator's annual Communications Market Report found 47.7% of households only have a mobile phone and no landline.

That figure has jumped from 39% in 2012.

Ofcom said in 1998 - the first year it conducted the survey - that just 22% of households only had a mobile.

"Landlines are clearly becoming a thing of the past," said James Barford, author of the Ofcom report.

"In 1998, the majority of phones in the UK were landlines, with only 22% of households having mobiles as their only phone.

"Fast forward to today and the situation has radically changed - with nearly half of all households now relying solely on mobiles."

The study also revealed that 92% of people now own a mobile, a jump from 88% last year.

This proliferation of mobiles has helped fuel a 28% jump in the amount of time each day that people spend on phones - from 88 minutes to 114 minutes each day over the past year, Ofcom said.

The study also showed that texting is the most popular activity on mobiles - one in five texts are sent or received every day, with the typical mobile user sending 41 texts each month.

In contrast, the number of voice calls made on mobiles has fallen for the first time, dropping from 102 calls each month to 96.

Ofcom said this showed that voice calls were "becoming a less important part of the mobile experience".

The study also revealed that nearly three-quarters (71%) of people have a smartphone, while 4G coverage now reaches 90% of the UK population.

But the report warned that not everyone had benefited from the move to digital, with 10% of the UK's geographical area - land and sea - lacking 4G coverage.

Air China has launched its $1.3bn (£820m) float on the London Stock Exchange, becoming the first Chinese airline to list in the UK.

The company sold about 4.5 billion shares at 67p each, valuing the total stock at £802 million.

The shares began trading in London on Wednesday morning, and were trading up 3% at 69.75p at 1305 GMT.

The flotation is a rare example of a Chinese company choosing to list in London following a string of high-profile cancellations.

There are growing concerns in the UK that Beijing is trying to discourage Chinese firms from listing in London, which until recently was the world's most popular venue for initial public offerings (IPOs).

In the six months to the end of June this year, a total of 13 Chinese firms cancelled London IPO plans, according to data from Refinitiv, higher than the 11 that scrapped them in the first six months of last year.

Air China's listing comes as the UK government has been trying to calm investor jitters ahead of Brexit on 31 October.

The airline, which has a fleet of 580 aircraft, is headquartered in Beijing and is a member of the Star Alliance.

It flies to more than 170 destinations, with a particular focus on China's fast-growing domestic market.

Air China's listing is a secondary listing, with the company already listed on the Hong Kong and Shanghai stock exchanges.

The firm said it would not be raising any new money from the London float, but would instead be allowing existing shareholders to sell their shares.

About eight per cent of the company is being made available in the float, which is expected to raise about £65 million for the selling shareholders.

The company's two largest shareholders are the China National Aviation Holding Company Ltd, which owns 28.1%, and Citic Group Corporation, which owns 18.5%.

The airline has been hit by the coronavirus pandemic, which has led to a sharp decline in air travel.

In the first half of the year, it carried just over 11 million passengers, down 55% from a year earlier.

It reported a net loss of about CNY2.5 billion (£293 million) in the first half of 2020, compared with a net profit of CNY1.3 billion (£162 million) a year earlier.

MPs have questioned the judge's decision to hand down a life sentence to a man who murdered an MP.

WA Corke, who killed Jo Cox, was given a minimum term of 35 years in December.

The Sentencing Council said it will examine whether the sentencing guidelines for murder are "fit for purpose".

Its statement came after a number of MPs raised concerns over the "vague" and "incomprehensible" law.

The Labour MP for Batley and Spen, who was pregnant, was attacked by Corke in Birstall in June 2016.

He was charged with her murder and the murder of Labour councillor Bernard Carter outside a library in Birstall.

At the time of the attack, Corke gave his name as "Death to Traitors, Freedom for Britain", which was also written on his baseball bat.

He was sentenced to life imprisonment with a minimum term of 35 years, which is variable and can be increased or decreased depending on behaviour.

The judge said the minimum term would have been 30 years but it was increased because the murder was "a terrorist act" and carried out "in pursuance of extremist ideology".

On Friday, Labour MP Yvette Cooper, who chairs the Home Affairs Select Committee, tabled a debate on the sentencing guidelines for murder, calling them "vague and incomprehensible".

She said the law needed to be changed so the public could have confidence it acted as a deterrent.

Her comments were echoed by Tory MP Bob Seely, who said the law was an "absolute mess" and needed to be simplified.

The Sentencing Council said it will examine the sentencing guidelines over the next few months "to ensure they are fit for purpose and clearly articulated".

"This review will commence shortly and the council will engage with stakeholders ahead of publishing any changes to the guidelines," it added in a statement.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: "The justice system has always allowed for sentences for violent crimes to be increased or decreased in accordance with behaviour, and this was a rare case because of the terrorist connection."

They added that the ministry had asked the Sentencing Council to "keep the guidelines under review".

Britain's former Prime Minister Tony Blair has urged the current government to delay the next budget until after the local elections in May.

The ex-Labour leader, who led his party to a landslide victory in 1997, wrote in The Times that the "budget should be after the local elections".

His comments came as Prime Minister Gordon Brown prepared to fly to Washington for talks with President Barack Obama on the global financial crisis.

In his first major interview since leaving office 10 years ago, Mr Blair told the BBC that the "world has changed" and that Britain had to become "more adaptable" to deal with the "new world".

The MP for Sedgefield also said the government had to become "more decisive" in improving public services.

In his Times article, Mr Blair also warned that the upcoming budget - expected on 22 April - would be seen as a "pre-election budget" whatever the government said.

He wrote: "The budget should be after the local elections.

"Frankly it's inevitable that it will be seen as a pre-election budget - Labour panicking as the polls move against it."

Mr Blair also warned that the economic downturn would hit the party at the polls - but that Labour could still win if it pursued the "right policies".

He wrote: "The downturn will affect Labour, but elections are not only about the state of the economy.

"They are about which party has the right approach for the times we live in - and Labour does."

Mr Blair also warned his old ally Mr Brown that he should not copy the "big tent" approach of the Tory leader, David Cameron.

He said that the "risk" to Labour was that it would "copy the Tory approach" and that this would be a "recipe for electoral oblivion".

The ex-PM added that Mr Cameron's approach was to "move to the centre ground and then sweep up the centre ground as the Liberal Democrats collapse".

But he said that if Labour did the same it would mean the party had "given up" on the values that it stood for.

Hollywood studios are to sue individuals who watch copyrighted material without paying, regardless of whether they actually download it.

The Motion Picture Association (MPA) said it would focus on "online marketplaces of infringement".

The announcement comes after six major film studios sued Dragon Media, which operates several websites offering movies and TV shows for download.

The legal action has been welcomed by the British Phonographic Industry (BPI), which said it would "shine a light" on the issue.

In a statement, the MPA said: "Given the billions of dollars lost each year to piracy, legal action is appropriate.

"We intend to step up our efforts to go after the marketplaces, rather than the end user."

It said that legal action would "only be taken against sites that demonstrate a clear intent to infringe".

The MPA, which represents six major film studios including Sony and Warner Bros, did not name the sites it intended to target.

But in its legal complaint against Dragon Media, it named several sites, including Movielinkr, Movieparadise, and Watchmoviesfree.

These include torrent websites, streaming services, and sites offering movies and TV shows to download.

The MPA claimed that all the sites named "collectively receive tens of millions of visitors each month".

"We recognise that the internet gives consumers incredible choice and easy access to a wide array of legal movie and TV content," said Chris Marcich, chairman and chief executive of the MPA.

"Unfortunately, it also provides a gateway for criminal organisations to exploit the hard work and creativity of those who work in the motion picture industry."

The MPA has previously sued individuals in the UK who it accused of downloading films, including a man from Norwich who was ordered to pay £16,000 in damages.

However, the focus on "online marketplaces" rather than individuals marks a shift in strategy.

The British Phonographic Industry (BPI), which represents the UK's recorded music industry, said it welcomed the announcement.

"We have long argued that the operators of these sites need to be held accountable," said BPI chief executive Geoff Taylor.

"The action taken by the MPA is a welcome step forward in shining a light on the extent of illegal online infringement, and those who enable it."

Dragon Media did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

Greek pole vaulters Ekaterina Stefanidi and Andrej Melu have had their appeals against suspensions from the sport's governing body, cleared by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas).

Stefanidi, who won gold at Rio 2016, and Melu had been suspended by the International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) in June last year for allegedly violating anti-doping rules.

The IAAF said at the time that the athletes had allegedly missed four out-of-competition tests between June 2017 and January 2018.

But Cas said the suspensions were "not necessary" and that there was "insufficient evidence" that the athletes had ever missed a test.

In a statement, Cas said the IAAF's "failing to properly serve notices" to the athletes for the tests in question was an "obvious" and "critical" flaw in the process.

Both athletes have consistently denied doping violations and have said they were not at the addresses provided to the doping control officers on the day of the alleged missed tests.

Cas' ruling said the athletes - who have been cleared to return to competition immediately - had provided "reliable telephone data" to show they could not have been at the addresses provided to doping control officers on the days of the tests.

The athletics body said it would not appeal against the Cas' decision.

In a statement, Stefanidi, who also won bronze at London 2012, said she was "delighted" with the outcome.

"I have said from the beginning that this case was not about whether I was a clean athlete or not, but about the procedures that should be followed in anti-doping," she said.

"Unfortunately, these were not followed and this decision shows that. I'm looking forward to getting back to training and competing again as soon as possible."

Mikhail Khodorkovsky is seeking $28bn in compensation for his firm's breakup and for being detained and jailed for a decade.

Yukos, once Russia's largest oil company, was broken up after being hit with huge tax bills.

Mr Khodorkovsky said the suit was "to defend my good name and my rights".

The suit claims that Russia violated the Energy Charter, a global energy treaty, by expropriating Yukos.

"I decided to file a claim today to defend my good name and my rights, as well as the rights of all Yukos shareholders," Mr Khodorkovsky said at the ICSID.

"I hope that the Russian authorities will realise that their unlawful behaviour has consequences."

Yukos, once the largest oil producer in Russia, was broken up after the government issued huge tax claims against it.

The firm owed billions in back taxes, according to the Russian authorities, although Yukos said the claims were politically motivated.

Yukos' assets were sold to state oil company Rosneft and private firm Gazprom Neft.

Mr Khodorkovsky, who had employed former Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev as a consultant, was Russia's richest man at the time of his arrest in 2003.

He was found guilty of fraud and tax evasion and sentenced to 10 years in jail.

He was released in 2013 and flew to Switzerland, where he had lived prior to his imprisonment.

The Russian government has previously indicated it would not recognise any claims by Yukos.

"The suit will not be without consequences for Khodorkovsky himself," said Vladimir Milov, a former deputy energy minister and an adviser to Mr Khodorkovsky.

"He is not any more a Russian citizen, but the chances are high that he will not be able to travel to Russia anyway. So it is not a matter of choice for him."

Richest 1% of Colombia's population has grabbed nearly half the money set aside for the nation's anti-poverty programme, alarming officials in a country where wealth inequality is among the widest in the world.

The enriched families withdrew nearly $750m (£656m) from the so-called "solidarity dividend" over the past six years.

The dividend is paid by the government from taxes on the nation's largest banks and telephone and utilities companies.

It is meant to help some of Colombia's neediest citizens.

But the fund has instead become a windfall for the wealthy, according to the head of the national tax office, Juan Carlos Velez.

"This is unacceptable," he told local media. "We are going to implement measures to avoid this happening again."

The fund was set up more than 20 years ago as part of a landmark peace deal between the government and guerrilla group, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc).

But in recent years the rules governing the programme have been loosened and the money is now used by some as an alternative pension scheme, or to pay for private education and healthcare.

The head of the tax office plans to restrict the use of the funds, and increase controls over them.

Several former directors of the fund have been accused of taking bribes in exchange for allowing wealthy Colombians to withdraw money.

One former official was arrested last week as part of the investigation.
The fund is officially called the Solidarity Intergenerational Savings Programme, and was modelled on a similar scheme in Chile.

It is funded by a tax on the largest local and foreign companies operating in Colombia. The money is meant to incentivise businesses to invest in the country.

Colombia has one of the highest rates of wealth inequality in the world, according to the World Inequality Report 2022.

The report found that the top 1% of earners in the country earn more than 20% of the total national income.

Drink driving 'a diversion' from dangerous drugs

A public health expert has said that enforcing laws against drink driving is "a diversion" from dealing with the much greater dangers posed by drugs.

Prof David Nutt said that the focus on drink driving "distorts" public awareness of the risks on the roads.

He said most accidents were caused by drivers on legal drugs, particularly benzodiazepines, found in prescription drugs such as Valium.

The professor of neuropsychopharmacology said traffic officers should "start looking for drugs in the same way" as they do for alcohol.

Prof Nutt's comments come after a man was arrested this week for allegedly driving whilst over the legal limit for cannabis.
The driver, who crashed into a parked car and then a tree, said he felt "uncomfortable" driving as he was high, but that it was "not illegal".

Police said they believed to be the first person in the UK to be arrested for drug-driving.
The government has announced that laws will be introduced next year to criminalise the behaviour.

Prof Nutt, who was sacked as the government's chief drug adviser for stating that taking ecstasy was no more dangerous than riding a horse, said current policies on drug driving were "a complete waste of time".

"We have got a really serious problem with drug driving but because it's a difficult problem to solve we are not going to solve it by pretending it's not there with another diversion on drink driving," he said.

"We need to be a lot more honest with people. Most of the drugs which are causing problems on the road are legal drugs and the police need to start looking for drugs in the same way they look for alcohol."

Prof Nutt said the greatest threat to road safety was the combination of benzodiazepines and alcohol, followed by anti-depressants and cannabis.

The professor, who is also the chairman of the Independent Scientific Committee on Drugs, said drug driving was "a far greater problem" than drink driving.

He said: "The problem is it's difficult to do because most drugs are legal.

"The second thing is it's very difficult to measure drugs in the body in the same way you can measure alcohol in the body."

Prof Nutt said random testing of drivers, similar to that for alcohol, could be a solution but it was "a difficult thing to implement".

New training aid could help golfers improve their swing by enabling them to see and feel the correct movements.

To achieve a better golf swing, you need to maintain flexibility and strengthen the right muscles. However, it can be difficult for beginners to coordinate the movements needed for a perfect swing.

Now help could be at hand thanks to a new training aid that has been compared to having a second pair of hands.

The Moving Mobile helps golfers coordinate the sequence of movements needed for a perfect swing and offers immediate feedback on their posture and position.

 Tested by BBC London's golf enthusiast Justin Webb, the device could help frustrated golfers who are struggling to master the moves needed to hit the ball long and straight.

Initially, it looks like an ordinary club but closer inspection reveals a flexible shaft about two-thirds of the way down.

This moves like a fishing rod, allowing you to feel a slight resistance as you hit imaginary balls.

The heavier end of the shaft must be held firmly with the left hand and the movement of the shaft then helps get the feel of the correct swing motion.

"It's about getting the sensation of the correct move and feel for a better swing," said Peter Dawson, the director of the Golf College in Hertfordshire, who demonstrated the device to BBC London.

"It helps get the feeling of the weight and the timing of the backswing and helps get the transition going from the backswing to the downswing."

The Moving Mobile can help improve a golfer's swing tempo, ensuring it is not too fast or too slow. It can also be used as a warm-up tool before playing a round of golf.

"It's a way of getting that feeling of tempo and rhythm back into the hands," said Mr. Dawson.

"It's a bit like having an extra pair of hands to help you."

The concept is similar to shadow swinging - where you pretend to hit balls to get the correct muscle memory - but offers more feedback on any mistakes.

And unlike a normal club it does not feel unnatural as you can actually feel the shaft bending as you make a swing.

Tata Steel aims to cut up to 15,000 jobs in Britain over the next decade as part of a restructuring plan.

The company, which employs about 20,000 people in the UK, said it had begun consultations that could lead to compulsory redundancies.

Unions said they were "disappointed" and called on the company to improve its offer on jobs and investment.

As part of the plans, Tata Steel is also selling its specialty steel making operation in South Yorkshire. It employs about 1,000 people and the potential buyer has until early October to submit a proposal.

The steelmaker has been hit by the coronavirus pandemic, as well as high energy prices and the closure of its main blast furnace at Port Talbot in south Wales last year.

Port Talbot's future was secured in March when Tata Steel signed a deal with the Welsh government to stay open.

As part of the latest plans, the company is aiming to deliver another £50-65m of annual savings to its European operations by the end of March 2026, on top of the £65m it aims to achieve this year.

Its British operations have been losing £1m a day, with steel demand hit by the recession triggered by the pandemic and global steel over-capacity.

The company said it had begun a consultation with union representatives on proposals that would see it lose a further 7,000 jobs in the UK by the end of the decade, on top of the 8,000 it has already cut over the last 10 years.

It also plans to sell its speciality steels business, which makes steel for the automotive industry, as well as several sites including Teesport, Dalzell and Clydebridge.

Unions have called for the UK government to take action to support the industry.

Community union national officer, Mark Richards, said: "The announcement on possible further reductions is disappointing.

"The company must improve its offer on jobs and investment to justify the faith it wants the government and unions to put in its future. The sector crisis cannot be allowed to continue."

Gareth Stace, director of UK Steel, said: "The UK steel sector is significantly more efficient than our global competitors yet we still lose money making steel here in the UK.

"That is because we pay far higher energy costs and far higher carbon costs than our competitors. That is why we are saying to the government they need to take action to help the sector."

The future of the Scottish fishing industry has been assessed by a group of MPs.

The Scottish Affairs Committee concluded that it did not support the UK government's plan to hand management of fishing quotas to an independent Scottish state.

The UK government plans to publish a fisheries bill within the next year, which would pave the way for the devolution of fishing quotas - a move supported by the Scottish government.

But the cross-party committee said there was a lack of evidence that divided management of fishing quotas would benefit the industry.

The committee's report also called for a clearer picture of the future UK-Scotland relationship in the wake of the Brexit deal.

And it recommended that the two governments reach an agreement that would allow Scottish fishermen to continue to access fishing grounds in Norwegian and Icelandic waters.

Committee chairman Pete Wishart said the report was concerned that the UK government's approach to fisheries management was "too narrowly focused" on the question of quota only.

"There is a lack of evidence to demonstrate that dividing up the management of fishing quotas between the UK and an independent Scottish state will deliver tangible benefits for the Scottish fishing industry," he said.

"Similarly, the impact that divided management will have on fisheries science is unclear.

"We heard concerns that there is a risk of fisheries science being compromised if the UK and Scottish governments collect data and carry out assessments separately.

"The UK government must urgently address these concerns as part of its fisheries bill, due to be published this year."

Mr Wishart added that there were still significant questions about the future UK-Scotland relationship, following the end of the Brexit transition period.

He said it was vital that an agreement which allowed Scottish fishermen to continue to access fishing grounds in Norwegian and Icelandic waters was reached.

"Both the UK and Scottish governments need to work together to resolve the issues that have been raised by the fishing industry and ensure that the sector gets the best possible deal in the post-Brexit era," he said.

The report comes after the committee visited harbours and fisheries around Scotland, and heard directly from those working in the industry.

It also comes after the Scottish Affairs Committee visited Norway and Iceland to see how the UK compares to two of the UK's nearest neighbours in the fisheries management.

The committee concluded that the UK was outperforming Iceland and Norway in several areas, including in the regularity of fisheries science and the amount spent on fisheries management.

Jamie Foxx and Hilary Swank have won the top acting awards at the US Golden Globes.

Best drama film went to Babel, while Stephen Frears' The Queen was named best film, musical or comedy.

Frears accepted the prize, saying he was thrilled that the movie - about the death of Princess Diana - had been so well received.

"I hope it has honoured the memory of someone who was very special and whose death was very sad," he said.

The awards are voted for by the 87 members of the Hollywood Foreign Press Association (HFPA), a group of overseas journalists based in California.

Best actor in a drama went to Foxx, who played a hit man in the film Collateral.

He dedicated his award to the city of his birth, Houston, Texas, which has been hit by Hurricane Katrina.

"I wanna say prayers out to Louisiana and Texas," he said. "That's where I'm from. I never thought I'd be standing up here."

Best actress in a drama went to Swank, who played the part of cancer patient Betty Anne Waters in the film Conviction.

"Never ever give up on your dreams, because if you do, you'll regret it for the rest of your life," she said.

Best director went to Martin Scorsese, for The Departed, which also won best film drama.

The Departed also won awards for Leonardo DiCaprio and Jack Nicholson, while Christopher Plummer won best supporting actor for The Painted Veil.

Best television drama went to the HBO series Big Love, and its star, Bill Paxton, won best actor in a television drama.

Liverpool manager Rafael Benitez has said he is happy with the way his team played in their 3-0 win over Portsmouth in the FA Cup fifth round. Benitez said:"For me, it was a professional performance. In the first half we were in control and created chances but in the second half we became a little bit nervous and gave them hope. But overall it was a good performance and to get through is important for the club and the supporters."

The Reds had dominated the first half without scoring, with Fernando Torres wasting the best chance of the opening period when he scooped over the bar from eight yards. But Liverpool went in front nine minutes into the second half when David Ngog scored from close range after Portsmouth goalkeeper David James had fumbled a shot from Torres. Ryan Babel doubled the advantage five minutes later with a close-range shot after good work from Steven Gerrard and Torres.

Benitez said:"We created lots of chances in the first half and the most important thing is to take them in the second half. We were playing against a good team, they have some great individuals and they can cause problems. In the end, the scoreline could have been bigger but sometimes as a manager you have to control the game and not rush things too much."

The Spanish manager was not happy with the performance of the referee, Mike Jones, for failing to award a penalty when Gerrard was brought down in the area by Portsmouth's Kevin Dillon. Benitez said:"It was a clear penalty. The referee said that Dillon got the ball but it was a penalty. If you analyse the situation afterwards maybe the referee is right because Dillon touches the ball but the player is in the process of making the movement and it is a penalty. The referee was not in a good position."

Benitez also confirmed that he will be without the services of midfielder Javier Mascherano for four weeks after the player picked up a hamstring injury in the second half.

Leonardo DiCaprio has finally won his first Oscar, decades after his film debut. The star, who has acted in more than 30 films, picked up the best actor gong for his role as Hugh Glass in The Revenant at the 88th Academy Awards in Los Angeles. It was his sixth nomination for an Academy Award, having previously been shortlisted for his parts in Titanic, Blood Diamond, Catch Me If You Can, The Wolf Of Wall Street and Inception.

Many believed that his luck had changed this year, as he had already won a Golden Globe, a BAFTA and a Screen Actors Guild Award for his lead role in the Alejandro González Iñárritu-directed wilderness drama. His win was widely applauded by his peers, with many stars taking to the stage to shake his hand or offer congrats hugs. "It's been a journey," he said, "I've been so fortunate to work with some of the most talented, visionary people who have made this possible."

He thanked his team, including his manager and lawyer, before turning his attention to climate change - a cause he has been championing for many years. "Climate change is real, it's happening right now," he said. "It's the most urgent threat facing our entire species and we need to work collectively together and stop procrastinating."

DiCaprio said that "we need leadership" to protect the planet, before mentioning France and India's recent efforts to do just that. "Our next generation depends on us," he said, before concluding by thanking his parents "who have always taught me to chase my dreams".

DiCaprio started his career on the TV soap opera Santa Barbara before making his film debut in Critters 3. He has since acted in a number of major films, including This Boy's Life, Romeo + Juliet, Titanic, Inception and The Great Gatsby.

DiCaprio's off-screen contributions have been extensive. He has been a United Nations Messenger of Peace since 2014, working to help communities adapt to climate change, and raise awareness about environmental conservation. He has also funded a number of environmental projects, including the recent $43m purchase of a large chunk of land in Argentina, which will be turned into a wildlife reserve. A passionate supporter of the environment, in 2010 DiCaprio hosted a charity ball for his foundation, which raised $45m to help protect the planet.

Robots have been programmed to be polite, with researchers developing "robotiquette" rules for them to follow.

They have taught machines to wait their turn, allow others to go first at junctions, and even say "thank you" when other robots let them pass.

It has been developed by scientists at the University of Washington in the US.

Their findings were presented at the Conference on Robot Learning in Montreal, Canada.

The researchers created an "etiquette" curriculum, with a series of social norms, that they believed would be useful for robots in shared spaces.

These included not cutting in line, and allowing robots carrying heavy loads to go first when passing through a door.

They then taught their "polite" robots these rules via trial and error, rewarding them for following the rules and not for transgressions.

Lead researcher Dr Emily Lim said the idea was to make robots "more useful and relatable" to people.

"We're all accustomed to following certain social norms, such as saying 'thank you' or waiting at a crosswalk," she said.

"Our robots need to follow similar norms in order to fit into our shared spaces."

The team developed software that allowed the robots to learn the "hidden rules" of human behaviour, through trial and error.

Over time, the robots learned to wait, and let other robots pass first, at junctions, and were rewarded for following the rules.

Dr Lim said the technology could be used in public spaces, including in hospitals and care homes.

She said it could also help robots work more effectively alongside people in factories and other workplaces.

"Our goal is for robots to be able to learn from and co-exist with humans, and following social norms is an important step toward that," she said.

The Old Trafford crowd protested against the Glazer family throughout United's final home game of the season against Brentford on Tuesday.

Supporters also stopped traffic on the M6 motorway and outside the ground before the game, while thousands more voiced their opposition to the Americans in a boisterous atmosphere throughout the 1-1 draw.

The Glazers, who completed a leveraged takeover of United in 2005, have seen the club's debt rise to well over £1bn.

They have also been accused of not investing in the team, with United's last Premier League title coming in 2013.

A United statement released before the Brentford game said the club "heard" the fans' protests "loud and clear" and acknowledged the need for a "stronger and closer relationship" with supporters.

That move appeared to be an attempt to head off a vote of no confidence in the directors by the Manchester United Supporters Trust (MUST), which gave its support to the protests.

But Avram Glazer, who was at the game on Tuesday, has now gone further in a statement released to the Manchester Evening News.

He said: "You expressed your dissatisfaction with the management of the club - and we hear you.

"You voiced your frustration with our ownership - and we hear you.

"You shared your desire for us to build a winning team - and we hear you.

"While there has been progress on and off the pitch, we know we have not lived up to your expectations of us as owners - and for that we apologise.

"Manchester United has a proud history of success on the pitch. Our focus as owners is to return that success.

"We understand you want to see regular investment in the team, and that is what we are committed to doing."

The statement was also posted on the club's official website.

United have not challenged for the Premier League title since their last victory under Sir Alex Ferguson in 2013.

The club finished sixth in the Premier League in 2021-22, with a lack of investment in the squad cited as a major reason for their slide down the table.

Fans protested throughout the season, but their anger intensified in recent weeks as United's hopes of qualifying for next season's Champions League faded.

A student who has been blind since birth can now see colours, following a groundbreaking surgery. The surgery involved a unique "tongue display" which stimulated the brain, enabling the patient to see colours.
The patient, who was born with a form of congenital blindness that affects 1 in every 10,000 people, underwent the experimental surgery in November last year.
The operation, which was led by Dr. Ron Pelias, assistant professor of ophthalmology at Stanford University, stimulated the tongue's nerve fibres, which in turn stimulated the brain's visual cortex, allowing the patient to perceive colours.
"We're trying to work out the neural mechanisms of colour vision by stimulating the brain in this very precise way," said Dr Pelias.
The patient can now see colours, but still does not have any form of visual acuity, meaning they can't see shapes or outlines.
The surgery was carried out on a patient with complete colour blindness and involves a small, 1.5mm square electrode, which is placed on the tongue.
The electrode is linked to a small, wearable computer, which transforms images from a camera into "tongue maps", consisting of eight different regions, each stimulated by a different colour.
When the patient looks at an object, the computer converts the image into a "tongue map", which stimulates the brain in such a way that the patient can perceive colours.
"We're trying to stimulate the brain so that it interprets stimuli as colour, by coaxing neurons in the brain to respond in a way that would normally only occur when a sighted person sees colour," said Dr Pelias.
The device needs to be calibrated against a "tongue colour chart", which the patient uses to tune the colours on the device, ensuring they are seeing the right colours.
So far, the patient has been able to identify colours in experiments, but the team is still working on improving the clarity of the images produced.
"This is a very early stage of the research. We're a long way from understanding how the brain encodes colour and even further from understanding how to restore that ability through electrical stimulation," Dr Pelias said.
"But it's a very exciting proof of concept that brings us a little bit closer to helping patients with congenital colour blindness."
The team hopes to carry out the procedure on other patients in the future and believes the technology could also be used to help people who have lost their sight to retinal degeneration.

Microsoft has launched a new version of its Windows operating system in India, aimed at curbing software piracy.

Windows 10 "Core", as it has been named, is an edition of Windows 10 that contains minimal features. While users will be able to run apps, they will not be able to access Microsoft's Windows Store to download programmes.

The move aims to offer a low-cost alternative to Windows, making it easier for Microsoft to compete with cheap pirated versions of its software, which are widely used in the country.

It also hopes the new version will encourage users of pirated Windows to move towards legal versions, by offering a more affordable option.

"It has always been our endeavour to ensure that customers have the best possible experience on our platform, and as a part of this, we are bringing the Windows 10 'Core' edition to India," said Bhaskar Pramanik, chairman of Microsoft India.

Search wars hit desktop PCs

Google and Microsoft are battling for desktop search supremacy -- but are desktop users ready for search?

That's the question both companies are hoping to answer with new desktop search applications designed to help users find anything stored on their PCs.

Google has introduced Google Desktop Search, a free application that scans the contents of a PC and displays find results in a Google-style page.

The application, which works on Windows machines, indexes the contents of a PC's hard drive, including email archives, and allows users to search them quickly.

Microsoft, which introduced its own desktop search tool, Windows Desktop Search, as a downloadable beta application last year, plans to release the final version of the product, also for Windows PCs, later this year.

Unlike Google's offering, Microsoft's will be integrated with the next version of Windows, code-named "Longhorn," due out sometime in 2006.

Google's move has raised the stakes in the ongoing battle between the two companies for search dominance.

Microsoft is still well ahead of Google in overall search share with more than 62% of searches conducted in the US performed on Microsoft sites, according to latest data from ComScore Networks.

But Google is nipping at its heels. In February, Google sites accounted for 34.6% of US searches, up from 30.5% a year ago, ComScore said.

Now the two companies are battling for search supremacy on the desktop.

Microsoft has had a desktop search tool since 1995, when it introduced Windows 95.

But Google's new tool is seen as a significant upgrade, since it allows users to search information stored in many different applications, including Outlook, Outlook Express, and Netscape Messenger, as well as PDF and Word files.

It also lets users search across multiple PCs -- a boon for businesses.

All of this has Microsoft scrambling to catch up.

"Google has jumped into the desktop search market in a way that is sure to get Microsoft's attention," said Matt Rosoff, an analyst with Directions on Microsoft, a research firm that tracks the software giant.

"It's clear that Google views desktop search as a platform, and Microsoft will have to respond," he added.

The number of jobs created in the US in January was much higher than expected, according to official data.

Figures from the Labor Department showed that the US economy added 678,000 jobs during the month, beating predictions of 400,000.

It said employment continued to trend up in leisure and hospitality, in professional and business services, in manufacturing and in construction.

But the data also showed that the unemployment rate had edged up from 3.9% to 4%, partly because of a surge in people entering the labour market.

Average hourly earnings for all workers also increased, rising to 5.1% compared with a year earlier. But compared with December, they fell by 0.5% to $32.09.

"This was a solid report with a very strong headline number and is likely to be well received on Wall Street," said Richard Flynn, managing director at Charles Schwab.

"The unemployment rate did edge up, but it was for good reasons as more people entered the workforce, and the participation rate rose as well.

"With earnings growth remaining steady and the Fed's inflation target still distant, there is no reason for the central bank to accelerate its tightening cycle."

The jobs data follows on from Wednesday's inflation report, which showed that prices rose by their fastest rate in 40 years in December, increasing by an annualised 7%.

The strong jobs growth also comes in the wake of December's mixed jobs report, which showed a loss of 227,000 jobs in the month. That figure was revised up to a gain of 768,000.

In the report for January, the Labor Department said that job gains had occurred in several industries, including leisure and hospitality, professional and business services, retail trade and manufacturing.

Construction employment continued to trend up, rising by 4%, or 78,000, in January, with job gains occurring in both residential and non-residential construction, the report said.

But it added that employment in local government education declined by 63,000 in January, mainly because of job losses in elementary and secondary schools.

The report also showed that the number of unemployed people rose by 187,000 to 6.1 million in January, while the labour force participation rate increased by 0.2 percentage points to 62.4%.
