It was seemingly inevitable that the internet would transform the way we give and receive presents but the extent of that change is surprising. Seven out of every 10 pounds spent on UK Christmas gifts now originates online, a proportion that has doubled over the past decade, according to the Centre for Retail Research.

This shift has produced a boom in the fortunes of online retailers, yet another example of the upheaval in "the high street" as traditional retailers struggle to keep pace with the move to smartphones, tablets and computers.

The research, which was commissioned by payment services provider Worldpay, found that £19.3bn was spent online on Christmas gifts in the UK last year, a rise of more than £2bn on the year before.

Much of that growth is being driven by the rise of mobile phones as shopping devices. Worldpay chief executive Philip Jansen said: "Over the past few years we have seen a significant increase in the use of mobile phones for online shopping, accounting for 52% of online sales in 2017, compared with 39% in 2015."

The most popular items purchased via mobile phones were clothes and footwear (£7.3bn), followed by games, toys and "hobby" goods (£4.8bn), and books, newspapers and stationery (£4.4bn).

Worldpay predicts that by 2021 the value of online sales will have reached £43bn, accounting for 42% of all retail sales in the UK.

Yet despite the rise of internet shopping, the research found that many consumers still prefer to make their final purchase in a shop. Two-thirds of those who research gifts online still buy them in a store.

"The high street is still very important as a place to touch and feel the product, and importantly, for consumers to engage with the brand," said Mr Jansen. "But the in-store experience needs to be seamless to cater for the 'always-on' consumer who wants a fully integrated shopping experience across all channels."

John Baulch, a director at the Centre for Retail Research, said: "The high street is changing from what it was 10 years ago. It is all about experiences: you can go and have your hair done, you can have a coffee, you can meet your friends.

"The problem is that the multi-purpose nature of the high street is not compatible with the internet, which is very functional. If you are looking for something specific, you are far more likely to go online."

The film's distributors submitted a trailer for Passion, which depicts Monroe's fictionalization of her troubled private life, for inclusion on the BBC's main channels. However, the broadcaster decided that the trailer was politically biased and could be construed as an endorsement of Christianity. 

A BBC source said the broadcaster did not believe the trailer was "objective" because its narration contained the phrase "Jesus Christ". The source added: "It was decided that the trailer was political and, therefore, should not be broadcast. "It's not unusual for political trailers to be submitted for BBC broadcast, and equally it's not unusual for them not to be broadcast. "In this case, the trailer was deemed to be biased and, as such, it was not shown on our networks." The BBC's decision has sparked a debate about whether the corporation has taken an overtly political approach to the trailer.

Martin Freeman, the actor and comedian who is a supporter of the Conservative Party, criticized the decision on Twitter, saying: "Jesus Christ indeed, the BBC won't run the trailer for Passion because they think it's too political. "So essentially any reference to Jesus is political but the many references to Stalin in Wolf Hall are just part of the general historical context. Seems odd. 

Freeman's comments were criticized by some Twitter users, with one person writing: "Not sure you're qualified to comment on this, Martin. You're not an expert on everything, despite your many talents. Let the experts do their job." 

The BBC's decision comes after it was revealed that John Whittingdale, the Culture Secretary, had written to the broadcaster demanding that it improves its coverage of religion. In the letter, Whittingdale said the BBC's output on religion was "too narrow" and "should reflect a faith perspective". The trailer for Passion will still be shown on other channels, such as ITV and Channel 4.

The work of a private research institute that has been linked to far-right activist and YouTuber Lauren Southern has been deemed "highly suspect" by an alliance of scientists. 

The Centre for Countering Digital Hate (CCDH) - which fights against hate speech online - obtained leaked documents showing that Southern, real name Kelly, worked for the Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD), an organisation focused on "the study of contemporary antisemitism". 

According to the CCDH, the ISD's work, like Southern's, is "highly suspect and frequently violates basic research ethics and journalistic standards". They obtained Google Drive and Dropbox links that they say show how the ISD works closely with Southern, who they describe as an "influencer and activist". 

The 25-year-old Canadian has a history of posting anti-Muslim and anti-immigrant content on social media and was deported from the UK last year after she planned to enter the country to film a documentary on sharia law. She was held by authorities for nine hours and subsequently denied entry to the UK. 

The ISD, which has links to the neocon think tank the Henry Jackson Society, was founded by strategic communications consultant Ed Husain. It has received funding from the US State Department, the UK's Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, and the European Commission. It claims to have "worked on projects in over 50 countries". 

In a series of tweets, the CCDH said the leaked files show that the ISD shared work with Southern, who they claim "has promoted conspiracy theories and fabricated news". They also alleged that the ISD covered up its relationship with Southern and failed to disclose its ties to the Henry Jackson Society. 

The CCDH said it has passed the files to the academic community for verification. 

In response to the leak, an ISD spokesperson said the files had been "selectively leaked as part of an orchestrated campaign" and that the organisation "has never worked with or for Lauren Southern in any capacity". 

They added: "We completely refute the outrageous allegations that we have in any way covered up our work, or that it is 'highly suspect'. We are a independent think tank, producing independent research on a range of issues, including online hate, anti-Semitism, and extremism." 

The spokesperson also said the organisation had a "commitment to the highest standards of research integrity and transparency".

According to a leaked recording obtained by The Observer, UKIP’s deputy chairman and prospective parliamentary candidate, David Kurten, suggested that the party could sue defectors who publicly criticised UKIP and defected to Veritas.

In the recording, Kurten is heard saying that UKIP could "potentially" pursue legal action against Simon Bennett, a former UKIP treasurer who publicly criticised the party and joined Veritas.

The recording of Kurten's remarks was made at a meeting of UKIP members in Hertfordshire on September 11. According to the Observer, the meeting was called to discuss the recent defections of high-profile UKIP members to Veritas, a new party founded by former UKIP leader Gerard Batten.

At the meeting, Kurten reportedly suggested that UKIP could sue defectors for breach of contract, claiming that the party's code of conduct requires members to give a month's notice before leaving UKIP.

It's 2023, and we're now well past the tenth anniversary of the introduction of the iPhone by Apple in 2007. That device, more than any other, was the catalyst for the mobile revolution. It seemed to appear out of nowhere, yet simultaneously felt like it had been around forever. The same is true of the way we interact with the web. It now feels like second nature to reach for our phones instead of our laptops when we want to visit a website. Yet, it's easy to forget that the first iPhone was only released ten years ago.

In the previous decade before the iPhone's arrival, web design had already gone through one major revolution. In the 1990s, websites became much more sophisticated and interactive, with the introduction of HTML tables, which allowed web designers to move beyond the constraints of HTML's original layout techniques and create more visually appealing pages. The industry saw an explosion of websites using these new techniques, offering a more enjoyable user experience.

However, these early websites were designed to be viewed on desktop computers, with monitors that were much larger than the screens on mobile phones. As a result, when the iPhone was launched in 2007 and mobile web browsing became possible, these websites looked terrible. Text was illegible, images were distorted, and interactive elements were impossible to use. Clearly, a new approach to web design was needed.

In the next decade after the iPhone was released, web design underwent a radical transformation, with a focus on mobile-friendliness and usability. Designers created websites that were touch-friendly and easy to use on small screens. As mobile phones became more and more popular, websites had to keep up.

Today, mobile traffic accounts for more than half of all internet traffic, and the importance of mobile-friendly design is clear. Websites that are not optimized for mobile devices risk losing traffic and revenue.

Throughout this decade of change, one principle has remained constant in good website design: the need to create a seamless user experience. From the early days of the web to the present day, websites that are easy to use and navigate have always been popular with users. As technology continues to evolve, we can expect to see even more innovative and intuitive website designs in the future.

Sajid Javid has rejected suggestions the Conservative Party is on the verge of splitting after criticism from one of its most high-profile MPs.

Mr Blunt, MP for Reigate, has urged his party to embrace pro-Brexit supporters - including those who voted for Jeremy Hunt in the Tory leadership contest.

But Mr Javid accused him of "backseat driving" and said the Conservative Party was "getting on just fine". 

He added that the party was "more united than ever" and that he had "never seen that". 

In an interview with The Telegraph, Mr Blunt said the party could lose up to 400 seats unless it "opens its eyes" to changes needed to win the next election.

The Conservative Party has held onto power as a minority government since the last election, but many of its MPs represent constituencies that voted to leave the European Union - including Mr Blunt.

Mr Hunt, who finished second to Boris Johnson in the leadership contest, won the backing of many pro-Brexit MPs and members. 

But since the result was announced, some Conservative MPs have expressed concern that the party is not doing enough to embrace figures like Mr Hunt.

Mr Blunt told The Telegraph that the party "needs to open its eyes and realise we're in danger of losing 400 seats".

He added that the party had "got itself into a position where it is ignoring everybody who voted for Jeremy Hunt".

A blind student from Bristol, UK, says he "hears in colour" after receiving a bionic eye. Tom Williams, 25, has only ever seen shadows and shapes – but now, after receiving the implant, he can identify colours in food and on clothes. The retinal implant goes over the top of his eye, with a video camera feeding information to a microchip which then sends signals to electrodes on the retina. It does not restore vision but allows Mr Williams to detect light and shade and determine the presence of motion.

The device was developed by the company Second Sight, and while it has been available in the US for some time, it is yet to be approved for use in the UK. It has been used in more than 300 people. The device was originally designed for people with a condition called retinitis pigmentosa, which affects the cells that detect light in the retina. However, it has also been tried with success in those with total blindness. 

Mr Williams has optic nerve hypoplasia, a condition where the optic nerves are underdeveloped. He hopes to gain even more sensation through training on the device. Currently, he uses a long cane to get around and listens to the sound of his footsteps to judge where he is.

"I knew it was going to be an extremely slow process, but I was willing to give it a go to help the next generation of visually impaired people," he told the BBC. "However, the sensations I experienced were much quicker and stronger than I expected. Being able to see motion and detect shades of grey has been amazing, but the colour is really something else."

Mr Williams is a classically trained musician and he immediately recognised the difference in colour on his piano keys.

"To be able to see the difference between my black and my white keys on the piano, and to see if my shirt is white or grey, is amazing," he said. "It's a whole new world." 

Mr Williams' bionic eye has a small video camera which is held on top of his eye by a magnetic clasp. This camera sends information to a microchip, which then transforms this data into signals that are sent to electrodes on the retina. The electrodes stimulate the retina's remaining cells, allowing the user to see. 

While the device does not provide the same vision as 20/20 eyesight, users can detect light and motion, differentiating between shades of grey and, in some cases, colour.

The actress Nicole Kidman has won a legal battle with a photographer she accused of stalking her, after a six-year fight.

Brian Walski had denied allegations that he pursued the Oscar-winning actress for many years, both at her home in Australia and in the US.

But a jury in Los Angeles has found him liable for invasion of privacy and stalking, awarding Kidman about $250,000 in damages.

"I thank the jury for their hard work and their thoughtful verdict but most of all I thank my family and friends who have stood by me through a terrifying battle," the actress, 54, said in a statement after the verdict.

Walski, 52, denied all allegations against him at trial, insisting he was not obsessed with the actress.

But the jury found that the photographer had indeed followed Kidman repeatedly since 2004, both in Australia and in Los Angeles. They awarded the actress $125,000 in economic and punitive damages, as well as $125,000 in legal fees.

Walski's lawyer Steve Vinderman said he would appeal the decision.

"We're obviously disappointed with the verdict," he said. "Mr Walski is favourable to continue this matter to trial."

Lawyers for the actress had told the court that Walski had shown up at Kidman's holiday home in Australia nine times in 2013 and 2014, and had followed her to Nashville, Tennessee, where he was arrested for trespassing.

Walski admitted to the Nashville incident but denied it had anything to do with the actress. He said he had been in the area for a wedding and showed up at the house because he was lost.

The photographer also denied pursuing Kidman in the US in 2017, despite a police report she filed in which she said she saw him outside her daughters' school several times.

The actress testified that she had been "paranoid" for years, and had slept with a gun for fear that Walski would break into her home.

The release of the documentary "Michael" signals the "end of an era", according to fans of the King of Pop, Michael Jackson.

The documentary, which premiered at the Sundance film festival, is billed as the final film in a trilogy, concluding over a decade's work by director Andrew Eastick.

But fans who have followed the singer's career believe the documentary could signal other things.

"It is the end of an era - the era of Michael Jackson, the greatest musician of a generation," one fan told the BBC.

"He survived the Beatles - yes the Beatles were huge but they hadn't anything like the global appeal of Michael Jackson," they added.

Another fan said: "He elevated pop as an art form and remained relevant even after his death.

"He's the greatest performer of all time and this documentary underlines that. He is the epitome of cool."

But the fan, like many others who have been raving about the documentary on social media, believes the film signals more than just the end of Jackson's era.

"For me it signals the end of an era for documentaries," they said. "It is brilliantly and beautifully made.

"It is respectful, and allows his work to speak for himself. He was an extraordinary talent and this reflects that."

While some fans remain convinced Jackson's career spanned eras, the term "era" usually refers to a period of time within a musician's career when they produce music with a distinct style, and signal a new phase in their work.

The term can also refer to the length of a musician's career, and signal that a person's work is done. 

Eastick's previous documentaries, "This Is It" and "Living With Michael", focused on Jackson's preparations for his final concerts, and the behind-the-scenes drama during the making of his album "Bad". 

"Michael" includes never-before-seen archive footage of the singer, and explores his legacy. 

Eastick said it was important to "show respect" to the singer, "a flawed genius".

"We wanted to show the man, not as anyone wanted to see him, but as he was," he told the BBC.

"He was a genius on many levels, not least of which was his ability to connect with audiences."

By selling dollars, Asian central banks are able to provide their own currencies with support, and temper the rush to sell emerging market currencies.

Beijing-based online gaming company Shanda has bought a minority stake in China's leading online news provider, Sina.

Shanda paid $84m for a 4.6% stake in Sina, according to a statement posted on the website of the Shanghai Stock Exchange.

The investment comes as Shanda, which has suffered from falling profits this year, moves further into the media business. 

Last month, the company launched a joint venture with China's largest broadcaster, CCTV, to run a pay-per-view entertainment website.

The deal may also help Sina, whose news websites have suffered from a government crackdown on the media.

Last month, Sina's chief executive, Charles Chao, told the Wall Street Journal that the company was seeking strategic investors.

"We need to bring in partners to develop our diversified businesses," he said.

Will Shanda's move pay off?

Shanda's profits have been hit this year by the slowing Chinese economy and a crackdown on online gaming by Chinese regulators.

The company posted a 94% fall in third-quarter profit last month, and said it did not expect its performance to improve in the final months of the year.

Last month's launch of the joint venture with CCTV, named China Entertainment Television, could help Shanda turn its fortunes around.

The venture plans to offer online streaming of movies and TV shows for a fee, as well as other entertainment services such as online karaoke.

Founded in 1998, Sina is one of China's best-known internet companies.

Its news websites, including Sina.com, were extremely popular until a government crackdown on media last year.

Regulators forced the company to suspend its popular microblog service Sina Weibo for 15 days last year, and it has continued to face restrictions.

However, the company has moved to diversify its business, and now makes most of its money from its online advertising and electronic payment services.

Sony, meanwhile, is hoping to entice gamers with a new motion-sensing controller and a slate of upcoming titles, including Grand Theft Auto IV and Metal Gear Solid 4.

Steve W. Bell, who suffered from diabetes and other related health problems, died unexpectedly at his home early on Saturday morning, according to a spokesman for the fast-food company.

Mr Bell, who was chief executive of McDonald's UK, was considered a rising star in the company's global hierarchy and seen as a possible successor to Ralph Alvarez, the outgoing chairman and chief executive.

McDonald's confirmed the death, saying Mr Bell was a valued member of the company's management team.

"He was a brilliant marketer and talented executive who played a major role in the development of McDonald's UK," it said in a statement.

"His contribution to the growth of the business over the last 10 years, during which time the company has doubled in size, been hugely significant."

Mr Bell joined McDonald's in the UK in 1996, taking over as chief executive three years later.

He transformed the way the company marketed itself, making greater use of television and other media and increasing its advertising budget from £19m to £58m.

Sales at McDonald's restaurants in the UK rose from £1.86bn to £2.8bn over the same period.

Mr Bell also forged partnerships with Disney, the BBC and the Premier League football clubs to reach a wider audience.

A strong advocate of healthy eating, he launched a range of salads and fruit bags, and improved the nutritional content of Happy Meals.

Last year he oversaw the opening of the chain's 1,000th British restaurant in Sheffield.

Mr Bell, an American by birth, lived in Oak Brook, near Chicago, with his wife and three children.

He is survived by his wife Karen and three children, Lauren, 24, Nicole, 22, and Steven, 20.

I hit a lot of fairways, a lot of greens and holed some nice putts here and there," said McIlroy, who won the FedEx Cup in September 2022. McIlroy won the Abu Dhabi HSBC Championship in 2009, 2010 and 2011. It is the first time he has successfully defended a title on the PGA Tour. Im, who will be defending his Genesis Invitational title in Los Angeles later this month, finished second in Abu Dhabi last year and third in 2020. England's Tommy Fleetwood was in a three-way tie for third place with American Collin Morikawa and Norway's Viktor Hovland.

Italy have plenty of reasons to feel confident as they prepare to face England in their Euro 2020 quarter-final on Saturday.

Not only do they have a fully fit squad to choose from, but the way they swept aside a highly rated Belgian team 2-1 in the last 16 gives them a timely boost.

And as manager Roberto Mancini pointed out on the eve of the game at Wembley, his team have another important weapon in their arsenal: the ability to hurt England from set pieces.

It was, after all, a stunning free-kick from Leonardo Spinazzola that sparked them into life against Belgium, equalising just before half-time to silence a raucous crowd in Rome. 

And with England having a tendency to switch off at set plays – as shown in their nail-biting 2-1 win over Germany in the last 16 – it is certainly a chink in their armoury that Italy plan to exploit.

His header from Marco Verratti’s cross was inches away from giving Italy the lead against Belgium, and he is due a goal at this tournament after working tirelessly in the opening group games.

Immobile, who scored 36 goals in 38 games for Lazio last season, is likely to be Italy’s biggest threat on Saturday.

Ferguson has put his faith in youth by naming six teenagers in his 25-man squad for the Europa League clash with AZ Alkmaar on Thursday. "For me, it is a positive because players in this moment have to make sure they are ready to play, because if not, they will be left behind. "That is what I expect and if players bang the door down, they will get opportunities." 

Among the six teenagers in the squad is 16-year-old Ben Knight, who made his debut off the bench in Sunday's 2-2 draw with Kilmarnock. Brent Council has told a Wembley firm it must not make a profit from a planned homeless shelter next to Stonebridge Park Station. The authority has been under increasing pressure to allow a site to be used for a temporary overnight shelter after a string of high-profile cases of rough sleeping in the borough. 

It identified an unused building near Stonebridge Park Station as a potential site but has now received a legal letter warning that a planning condition preventing profit cannot be enforced. The condition was included in plans approved in 2015 for the site, which is owned by a firm called Project Urban. 

In summer, the council served the owners with a notice ordering them to open the doors to homeless people, arguing that a lack of suitable hostel beds in the borough was a special circumstance that overrode the condition. The letter, sent by Project Urban's lawyers last week, argues that the planning condition is valid and should be enforced. 

"There is no credible evidence... that the application would result in an unacceptable windfall profit," it says. "There is no justification for the council's attempt to override the condition... and its attempt to do so is an unlawful interference with Project Urban's rights." 

The letter, sent on October 7, adds that the council has not provided any evidence to support its case and that its notice is "an unlawful decision and should be withdrawn". 

A Brent Council spokesperson said: "The council stands by its decision and remains confident that its approach is both legally and morally right. "We have a duty to provide accommodation and support to all rough sleepers in the borough and have been working tirelessly with our partners to bring this to fruition. "We have been talking with the site owners for several months about using the premises as a night shelter and remain open to discussions."

China has kept a tight rein on credit in the last few months, with total social financing falling significantly compared to last year. Experts say the government is cautious about stoking inflation, and does not want to add to problems with the country's property sector. But economists say local governments and businesses are starved of cash, and China's economy is paying the price. The decline in social financing has been consistent despite four interest rate cuts since last year. In September, total social financing was down 22% from a year earlier, at 1.35 trillion yuan ($203 billion). Meanwhile, M2, a broad measure of money supply, is growing at its slowest pace in nearly three decades. 

China's economy is already suffering its slowest growth rate in nearly half a century. In the third quarter, GDP increased by 3.9% year-on-year, down from 7.9% in the same period the previous year. And the latest data suggests the economy is slowing further, with retail sales growing 2.5% in September from a year earlier, down from 8.5% in March. Meanwhile, industrial output grew by just 3.1% year on-year in September, down from 6.3% in March.

Most of the loans issued in September went to solvent firms, including property developers, according to central bank data. But economists say these companies are not keen on borrowing, as they already have cash tied up in projects that are not selling well. Many local governments are also under pressure after lavish spending on infrastructure projects in past years. 

Experts say the central bank is being very cautious about pumping more money into the economy, for fear of stoking inflation. Rising prices are a political sensitive issue for the government, as households have seen their cost of living rise rapidly in the last few months. Food prices have climbed as a result of the Russia-Ukraine war, and consumers are also feeling the pinch from rising energy and transport costs.

The property sector has been a major driver of China's economic growth in recent years, but the government has introduced a string of measures to curb speculation and slow the sector's growth. Real estate loans made up just 6.9% of all loans issued in September, down from 12.3% last year, according to the central bank. 

The government has also been trying to reduce its reliance on real estate, and promote other sectors, including consumption and services. But experts say these sectors are not yet strong enough to drive the economy forward.

One Labour MP, who wished to remain anonymous, said there was a "real sense of worry" within the party. They argued the shift would "play into the hands of people who want to portray Labour as anti-Semitic".

This policy shift has led to accusations from Labour's political rivals that the party is, effectively, copying the Conservatives.

One former minister told the BBC that the Labour Party was "taking the Tories' playbook". They argued that Labour was "copying the Conservative Party – even using language that sounds like Boris Johnson".

"For so long, the Labour Party said very little about the Middle East – and that's not good enough," he said. "We're starting the conversation again – and we're putting Labour values at the heart of it."

The question now is whether this new approach will help the party win back voters – and whether it might also lead to further accusations of antisemitism.

Britain's pollsters are facing their first serious test of the 2023 general election campaign, with one firm seeing a dramatic crash in its accuracy scores and another threatened with legal action over its methodology.

Polling has helped transform election campaigns over the past 50 years, giving journalists and politicians a guide to how the public are likely to vote and offering predictions on which parties will win seats.

But after a decent start to the election cycle, the polls have begun to show signs of instability, with several surveys recording a dramatic narrowing in the Labour lead over the past month.

The data has prompted speculation about whether the industry's biggest players - YouGov, Savanta ComRes, Ipsos MORI and Kantar - are accurately reflecting the state of the electoral race.

One firm - Panelbase - has already seen its accuracy ratings crash amid concerns over its methodology.

And another - Lord Ashcroft Polls - has faced criticism over its approach to weighting its data, with Labour threatening to refer it to the statistics regulator.

In recent months, Pollbase has seen its average statistical accuracy rating - as calculated by the pollster's rivals - plunge from 73% to 54%, according to the Pollster website.

Film-maker Morgan Matthews says it is "difficult" to get investors interested in campaigns for social good.
His documentary about school bullying, Defiance, is one of five short films nominated for best live action short at this year's Oscars.
But he said it was "very difficult" to get backing for the project as it "didn't fit the model" of what investors usually backed.
Matthews, 34, said he had to "beg, borrow and almost steal" to get the film made.
His film tells the story of a young victim of bullying who brings her tormentor to justice.
It features an appearance from Game of Thrones star Peter Dinklage, who also voices the audiobook of Matthews' original novel on which the film is based.
Matthews, who previously directed the well-received documentary Life in a Day, said it was hard to "get the balance" right between "making a film that is entertaining and makes you think".

It was spring 1995, and a team of us at the BBC were charged with creating the corporation's first web page. My colleague Richard Taylor and I were put in charge, and we set up a skunkworks lab to investigate this new phenomenon.

We were lucky. Despite the vast reach of the BBC, the organisation had, in those days, a relatively small number of people involved in new media. So our team of about 12 was able to control the agenda. We were joined by Martin Freethy, a brilliant young programmer who had been recruited from Oracle, and Anthony Howard, a designer who instantly understood what we were trying to do.

We were not trying to do anything very grand. All we wanted to do was make sure the BBC had a web presence. But we were fortunate in having an enlightened manager, Alan Chesters, who understood this new medium and gave us pretty much free rein.  

We were also lucky that the web was so new that nobody really understood it fully, which meant we could pretty much make it up as we went along.

And so we did. We took all the things we liked about the emerging web landscape – the things that seemed to make the most sense – and built a site that had most of the elements you would recognise in the BBC's web presence today: a top menu, a sidebar of links to internal pages, and a big promotion on the homepage to a major news story. We added some other things that were novel at the time, such as a site-wide search engine and a daily updated list of "what's new".

And that was about it. We weren't trying to "design" the site, because the idea of "user experience design" hadn't been thought of yet. Nor were we trying to produce a "brand" experience, because again, that idea was still far in the future. In fact, the word "brand" wasn't even used much in the BBC.

But despite this lack of design thinking, and working with incredibly primitive tools, it seemed to us that the site we were producing had a certain something. In fact, looking back at it now, it seems pretty clean and crisp, and not that far off what we produce today.

A student who has been blind since birth can now see colours, following a groundbreaking surgery. The surgery involved a unique "tongue display" which stimulated the brain, enabling the patient to see colours.
The patient, who was born with a form of congenital blindness that affects 1 in every 10,000 people, underwent the experimental surgery in November last year.
The operation, which was led by Dr. Ron Pelias, assistant professor of ophthalmology at Stanford University, stimulated the tongue's nerve fibres, which in turn stimulated the brain's visual cortex, allowing the patient to perceive colours.
"We're trying to work out the neural mechanisms of colour vision by stimulating the brain in this very precise way," said Dr Pelias.
The patient can now see colours, but still does not have any form of visual acuity, meaning they can't see shapes or outlines.
The surgery was carried out on a patient with complete colour blindness and involves a small, 1.5mm square electrode, which is placed on the tongue.
The electrode is linked to a small, wearable computer, which transforms images from a camera into "tongue maps", consisting of eight different regions, each stimulated by a different colour.
When the patient looks at an object, the computer converts the image into a "tongue map", which stimulates the brain in such a way that the patient can perceive colours.
"We're trying to stimulate the brain so that it interprets stimuli as colour, by coaxing neurons in the brain to respond in a way that would normally only occur when a sighted person sees colour," said Dr Pelias.
The device needs to be calibrated against a "tongue colour chart", which the patient uses to tune the colours on the device, ensuring they are seeing the right colours.
So far, the patient has been able to identify colours in experiments, but the team is still working on improving the clarity of the images produced.
"This is a very early stage of the research. We're a long way from understanding how the brain encodes colour and even further from understanding how to restore that ability through electrical stimulation," Dr Pelias said.
"But it's a very exciting proof of concept that brings us a little bit closer to helping patients with congenital colour blindness."
The team hopes to carry out the procedure on other patients in the future and believes the technology could also be used to help people who have lost their sight to retinal degeneration.

Film-maker Nora Fingscheidt says it took three years to persuade the German actor to take the lead in her debut feature. But it was worth the wait. Michael is a powerful, gripping film, and Kross gives one of the year's best performances.

It's a film with a tricky balance. On one level it is a tense, finely crafted thriller, on another a heartbreaking study of a disturbed young man's descent into violence. But it's also a story about responsibility, about a society that turns a blind eye to bullying and then is surprised when the consequences are tragic.

The title character, Michael, is a sensitive, soulful boy who becomes the target of bullies. He withdraws into himself, and his classmates sense a vulnerability that only makes their harassment more vicious. They post humiliating videos of Michael on the internet, and even his single mother, whose own vulnerability makes her over-reliant on the sympathy of strangers, seems unable to help.

Isolated and angry, Michael starts to see a counsellor, but even here he cannot escape his classmates' mocking online comments. His emotions simmering, the stage is set for a showdown that neither he nor those around him will escape unscathed.

Fingscheidt, who also wrote the script, deftly handles the material, playing with time and perspective to build the tension, but never resorting to cheap tricks or manipulative devices.

She shows rather than tells, inviting the audience to interpret the events, to fill in the blanks, to understand the character's pain. At the centre of it all is a remarkable performance from Kross, his fragility counter-balanced by a simmering rage. It is a performance that asks us to consider not just the consequences of bullying, but also the complexities of the bully himself.

If there is a flaw in the film it is that it sometimes feels as if we are being invited to feel too much sympathy for Michael. He is a complex, troubled character but, in the end, it is hard not to feel that he gets away with murder. 

Still, this is an impressive, accomplished debut. Fingscheidt shows a confidence and maturity behind the camera, a willingness to trust the audience to keep up, to think for themselves. There is an assurance to the filmmaking that you don't often see in a first-time director.

Asian banks have helped the dollar recover from its worst sell-off in weeks as worries about the US economic outlook pushed investors towards the relative safety of the world's primary reserve currency.

The dollar had skidded to an almost three-year low against a basket of currencies following the Federal Reserve's dovish shift last week.

But it has since bounced back more than 1.2% ahead of the Fed's policy meeting on Tuesday, where policymakers are expected to signal that they will raise interest rates in September.

"The dollar's recovery this week has been more pronounced in Asia, where the banks seem to have played a key role," said Mazen Issa, senior foreign exchange strategist at TD Securities.

"This could be attributed to month-end or quarter-end rebalancing flows, but the magnitude of the move suggests spot dollar-selling from regional banks," he added.

The dollar's rebound began in Asia on Tuesday last week, when the Korean won fell more than 1% and the Singapore dollar hit a one-year low.

The won recovered from its lows after the country's central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market, while the dollar also rose against the Singapore dollar.

Asian currencies have been among the best performers so far this year thanks to the region's economic recovery from the Covid pandemic and attractive yields.

But the dollar's rebound this week has swept across the board, with the exception of the New Zealand dollar, as markets bet that the Fed will hike rates twice before the end of the year.

On Monday, the dollar hit a one-month high against the euro, with the single currency also hit by a dovish stance taken by the European Central Bank.

"We expect the dollar recovery to extend in the near term," said Carol Kong, a currency strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA).

"The Fed is expected to reiterate its commitment to raising rates this year and slowing the pace of balance sheet runoff, which should help support the dollar," she added.

Led Zeppelin took the next three places with IV, Whole Lotta Love and Led Zeppelin II.

Paranoid was the Birmingham band's second album and featured the hit singles Iron Man and Paranoid.

It was also the first appearance of the classic Sabbath lineup of Iommi, Ozzy Osbourne, Bill Ward and Geezer Butler.

Following its release in September 1970, the album went on to reach number one in the UK and sell more than four million copies worldwide.

Nuclear dumpsite plan attacked

 Critics say scheme to store nuclear waste in Utah desert is unsafe.

Protesters have rallied against plans to develop a nuclear waste dump in Utah's remote west desert, with demonstrations in the state's largest city and at the Utah State Capitol.

About 300 people gathered in Salt Lake City on Saturday to hear speakers oppose the plan that would bring up to 44 tons of nuclear waste daily to the state.

A larger protest was held in the tiny town of Milford, near the Nevada border, where a rail line could be used to ship the waste.

The plan is to store up to 77,000 tons of nuclear waste on a 1,600-acre (647-hectare) site at Crescent Junction, Utah.

It is a remote area, about 150 miles (240km) south of Salt Lake City and 40 miles (65km) from the Nevada border.

The site is near the Great Salt Lake and on the edge of the Wasatch Plateau. It is about 140 metres (459 feet) above sea level.

The waste would be transported by train. Officials say it would be secured in stainless steel tubes and placed in specialised containers.

Once the waste arrives, it would be stored above ground in concrete and steel containers for up to 40 years.

Once hailed as the most popular star in the world, Johnny Depp seems to have lost his mojo. His once-upon-a-time box office allure, so powerful that it prompted one fan to tattoo the actor's face on his calf, has proven to be temporary. Depp's once-promising career as an A-list leading man has faltered. His last four films have flopped. 

When Depp joined the ranks of Hollywood's top-earning actors, pocketing $75m for the fourth instalment of the Pirates of the Caribbean franchise in 2010, it seemed he had reached the pinnacle of his career. But revenues declined with each subsequent sequel and Disney finally threw him overboard in 2018. 

The franchise, which raked in $4.5bn at the box office, was Depp's ticket to eternal fame. Instead, his career went into freefall. His vanity project, City of Lies, sank without a trace in 2017. The much-delayed Sherlock Gnomes, in which he voiced the title character, barely scraped in at the box office in 2011. 

Depp's next outing was as the infamous mobster Al Capone in the biographical crime film Fonzo. Except, instead of making a beeline for cinemas, the film went straight to video on demand. The same fate befell Depp's latest project, Minamata, which premiered at the Berlin Film Festival in February 2021, more than a year after being shot. 

Depp's private life may be to blame for his professional demise. Legal woes have mounted. He is suing his ex-wife, Amber Heard, for defamation over a Washington Post op-ed she wrote about surviving domestic abuse. She countersued. 

High-profile supporters, including his ex-girlfriend Vanessa Paradis, and longtime collaborator Tim Burton, have rallied around him. But others have been less willing to back the actor. Depp has been dropped from Warner Bros' Fantastic Beasts franchise and replaced by Madds Mikkelsen. 

The star, who was estimated to be worth $450m in 2016, has seen his wealth squandered. As he prepares to face Heard in court in April, things are only getting worse for Johnny Depp.

Downloads have entered the US singles chart for the first time ever, in a groundbreaking move for the music industry. The change, which was announced by Billboard, the company that compiles the chart, is the result of a dramatic shift in how people listen to music and reflects the growing dominance of streaming services such as Spotify and Apple Music.

Until now, the US Hot 100, the most influential music chart in the country, has been based on sales and radio play. But from now on, streaming will account for 50% of the chart, with sales and radio play making up the other 50%.

The move is significant because it means that songs will now be able to reach a far wider audience than ever before. Whereas before a song had to be purchased or played on the radio to chart, now all it takes is for enough people to stream it. This means that artists who might not have been able to get radio play or sell enough copies of their songs to chart can now find themselves in the upper echelons of the chart simply by gaining a strong streaming presence.

It also means that the chart will now be more reflective of the way that people listen to music today. More and more people are turning to streaming services as their primary means of music consumption, and this move by Billboard reflects that shift.

Some industry experts, however, have voiced concerns about the impact of streaming on the music industry. They argue that it is already difficult for new artists to achieve success in a market dominated by a few major labels, and that the new chart could make it even harder for them to break through.

Nevertheless, the move is likely to be welcomed by many artists and industry figures, who see it as a way of reflecting the changing landscape of the music industry and giving a platform to a wider range of artists. It remains to be seen whether the new chart will lead to any major changes in the type of music that is successful in the US, but it certainly marks a significant moment in the history of the music industry.

A controversial film about the life of Vincent Van Gogh has been withdrawn from a festival showcasing the works of the tortured Dutch painter.

'Vincent Van Gogh: A New Way of Seeing' was set to screen at the Van Gogh Festival in the Netherlands next month [July].

The festival's programme director, Koen Pijnenburg, said he hoped a solution could still be found to show the film, adding it was "a shame for the many festival visitors who bought a ticket".

He told AFP news agency the decision to pull the film was "not censorship" but rather a "decision of the board of the festival".

Controversy has raged over the biopic, directed by Russian Dmitry Kleiman, which uses actors in blackface to depict the Dutch painter and his contemporaries.

Kleiman, who is of Russian descent, told AFP news agency the film was not racist as it was "not about black people".

"It's about sick people who are in a mental hospital," he said.

The film depicts the painter's famous ear slicing incident, which he infamously achieved with a razor blade in 1888, giving rise to the popular myth that he used a knife.

Kleiman said the scene was recreated with the permission of the artist's family, and that it was important "to show how crazy he was and that he was hurting himself".

The director added that he himself had "a Afro-European background" and that he had put himself in the film.

On Wednesday, Dutch politician Henk Krol posted a clip from the film on Twitter, saying "how disgusting can this be?".

Krol, an MP with the centrist D66 party, added that the use of blackface was "unacceptable", and called on the Dutch culture ministry to withdraw its funding for the film.

The culture ministry said in a statement on Thursday that it had launched an investigation into the matter, and that "the images leave an unpleasant taste".

Kleiman hit back at the criticism on Thursday, saying: "I made a film about Van Gogh with actors wearing masks.

"It's not about black people, Africans or whatever. This is not racism. The one who is really racist here is you," he told Dutch news agency ANP.

This year, four films have made more than $100m, led by James Cameron's Avatar: The Way of Water.

But he also attributed the boost to a greater range of films, with the top 10 box office hits this year ranging from Marvel's blockbuster to the low-budget horror film M3gan.

"We are in this world where the movie theatre is becoming more and more a place for event movies," said Mr Dergarabedian.

"But alongside that, there is also a tremendous counter-programming opportunity. "

Box office in the US this year has been buoyed by a relatively small number of huge hits.

The top 10 films of the year have taken $5.3bn, which is $1.5bn more than the total taken by the top 10 films in 2021. 

But overall, the number of films that have made at least $100m in the US this year has fallen short of pre-pandemic levels.

Sir Anthony Corbett, the former controller of BBC Radio 2, has attacked the dumbing-down of television, arguing that it is misogynistic and favours the most stupid and coarse members of society.

Giving a lecture at Cambridge University, Sir Anthony, who was responsible for radio programmes such as Desert Island Discs and The Archers, spoke of his fears for the future of serious television.

He said television had taken a direction "completely contrary to the idea of an intelligent democracy".

The 83-year-old argued that there were some exceptions, such as Channel 4's coverage of the Iraq war, but that these were "becoming isolated islands in a sea of triviality".

"I worry about the future of serious television. I worry that it could disappear altogether," he said.

Sir Anthony criticised the trend towards reality shows and panel games, which he said allowed participants to behave badly towards each other, and the increasing use of sexualised female presenters in order to attract viewers.

"Is there any other explanation for the number of female presenters in mini-skirts presenting programmes about decorating your home or trying on clothes?" he asked.

"These are not role models for young women, nor for young men," he said. "They merely provide an excuse for more sexism and more exploitation."

The broadcaster argued that serious issues were being marginalised, saying that the BBC's flagship current affairs programme, Newsnight, had been pushed from its 10pm slot to midnight in Scotland.

And he claimed that an earlier generation of journalists would be "appalled" at the way news was presented now, with the emphasis on the visual rather than the story.

"In the old days, you had reporters who could write, and could describe what was going on. Now, the stress is on visual impact," he said.

"The priority is to get pictures, and the pictures are often shown repeatedly... with a voice-over which may have nothing to do with the pictures.

"I think the journalists of my generation would be appalled at the priorities, and the techniques, of many television journalists today."

Sir Anthony said he did not believe that television had been entirely taken over by "the stupid, the coarse and the venal".

But he added that it was difficult to attract large audiences for serious programmes, and that there was a danger that "the serious will disappear, and be replaced by the trivial".

The veteran Nigerian author, Buchi Emecheta, has died at 74.

Her debut novel, Concubine, was published in 1966, and she went on to become one of the world's best-known female writers, with more than 20 novels and several short stories and essays.

She died in London on Monday, her family said, without giving details.

"Buchi was a great storyteller and her books will continue to be read and loved by readers all over the world," they said in a statement released by the United Kingdom's Guardian newspaper.

The novelist had been suffering from breast cancer.

Her most famous books include The Joys of Motherhood, published in 1979, and Double Yoke, published in 1973. The latter was adapted for a film in 1982.

She was appointed officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in 2006 for services to literature.

Her novels, mostly set in Nigeria and featuring strong female characters, typically tackled issues such as polygamy and the role of women in society.

She once said of her writing: "If my books can help somebody, if they can make somebody understand somebody else's life better, then I have achieved something."

Born in Lagos in 1944, Emecheta moved to the UK with her husband in 1962. It was there that she began to write, following the breakdown of her marriage.

After the publication of her first novel, she would go on to publish at least a book a year.

One of her most recent novels, The New Tribe, was published in 2004. It told the story of a group of women who form a community in Nigeria, and their struggles with the traditions of marriage and family.

In a 2004 interview with the Guardian, Emecheta said she did not believe she had ever been properly recognised for her work.

"I don't think my books have been taken as seriously as they should be," she said. "Perhaps it's because I'm a woman. Perhaps it's because I'm black. I don't know."

The novelist Arthur Hailey could hardly have hoped for a more lavish tribute than the five-part television adaptation of his 1977 bestseller, Airport. It was the most expensive movie made up to that time, starred an array of major movie stars including Burt Lancaster, Dean Martin, George Kennedy and Helen Hayes, and was directed by the veteran master of suspense, George Seaton. The film was a huge hit, and its success helped make Hailey one of the bestselling authors of the late 20th century. By the early 1990s, his novels had sold more than 170 million copies worldwide, and had been translated into 40 languages. Hailey died in 2004, aged 84, but his work has not been forgotten. In the words of the writer Peter James, himself no slouch when it comes to popular crime fiction: "Arthur Hailey is the father of us all."

Hailey was born in Luton in 1920, the son of a wholesale jeweller. When the depression hit, the family fortunes changed dramatically, and Arthur found himself expelled from grammar school and sent to live with his aunt in Toronto. He mastered touch-typing and landed a job as a court reporter, and later as a journalist on the Toronto Star. His first novel, Dangerous Weapons, a suspense thriller about a nuclear missile hijacking, was published in 1959, when he was 40. But it was the novel Airport, published 14 years later, that really catapulted him to success.

According to the writer Robert Barnard, the secret of Hailey's success was his ability to make a thrilling story out of the banal. In Airport, he took the everyday scenario of an airport and made it the setting for an edge-of-your-seat drama that combined the threat of terrorist violence with more personal stories of romance and betrayal. The book was adapted for the screen by Hailey himself, in collaboration with the screenwriter Stirling Silliphant, and there was little scope for improvisation when it came to the script. The huge cast included Burt Lancaster as the managing director of Chicago's O'Hare airport, and Dean Martin as the pilot of the doomed flight. George Kennedy played the tough, no-nonsense airport chief, who managed to convey a great deal of information about aircraft procedures while issuing forth a steady stream of four-letter words. And Helen Hayes, fresh from her success in the stage and screen versions of Hello, Dolly!, played the grieving mother of a murdered girl, whose son is taken in by a religious sect.

For more than a decade, the BBC's Marc Settle has been worrying about the security of the many Wi-Fi networks he's been forced to connect to.

They're not just in coffee shops, but also in hotels, conference centres, and on trains.

"Some are completely wide open, and some have a flaky password that you can quickly glean from the guy at the front desk when you check in," he says.

So, what can be done to improve the situation?

"You basically have two choices," says Mr Settle.

"You can either stuff the network in a box, by using a VPN [virtual private network] app, or you can operate your own router as a firewall.

"The stuff-it-in-a-box solution is the easiest thing to do, but it's also pretty unsatisfactory," he says.

Once you're connected to the VPN, you have to be careful which websites you access, because your IP address is now hidden and you're effectively operating in secret online.

"VPNs are a little bit like the old days of Tor, when you had to carefully choose your browser to access the internet safely," says Mr Settle.

"It's better than nothing, but it's not a great solution."

Operating your own router as a firewall is technically challenging, he says, and you also need an internet connection that's stable enough to support it - which can be a problem on trains, for example.

So what can be done about the poor state of Wi-Fi security in public places and hotels?

The industry is slowly waking up to the problem, says Mr Settle, but change is slow.

"In the meantime, I'd like to see people thinking more carefully about security when they set these things up," he says.

"If you're running a network, please don't set the password on the front desk. And if you really must do that, make it a long password using all sorts of weird characters, not just 'hotelwireless'.

"And turn off guest access to the network unless it really needs to be on."

Career politician Robert Kilroy-Silk has quit the UK Independence Party, saying it has been "infected" by racism.

The former Labour MP said he had been subjected to "offensive" personal abuse since joining UKIP, but the main reason for his departure was the "toxic" atmosphere in the party.

In a letter to party leader Nigel Farage, he said he could not "in good conscience" stay in UKIP.

Mr Kilroy-Silk said the party had been "infected by racism".

The 69-year-old - who joined UKIP in April - said: "It has become clear to me that In UKIP, immigration and related issues have become a proxy for anti-Muslim feeling.

"This is toxic for our party, toxic for our country and toxic for our democracy. "

He said that when he joined UKIP, he had believed it could be a party "that seeks to reclaim the patriotic vote in this country from the extremists of left and right".

But he added: "It has become clear to me that UKIP has been infected by racism, with sometimes indistinguishable distinctions between far-right parties."

Mr Kilroy-Silk, who served as a Labour MP for Ormskirk between 1992 and 2004, said he had been subjected to "offensive" personal abuse since joining UKIP, which had been "monstrously unfair".

But he said this was not the main reason for his departure, which he described as "a matter of conscience".

In his letter to Mr Farage, he wrote: "I have struggled with these issues for many months, hoping that the leadership would succeed in changing the toxic atmosphere in UKIP.

"This has not happened. "

He said it was with "great sadness" that he was resigning from UKIP, and added: "I wish you and the party well."

In a statement, Mr Farage said he was "very sorry" to see Mr Kilroy-Silk go.

"He is a patrician figure but we have very different visions for the party," said the UKIP leader.

"We have said we want a non-racist, non-sectarian party and I am glad that Kilroy-Silk has made it clear that he thinks we have succeeded in that."

The BBC's flagship technology show, Click, recently ran a story about the MP3. They rightly pointed out that "whatever happened to the MP3?" The answer is simple: almost everything. Today, MP3 technology is everywhere. It's in your phone, your car, your home, your fridge, your watch, and your fitness tracker. There are billions of MP3-playing devices around the globe. Chances are, you're listening to an MP3 file as you read these words.

The MP3 story is an interesting one and worth retelling. The technology that delivers music to your phone or PC has a rich history and a bright future.

In the early 1980s, the Fraunhofer Institute in Germany developed a way to compress audio files. The idea was to reduce the size of audio files to enable faster transmission over the internet while retaining acceptable quality. At the time, there were many competing audio formats, but the MP3 stood out. It was developed by MPEG, the same group that gave us the MPEG video standard.

The first MP3 player was unveiled in 1997. It was a portable music player that could hold enough music to rival the Sony Walkman. The Apple iPod launched in 2001 and quickly became the world's most popular MP3 player.

Since then, MP3 has become the de facto standard for digital audio. It's used in every device that plays digital music, from your phone to your car. There are billions of MP3 files stored on devices and computers worldwide.

But the MP3 is more than just a file format. It's a technology that has changed the way we listen to music. It has made it possible for us to carry our music collections with us wherever we go. It has made it possible for us to share our music with friends and family. It has made it possible for us to discover new music.

The MP3 is here to stay. Thanks to ever-improving audio technology, the MP3 continues to evolve. We can expect to see higher-quality MP3 files and more features that enable us to do more with our music. That's why the BBC was right to ask, "whatever happened to the MP3?"
